Sensitivity & DSA — How they connect, what DSA really means

From your Understanding Noise Figure PDF + your lab procedure · What sensitivity is physically · How DSA is derived from sensitivity · Why modulation matters · Your exact numbers

DSA1 Receiver sensitivity — what it means physically, BLER threshold, lab measurement Intermediate click to expand▾
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
Sensitivity = kTB + 10·log(BW) + NF + SNR_req. This card explains what sensitivity means physically. For the full derivation including per-band DSA calculation, see DSA card.
→ For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

What sensitivity physically means

Sensitivity is the minimum signal power at the RU antenna port at which the receiver can still decode data at 5% BLER (3GPP threshold). It is not fixed — it depends on bandwidth, modulation, and band. The sensitivity formula is not an approximation — it is an exact derivation from thermal physics and information theory.

Sensitivity vs RSSI — the critical difference:
Sensitivity is a threshold — the floor below which decoding fails. RSSI is a measurement — the actual received power at any instant. During a sensitivity test you set EXM to exactly the sensitivity threshold and verify the RU can decode. In normal operation RSSI is whatever arrives — could be −70 dBm (UE nearby) or −105 dBm (UE at cell edge). Sensitivity defines where the floor is. RSSI tells you where you currently are relative to that floor.
Why bandwidth degrades sensitivity — the bucket analogy:
A wider channel (wider bandwidth) collects more thermal noise — like a wider bucket catches more rain. The signal power stays fixed but noise increases, so SNR worsens and you need a stronger signal to decode. 5 MHz sensitivity is 3 dB better than 10 MHz. 20 MHz is 3 dB worse than 10 MHz. This is why the DSA table has separate rows for each BW — same band, different thresholds.
BLER 5% — why this specific threshold:
3GPP defines sensitivity as the point where Block Error Rate = 5%. Below this, too many blocks fail and the system cannot sustain a call. At 5% BLER the link is just barely functional — this is the edge of coverage. The test is binary: inject at threshold power, count block errors, pass if BLER ≤ 5%. This is measured via the PRACH detection rate in your RCT — PRACH preamble either detected or not.
DSA2 Modulation vs sensitivity — FRC, SNR_required, why QPSK gives best sensitivity Intermediate click to expand▾
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
SNR_required is the last term in the sensitivity formula. This card explains what drives it: modulation order and coding rate. QPSK 1/3 gives the best (lowest) sensitivity — this is why FRC A1 is the standard sensitivity test.
→ For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

What is FRC and why it determines sensitivity

FRC (Fixed Reference Channel) is a 3GPP-defined test waveform with fixed modulation, coding rate, and resource allocation. Different FRCs test different capabilities. FRC A1 (QPSK 1/3) tests sensitivity because it gives the most robust link — maximum coverage, minimum signal requirement. The sensitivity number you compare against in your DSA table is always FRC A1.

Why QPSK 1/3 gives the best (lowest dBm) sensitivity:
QPSK has only 4 constellation points — they are spread far apart in the IQ plane. Even with heavy noise, the receiver can correctly decide which of the 4 quadrants the received symbol falls in. The 1/3 coding rate adds heavy redundancy — for every bit of data, 2 extra error-correction bits are sent. Together these give an effective SNR requirement of −1 dB, meaning the signal can be 1 dB below the thermal noise floor and still be decoded. This is why QPSK 1/3 gives the best sensitivity and is the standard for coverage-limited testing.
DSA3 DSA — complete picture: kTB → sensitivity → per-band offset → rev paths → before/after → MRC combining Advanced click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST DSA in one sentence: Because each frequency band (B1, B3, B8, B28, B41) has slightly different hardware quality, they each have a slightly different "hearing ability" (sensitivity). DSA is the lookup table that tells the test instrument exactly how loud to play the test signal for each band — so every band gets a fair test at its own correct threshold, not someone else's.

DSA — the complete story in one card

DSA stands for Dynamic Sensitivity Adjustment. It solves the problem of testing multiple bands with one test framework: each band has a different sensitivity because each band's hardware (LNA, duplexer, filter) has different noise figures. Rather than hardcoding different thresholds manually, DSA calculates a per-band offset from the sensitivity formula and instructs EXM to inject exactly the right power for each band automatically.

Step 1 — kTB: the physics floor
kTB = Boltzmann constant × Temperature × Bandwidth. At room temperature (290 K), in a 1 Hz bandwidth: kTB = 1.38×10⁻²³ × 290 × 1 = 4×10⁻²¹ W = −174 dBm/Hz. This is the absolute minimum noise any receiver can have — it cannot be beaten. For your 10 MHz channel: add 10·log(10,000,000) = +70 dB → noise floor = −104 dBm. For 5 MHz: +67 dB → −107 dBm. For 20 MHz: +73 dB → −101 dBm. Every 2× increase in bandwidth raises the noise floor by 3 dB.
Step 2 — System NF: what your hardware adds
Noise Figure is how many dB of extra noise your RX chain adds on top of kTB. Your chain (B1): cable 2.5 dB + duplexer 0.5 dB + pre-BPF 0.3 dB + LNA 2.0 dB + post-LNA components ≈0 dB = 5.75 dB system NF. The Friis formula shows that LNA dominates because everything after it gets divided by LNA's linear gain (×100). Everything before the LNA (cable, duplexer, BPF) adds its full loss as NF — this is why cable length matters enormously for sensitivity.

Per-band NF: B1=2.44 dB · B3=2.40 dB · B8=3.15 dB · B28=2.73 dB · B41=2.00 dB. B8 highest because 900 MHz LNA has higher noise, and the B8 duplexer has more loss at lower frequency. B41 lowest because TDD uses a T/R switch instead of a duplexer — less loss before the LNA.
Step 3 — Sensitivity: combining it all
Sensitivity = kTB_floor + 10·log(BW) + NF + SNR_required

SNR_required depends on modulation and coding rate. For FRC A1 (QPSK 1/3) — the standard sensitivity test — SNR_req = −1 dB. QPSK has only 4 constellation points spread far apart, so the receiver can decode it even when signal is 1 dB below the noise floor.

B1 worked example: −174 + 70 + 5.75 + (−1) = −99.25 dBm
B3 baseline: −174 + 70 + 5.71 + (−1) = −99.29 dBm (slightly better NF)
B8 worst: −174 + 70 + 6.46 + (−1) = −98.54 dBm (higher NF = worse sensitivity)
Step 4 — DSA offset: per-band correction
B3 is the reference baseline (DSA = 0). For every other band: DSA = Sensitivity_band − Sensitivity_B3. This gives the number of extra dB EXM must inject for that band to hit the correct threshold. The DSA values in your table (5 for B1, 8 for B8/B28) also include empirical corrections for path configuration differences (LB uses 2 RX paths vs HB 4 paths), flavour-specific gain settings, and actual measured hardware performance — not just the theoretical NF difference alone.
Step 5 — RX paths: what rev5/rev1/comb mean
Your AAU is 4T4R — 4 independent RX columns (A, B, C, D), each with its own LNA, cable, and ADC channel.

rev5 = Column A tested alone (single path, worst case for that column)
rev1 = Column B tested alone (independent verification of second chain)
comb rev3 = Columns A+B+C combined via MRC (Maximum Ratio Combining). MRC weights each chain by its SNR and sums them. Gain ≈ +3 to 4 dB over single path.
comb rev1 = All 4 columns A+B+C+D via MRC. Best possible. Gain ≈ +5 to 6 dB.

Why test single paths? Because MRC hides individual column failures. If Column C's LNA is dead, comb rev1 might still pass — A, B, D compensate. The rev5/rev1 single-path tests catch dead columns that combined results would mask. This is exactly what happened with AAU #510 — B1C and B1D showed dead in single-path but combined was degraded not zero.
Step 6 — before vs after: the 0.2–0.5 dB gap explained
In the DSA table, every measurement has a "before" and "after" value. The DSA offset is already applied before this comparison — these are NOT showing the DSA offset itself.

before = theoretical sensitivity from the formula (what physics says it should be)
after = sensitivity measured on real hardware after DSA correction

The 0.2–0.5 dB gap = hardware residual: connector insertion loss variation (±0.1 dB), LNA NF not exactly at datasheet (±0.1 dB), filter passband ripple (±0.05 dB), cable slightly different from assumed (±0.1 dB). A healthy unit shows consistent 0.2–0.5 dB residual across all paths. A gap suddenly becoming 2–3 dB on one path = hardware fault on that specific column. This is how you catch degraded LNAs and bad connectors at the measurement level without disconnecting anything.
📐 DSA Worked Calculation — B8 vs B3 reference (step by step)
Step 1: Compute sensitivity per band
Base: kTB = −174 dBm/Hz
BW(10MHz) = +70 dB → floor = −104 dBm
B3: NF=2.40 → sens = −104 + 2.40 − 1 = −102.6 dBm
B8: NF=3.15 → sens = −104 + 3.15 − 1 = −101.85 dBm
B1: NF=5.75 → sens = −104 + 5.75 − 1 = −99.25 dBm
B28: NF=3.70 → sens = −104 + 3.70 − 1 = −101.3 dBm
B41: NF=2.75 → sens = −104 + 2.75 − 1 = −102.25 dBm
Step 2: Compute DSA offset (vs B3 reference)
DSA = Sens_band − Sens_B3 (reference)
DSA_B3 = −102.6 − (−102.6) = 0 dB (reference)
DSA_B8 = −101.85 − (−102.6) = +0.75 dB
DSA_B1 = −99.25 − (−102.6) = +3.35 dB
DSA_B28 = −101.3 − (−102.6) = +1.3 dB
DSA_B41 = −102.25 − (−102.6) = +0.35 dB
Positive DSA = inject more power (band is less sensitive)
Step 3: How EXM uses DSA
Base injection = −95 dBm (arbitrary reference). EXM actual = Base + DSA offset.
B3: EXM = −95 + 0 = −95 dBm · B1: EXM = −95 + 3.35 = −91.65 dBm · B8: EXM = −95 + 0.75 = −94.25 dBm
After cable loss (−2.5 dB): power at RU port = EXM − 2.5 dB
B1 at RU port: −91.65 − 2.5 = −94.15 dBm → compare to sensitivity −99.25 dBm → 5.1 dB above → PRACH detects reliably

What every column in the DSA table means

Flavour / Band:
"Flavour" = which band combination config the RU is running (b1b3 = B1+B3 active, b1b3b41 = B1+B3+B41 active, etc.). Different flavours can have slightly different gain settings even for the same band because the RF front-end is shared between bands. This is why B1 DSA might differ between b1b3 and b1b3b41 flavours even though B1 NF itself does not change — the shared hardware context changes.
DSA (dB) — the offset column:
This is how many dB above the B3 baseline this band's sensitivity sits. DSA = 0 for B3 (it is the reference). DSA = 5 for B1 means B1 is 5 dB less sensitive than B3 in this flavour/BW combination — EXM injects 5 dB more power for B1 tests than it does for B3 tests. DSA = 8 for B28 means EXM injects 8 dB more. This correction ensures every band is tested at exactly its own correct threshold, not B3's easier threshold.
RX paths — why B28 has 2 instead of 4:
High-band (B1/B3/B41) uses 4 RX paths — all 4 columns (A/B/C/D) active. Low-band (B8/B28) uses only 2 RX paths — columns A and B only. This is a hardware design choice: the low-band RFFE only connects to 2 of the 4 columns to save cost and board space, since low-band coverage is wide enough that 2-path MRC is sufficient. This also means low-band combined sensitivity gain is only +3 dB (2 paths) vs +5-6 dB for high-band (4 paths).
before vs after — the 0.2–0.5 dB gap:
The DSA offset is already applied before the before/after comparison. These two numbers show:
before = sensitivity calculated purely from formula (theoretical, perfect components assumed)
after = sensitivity measured on your actual hardware after DSA correction

The gap is the sum of all real-world imperfections the formula cannot predict: connector loss variation (±0.1 dB), LNA NF tolerance (±0.1 dB), filter ripple (±0.05 dB), cable slightly different (±0.1 dB). All these add up to 0.2–0.5 dB on a healthy unit. When this gap suddenly becomes 2–3 dB on one specific path — that path has a hardware problem. This is how you pinpoint a bad LNA or connector without disassembling anything.
MRC — how the +5 dB combining gain works:
MRC (Maximum Ratio Combining) does not simply add signals — it weights each chain by its own SNR quality before summing. A chain with strong, clean signal gets high weight. A chain with a degraded LNA gets low weight automatically. The combined SNR in linear scale = sum of all individual SNRs. For 4 equal chains each at SNR = S: combined = 4S = 10·log(4) = +6 dB. In practice chains are slightly unequal so you get +5 to 5.5 dB. For 2 paths (LB): +3 dB. For 3 paths: +4.8 dB.

Key takeaway — what you should remember
Sensitivity = minimum power (at RU port, cable-loss corrected) for successful decode. Set by physics (kTB) + your hardware (NF) + your modulation (required SNR).
NF dominates = LNA is first in chain → Friis formula → LNA NF is system NF. Every other stage is negligible.
Cable loss = NF penalty = your 2 dB test cable before the LNA makes the system 2 dB worse. This is why you always subtract cable loss when reporting sensitivity — you are removing the noise penalty your test setup added.
DSA = the measured per-band sensitivity offset from a common reference. Derived experimentally. Stored in config. Used so the PRACH test threshold matches real hardware capability per band.
Modulation changes sensitivity by 17+ dB = QPSK 1/3 (A1, −102 dBm) vs 64QAM 3/4 (A5, −85 dBm). Same radio, same hardware, completely different sensitivity number. This is why your ul-rct-test results show different sensitivity per FRC scenario.
KTB K × T × B explained — what each constant is, why room temp is the reference Beginner click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST kTB in one sentence: −174 dBm/Hz is the absolute minimum noise any radio can have — it comes from the random jiggling of electrons in any warm object. You cannot engineer away from this limit. Every sensitivity calculation starts here.
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
kTB = −174 dBm/Hz is the first term in the sensitivity formula. This card derives it from first principles. The full chain showing how kTB feeds into sensitivity and then DSA is in the DSA card.
→ For the complete chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

Why −174 dBm/Hz is the absolute floor

Full numerical derivation:
P = kTB = 1.38×10⁻²³ × 290 × 1 = 4.002×10⁻²¹ watts
= 4.002×10⁻¹⁸ milliwatts
= 10·log(4.002×10⁻¹⁸) = −173.98 dBm ≈ −174 dBm/Hz

This is noise power in 1 Hz bandwidth. For any real channel add 10·log(BW_Hz). Common mistake: entering BW in MHz — 10·log(10) = 10 dB, not 70 dB. Always convert to Hz first.
Why 290 K is used even though your lab is warmer:
IEEE Std 60268 defines 290 K as the standard noise temperature for all NF and sensitivity specs. This is a measurement convention — it makes results from different labs and manufacturers directly comparable. At your actual lab temperature of ~298 K (25°C), the real noise floor is about 10·log(298/290) = +0.12 dB higher. This is small enough that all 3GPP specs are written using 290 K as the reference without correction.
🎯 Analogy: kTB is the sound of the universe itself

Imagine you are in a quiet room trying to hear someone whisper. Even if the room is completely soundproofed, you still hear a faint hiss — the hiss of air molecules randomly vibrating against your eardrum. That is thermal noise. In electronics: electrons in any resistor randomly jiggle because they have thermal energy (k×T). This jiggling creates tiny random voltages — the noise you can never eliminate unless you cool the component to absolute zero (−273°C). At 290K (room temp), this noise is exactly −174 dBm per Hz of bandwidth. Every RF receiver starts its noise calculation from this floor — it cannot do better.

Yes — −174 dBm/Hz is the minimum noise at room temperature
You said it exactly right. kTB = −174 dBm/Hz is the minimum possible noise at room temperature. It is not something you can engineer away. As long as your receiver is at 290 K (room temperature), every 1 Hz of bandwidth will contain at least −174 dBm of thermal noise power. The only way to go below this is to physically cool the receiver (cryogenic LNAs used in radio telescopes operate at 4–20 K and achieve noise floors approaching −190 dBm/Hz).
Why 290 K and not 300 K (25°C)?
IEEE defined 290 K as the standard noise temperature reference because it makes kT a round number: kT = 4.0×10⁻²¹ W/Hz exactly. At 300 K it would be 4.14×10⁻²¹ — messier. The difference is only 0.15 dB, negligible for engineering purposes. All 3GPP specs, all Keysight instruments, and all noise figure calculations use 290 K as the reference.

Friis formula — why LNA position is everything

Friis numerical calculation (all values in linear):
Convert each component: NF_linear = 10^(NF_dB/10)
Cable: 1.778, G=0.562 · Dup: 1.122, G=0.891 · BPF: 1.071, G=0.933 · LNA: 1.585, G=100 · PostBPF: 1.259 · Mixer: 5.012

NF_total = 1.778 + (1.122−1)/0.562 + (1.071−1)/0.501 + (1.585−1)/0.447 + (1.259−1)/44.7 + (5.012−1)/4470
= 1.778 + 0.217 + 0.142 + 1.309 + 0.006 + 0.001 = 3.45 linear = 5.38 dB
(Slight variation from 5.75 dB due to component tolerances and cable length — 5.75 is measured value)
The cable before LNA — your biggest variable in lab tests:
The 2.5 dB cable loss adds its full value to system NF because it comes before the LNA (no gain divides it). When you change cables, swap adapters, or use a different length cable between EXM and RU port, the system NF changes. Every 0.1 dB extra cable loss = 0.1 dB worse sensitivity = your test threshold moves by 0.1 dB. Always measure cable loss with VNA before any sensitivity test and subtract it from EXM output when calculating the power arriving at the RU port.
Why everything after the LNA is negligible:
LNA gain = +20 dB = ×100 linear. Post-BPF NF = 1.0 dB → linear 1.259. Its Friis contribution = (1.259−1)/100 = 0.0026 linear = 0.011 dB. Mixer NF = 7 dB → linear 5.012. Contribution = (5.012−1)/100 = 0.040 linear = 0.17 dB. These are completely insignificant compared to the 2.5 dB from the cable. This is why once the LNA is working correctly, improving anything after it gives virtually zero sensitivity improvement.
🎯 Analogy: the Friis formula is like a telephone game

Imagine passing a message (your signal) through a line of people. The first person in line can mishear the message and corrupt it — and everyone after will repeat the corrupted version louder. The second person can also mishear, but their error gets divided by how loudly the first person spoke (the LNA gain). By the time you get to the 10th person, their individual errors are completely drowned out by the first person's mistake. This is why the LNA (first active component) dominates the system NF — and why every millimetre of cable before the LNA directly costs you sensitivity.

The single most important rule from all of this
Everything before the LNA costs you sensitivity. Everything after the LNA is free.
→ Your test cable before the LNA: every dB of loss = 1 dB worse sensitivity
→ Your duplexer before the LNA: every dB of insertion loss = 1 dB worse sensitivity
→ Your connector quality before the LNA: loose connector = worse sensitivity
→ Your LNA itself: its NF determines the system. 1 dB better LNA = 1 dB better sensitivity
→ Your mixer NF: irrelevant — divided by LNA gain (×100)
→ Your ADC: irrelevant for sensitivity — quantisation noise is far below thermal noise
→ Your DU / software: irrelevant for NF — only affects required SNR (which depends on modulation)

16a RF path components — duplexer, BPF, LNA, VGA, mixer (every stage) Beginner–Intermediate click to expand▾

RF path components — duplexer, BPF, LNA, VGA, mixer, ADC

Component purpose and NF contribution (B1 RX chain):
Duplexer: separates TX and RX paths at antenna port. Insertion loss 0.5 dB → NF contribution 0.5 dB. TX rejection >50 dB (prevents PA from entering LNA).
Pre-BPF: rejects out-of-band blockers before LNA. Loss 0.3 dB → NF 0.3 dB. Worth it — without it, a strong blocker could compress LNA.
LNA: NF 2.0 dB, gain +20 dB. Most critical component. Sets system NF. GaAs pHEMT.
Mixer: NF 7 dB, but after LNA gain ÷100 = 0.07 dB contribution. Negligible.
VGA: variable gain ±30 dB range. AGC-controlled. Keeps ADC at −12 dBFS.
ADC: 12-bit, 74 dB SQNR, 122.88 MSPS.
TX path components — FHGW to PA:
DAC: converts digital IQ to analog. 16-bit, 122.88 MSPS. Clock from GPS-locked reference.
Upconverter: baseband IQ → RF. Mixer × LO frequency. IQ imbalance here → constellation rotation.
PA: GaN, Class AB, +43 dBm output, ~35% efficiency. Protected by: thermal shutdown, VSWR protection, over-current detection.
Duplexer: TX side routes PA output to antenna. Loss 0.5 dB from rated power.
Failure modes per component:
LNA dead → sensitivity fails, all columns for that band. LNA compressed (blocker) → NF increases, sensitivity degrades but LNA not dead. VGA/AGC stuck → RSSI reads wrong, may clip ADC. ADC_ADJUST wrong → RSSI off by fixed offset. PA degraded → TX power low, ACLR may worsen. Duplexer cracked → TX-to-RX leakage → RX desensitisation, possible LNA damage.
Duplexer / T-R Switch — first after antenna
In FDD (B1/B3/B8/B28): the duplexer simultaneously passes UL and DL on separate ports with >50 dB TX→RX isolation. It stops the PA's +43 dBm TX power from flooding the LNA input and desensitising the receiver. In TDD (B41): a T/R switch replaces the duplexer — faster switching, but cannot transmit and receive simultaneously on the same antenna.
BPF — Band-pass filter
Placed after the duplexer (and sometimes again after the LNA) to provide additional out-of-band rejection. Blockers passing through the duplexer with only 50 dB suppression are further attenuated, protecting the LNA from strong interferers that would cause compression and desensitisation. Also suppresses the image frequency before downconversion.
LNA — the most critical component
David: "you have here the LNA, right? Low noise amplifier... if we receive the signal in low power, we amplify it. This is why we have the LNA here."
The LNA amplifies the weak incoming signal (maybe −80 dBm from a distant UE) while adding minimal noise. By Friis formula: the first stage dominates system NF. A 3 dB NF LNA before a 10 dB NF mixer gives system NF ≈ 3.3 dB. Swap them, and system NF ≈ 10 dB — 6.7 dB worse sensitivity.
ParameterTypical valueWhat it means for your tests
Noise Figure (NF)1–3 dBDirect hit on REFSENS. +1 dB NF = −1 dBm sensitivity (worse). If REFSENS fails, check LNA NF first.
Gain15–25 dBAmplifies signal so ADC and mixer see it clearly above their own noise floors.
IIP3−5 to +10 dBm inputLinearity. Determines blocking performance (ACS test). Higher IIP3 = better ACS.
P1dB−10 to 0 dBm inputIf a strong interferer exceeds P1dB, the LNA compresses → receiver goes blind → desensitisation.
NEVER put any lossy component (attenuator, switch, long cable) before the LNA. A 2 dB attenuator before the LNA adds exactly 2 dB to system NF — halving effective coverage range. This is why your test cable connects directly to the RU antenna port for sensitivity tests.
VGA — Variable Gain Amplifier (AGC engine)
After the LNA, the VGA provides adjustable gain (typically −20 dB to +20 dB range). The AGC loop reads RSSI and adjusts VGA gain to keep the signal level at the ADC input within the optimal range — not too strong (clipping) and not too weak (buried in quantisation noise). David: "we calibrate the RF chain to make sure we are not compressing the ADC and we are not transmitting in too much low power."
Mixer + Local Oscillator (LO) — frequency downconversion
The mixer multiplies the RF signal (e.g. 1747.5 MHz for B3 UL) by the LO signal at the same frequency → output is the difference frequency = baseband (0 Hz for direct conversion / zero-IF architecture). Modern RUs use zero-IF: I and Q channels come out at baseband, 90° apart. Together they fully represent the complex baseband signal including both amplitude and phase.
LO phase noise directly limits EVM. Phase noise at 10 kHz offset from the LO causes ICI between adjacent LTE subcarriers (spaced 15 kHz apart). This is why EVM tests fail when the reference oscillator ages or runs too hot.
16b ADC — 11-12 bit resolution, dynamic range, dBFS, clipping Intermediate click to expand▾

12-bit ADC — dynamic range, SQNR, dBFS, clipping

SQNR and what 12 bits gives you:
SQNR (Signal to Quantisation Noise Ratio) = 6.02×N + 1.76 dB where N = number of bits. For 12 bits: SQNR = 6.02×12 + 1.76 = 74 dB. This is the ratio between the full-scale signal and the quantisation noise floor. 74 dB of dynamic range means signals up to 74 dB above the quantisation noise floor are cleanly digitised. A 16-bit ADC would give 98 dB — used in audio. RF systems use 12–16 bits because the VGA/AGC keeps the signal in a narrow range.
Operating point — why −12 dBFS is the target:
Operating at 0 dBFS (full scale) means any instantaneous peak clips → severe distortion → wrong RSSI, high EVM. Operating too low (−40 dBFS) wastes dynamic range — more quantisation noise relative to signal. −12 dBFS is the standard operating point: 12 dB of headroom for signal peaks above average, and 62 dB of SQNR still available below the signal. The VGA/AGC loop constantly adjusts gain to maintain this target.
Clipping — what happens and how to detect:
When input exceeds full scale (0 dBFS), the ADC output saturates at the maximum code (all 1s). RSSI reading wraps around or saturates at a wrong value. On EXA: flat-top distortion visible on spectrum (compressed waveform). In CLI: get_rssi returns a value close to 0 dBFS regardless of actual input power. Fix: reduce gain (check VGA/AGC settings, check if LNA is in compression from a strong blocker).
What the ADC does
The ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter) is the boundary between the analog RF world and digital processing. It samples the baseband IQ signal at the Nyquist rate and converts each sample to a binary number. David: "we are working with 12 bits. Sorry, 11 bits. It means 2 by 11 steps of resolution."
Resolution: N bits → 2^N amplitude levels 11-bit ADC: 2^11 = 2048 levels 12-bit ADC: 2^12 = 4096 levels SQNR = 6.02 × N + 1.76 dB 11-bit: SQNR = 68 dB dynamic range 12-bit: SQNR = 74 dB dynamic range
Dynamic range — exactly what David drew on the whiteboard
The ADC has a fixed input voltage range from minimum (noise floor) to maximum (full scale). David's explanation: "the dynamic range is the minimum value that the ADC is starting to see some power from the noise itself — to separate the signal from the noise. And the maximum value. This is called dynamic range."
ADC pointdBFS valueWhat happens
Full scale (clipping)0 dBFSADC output saturates. All values above this are clipped. Waveform peaks go flat. Severe EVM and ACLR degradation.
Operating target−6 to −10 dBFSSignal is well within range with headroom for PAPR peaks.
AGC target (typical)−20 to −30 dBFSComfortable operating point with large PAPR headroom.
Noise floor−68 to −74 dBFSQuantisation noise. Signals below this cannot be distinguished from noise.
Sensitivity point~−60 to −68 dBFSWhere signal just emerges from quantisation noise — the "blur" point David described.
dBFS — decibels relative to Full Scale
David: "DBFS is DB to full scale related to the maximum dynamic range of the ADC." All dBFS values are ≤ 0 dBFS. 0 dBFS = at the clipping threshold. −20 dBFS = 10% of full-scale voltage. −74 dBFS = at the ADC noise floor for a 12-bit converter.
The get_rssi CLI command returns RSSI in both dBm AND dBFS. The dBFS reading tells you where the signal sits inside the ADC's operating range. If dBFS is close to 0 → near clipping, reduce VGA gain. If very negative (−60 dBFS or below) → signal is weak, near noise floor.
David's clipping explanation: "you're cutting the information if you're transmitting too high. You got the information — if this is the time domain and this is the amplitude domain — you're cutting the information." The ADC chops the sine wave peaks flat → massive harmonic distortion → EVM and ACLR both fail catastrophically.
16c RSSI: two methods (CLI dBFS vs DU dBm), sensitivity point, your task Intermediate click to expand▾

RSSI — CLI dBFS method vs DU dBm method, when they disagree

CLI method — get_rssi N:
Reads the ADC digital output directly. Returns dBFS value (e.g. −12.5). Converted to dBm via: P_dBm = dBFS + ADC_ADJUST. Fast, per-column, direct hardware reading. Does not go through DU processing. Useful for: initial calibration, column-by-column fault isolation, debugging without DU. Limit: only as accurate as ADC_ADJUST calibration.
DU method — testmac rssi:
Reads RSSI computed inside the DU baseband after FFT processing. Averages power across active subcarriers. Includes interference contributions. Goes through eCPRI fronthaul → FHGW → DU. More representative of what the scheduler sees. More affected by fronthaul issues. Useful for: validating end-to-end chain, checking FHGW BFP accuracy, confirming what the network actually "sees".
Disagreement diagnosis — what each pattern means:
CLI accurate, DU off by 2–3 dB → FHGW BFP decompression issue or eCPRI timing problem → check FHGW firmware.
Both off from EXM by same amount → ADC_ADJUST wrong → re-run RSSI cal.
One column CLI wrong → hardware fault on that column (LNA, cable, connector) → inspect physically.
All columns drift together as unit warms → temperature compensation not set → check TEMP_COMP in hardware.json.
CLI varies but DU is stable → ADC channel mapping wrong in configuration.
Two RSSI measurement methods
David described two independent ways the system measures RSSI:
Method 1 — DU RSSI (dBm): After FFT processing, IQ samples flow to the DU via eCPRI fronthaul. The DU sums power across all subcarriers and computes RSSI in dBm. This is what your test automation reads from the OAM portal or DU CLI. Also: the DU calculates the "blur" (sensitivity point) from these same samples.
Method 2 — CLI RSSI at ADC (dBFS + dBm): The FHGW firmware measures power directly at the ADC output, before FFT or compression. Command: get_rssi. Returns 8 readings (ADC channels 0–7) in both dBm (gain-corrected) and dBFS (raw ADC reference). One reading per antenna element/RX chain.
The gap — and how it was closed
David: "We had a gap between the readings from the DU and the readings from the CLI. So we managed to close this gap by adding new features from the software side to the DU." The gap existed because the two methods have different reference planes, different gain compensation tables, and different averaging windows. The DU software update added calibration offsets to align them.

"Start first with basic uplink test to measure the sensitivity point, measure the RSSI point manually, and then provide the automation. We need to do it for each flavor, we need to do it for each band."

16d FHGW internals — FFT, BFP compression, eCPRI fronthaul timing Advanced click to expand▾

FHGW internals — BFP compression, IFFT, eCPRI, what can go wrong

BFP compression — why it is needed:
Raw 16-bit IQ for a 20 MHz 4T4R system: 4 columns × 2 (I+Q) × 1200 subcarriers × 14 symbols/ms × 16 bits = ~430 Mbps. Standard 10GbE fronthaul supports 10 Gbps — but with overhead, practical is ~8 Gbps. With BFP: each resource block (12 subcarriers) shares one 4-bit exponent, and each sample uses 9-bit mantissa instead of 16-bit. Compression ratio ≈ 9/16 = 56% → bandwidth = ~240 Mbps. Fits easily in 10GbE with margin.
IFFT — frequency to time domain:
The DU schedules which UEs get which subcarriers (resource blocks). It passes the frequency-domain IQ values per subcarrier to the FHGW. The FHGW performs IFFT (Inverse FFT) to convert this to a time-domain OFDM symbol. Then adds cyclic prefix (4.69 μs for normal CP). The resulting time-domain waveform goes to the DAC and then to the RF chain. For UL: the FHGW performs FFT (removes CP first) to convert received time-domain samples back to frequency-domain subcarriers for the DU to decode.
FHGW faults that cause RSSI discrepancies:
BFP expansion error: if the exponent bits are corrupted, the IQ amplitudes are wrong by a power of 2 → RSSI off by 6 dB steps.
IFFT timing: if FHGW IFFT timing drifts, the cyclic prefix overlaps with the data → inter-symbol interference → EVM increase.
eCPRI packet loss: dropped eCPRI packets cause missing subcarriers → DU sees lower RSSI.
Clock reference loss: FHGW loses GPS/PTP sync → frame timing drifts → TDD B41 DL/UL collision.
FHGW digital processing blocks
BlockUL functionDL functionWhy it matters
FFT / iFFTTime→frequency (OFDM demod)Frequency→time (OFDM mod)Converts between IQ samples and resource elements. FFT size = N subcarriers.
CP removal / insertionRemoves cyclic prefixAdds cyclic prefixCP absorbs multipath delay. LTE normal CP = 4.69 µs.
BFP compression14→9 bit IQ samples9→14 bit decompressionReduces fronthaul BW. Small EVM floor from quantisation.
eCPRI framingWraps IQ in Ethernet+timestampUnwraps, extracts timingTiming accuracy <260 ns. Errors cause time_offset test failures.
RSSI at ADCPower measured before FFT—get_rssi CLI reads this raw ADC power in dBFS.
BFP compression — why it matters for your tests
Block Floating Point (BFP) encodes a block of 12 IQ samples (one resource block) with a shared 4-bit exponent and individual mantissas. Going from 14-bit raw to 9-bit BFP adds quantisation noise equivalent to ~5 bits of resolution loss. This contributes a small but real EVM floor (~0.1–0.3% EVM) even with a perfect PA. Your EVM spec limits must account for this irreducible floor.
The IQ compression ratio directly affects fronthaul bandwidth. A 20 MHz LTE channel (100 RBs × 12 subcarriers) at 30.72 Msps, 14-bit IQ, 2 antennas = ~3.7 Gbps raw. With 9-bit BFP: ~2.4 Gbps. eCPRI over 10GbE handles this comfortably. This is why the fronthaul is specified at 10G/25G in O-RAN deployments.

M01 The Decibel & RF Power — dB, dBm, dBc, dBFS, link budget Beginner click to expand▾

dB, dBm, dBc, dBFS — the language of RF

Why RF uses logarithmic scale (dB):
RF signals span 13 orders of magnitude in power — from a 20W PA (+43 dBm) to a sensitivity threshold of −99 dBm. That is a ratio of 10^14. Working in linear watts is impossible. dB compresses this: every ×10 power = +10 dB, every ×2 = +3 dB. Adding gains in dB = multiplying in linear. Chain gain = sum of all block gains in dB.
dBm, dBc, dBFS — reference points:
dBm = power relative to 1 mW. 0 dBm = 1 mW. +30 dBm = 1W. −99 dBm = your RX sensitivity.
dBc = power relative to carrier. Used for ACLR (adjacent channel power vs carrier) and spurious. ACLR limit −45 dBc means adjacent channel must be 45 dB below the wanted signal.
dBFS = power relative to ADC full scale. 0 dBFS = ADC clipping. −12 dBFS = typical operating point. Converted to dBm via ADC_ADJUST in hardware.json.
Quick mental maths — dB rules to memorise:
+3 dB = ×2 power · −3 dB = ÷2 · +10 dB = ×10 · −10 dB = ÷10
+6 dB = ×4 · +20 dB = ×100 · +30 dB = ×1000
0 dBm = 1 mW · +10 dBm = 10 mW · +30 dBm = 1 W · +43 dBm = 20 W
−30 dBm = 1 μW · −60 dBm = 1 nW · −99 dBm ≈ your sensitivity floor
Why RF lives in logarithms
A base station may transmit 40 W; the signal it receives from a phone at the cell edge can be around 10⁻¹³ W — a ratio of ~100,000,000,000,000 to 1. You cannot reason about that range in linear watts. RF uses a logarithmic scale, the decibel, which compresses that range and turns multiplication into addition.
dB — the decibel is a RATIO
dB = 10 × log₁₀(P_out / P_in)
Memorise the toolkit: +3 dB = ×2 · −3 dB = ÷2 · +10 dB = ×10 · −10 dB = ÷10 · 0 dB = ×1
Build everything else by combining: +6 dB = ×4 · +13 dB = ×20 · +20 dB = ×100 · +30 dB = ×1000
dBm — absolute power (referenced to 1 mW)
dBm = 10 × log₁₀(Power_mW / 1 mW)
dBmActual powerContext
+43 dBm20 WYour RU TX output per port
+30 dBm1 W+30 (1W) is the anchor
0 dBm1 mWVNA source output, reference point
−69 dBm126 pW3GPP REFSENS limit Wide Area BS
−104 dBm0.04 fWThermal noise in 10 MHz at room temp
Rules: dBm + dB = dBm ✓ | dBm − dBm = dB (gain) ✓ | dBm + dBm = WRONG ✗ | Never add two absolute powers in dB.

The power_monitor tool on the FHGW reads power in dBFS (digital domain, before the DAC/PA). It is NOT dBm. You cannot convert without knowing the full gain chain.

📐 Worked examples — do these until they feel automatic
Q: EXA reads −16.7 dBm at BOB SMA. Coupler = −30 dB. What is antenna power?
A: P_antenna = −16.7 + 30 = +13.3 dBm = 21 mW per column
Q: PA gain = +43 dB. Input = −10 dBm. Output?
A: Output = −10 + 43 = +33 dBm = 2 W
Q: Cable loss = 2.5 dB. EXM outputs −95 dBm. Power at RU port?
A: −95 − 2.5 = −97.5 dBm
Q: Signal is 5 mW. Convert to dBm.
A: 5 mW = 5 × 1 mW → 10·log(5) = +7 dBm
Q: ACLR reads −42 dBc. Limit is −45 dBc. Pass or fail?
A: FAIL — −42 is 3 dB worse (less negative) than −45 dBc limit
Q: get_rssi returns −12.5 dBFS. ADC_ADJUST = −85. P_dBm?
A: −12.5 + (−85) = −97.5 dBm at RU port
M02 The 50-Ohm World — impedance, reflection, VSWR, return loss Beginner click to expand▾

50 Ω impedance — why it matters for every connector and cable

Why 50 Ω is the RF standard:
75 Ω minimises cable loss (optimal for coax). 33 Ω maximises power transfer. 50 Ω is the engineering compromise — acceptable loss, acceptable power handling, rugged connectors. The entire RF industry standardised on 50 Ω so equipment from different manufacturers connects without impedance mismatch.
What happens when impedance is not matched (VSWR):
When source and load impedances differ, part of the signal reflects back. VSWR (Voltage Standing Wave Ratio) measures this. VSWR = 1.0 = perfect match, zero reflection. VSWR = 2.0 = 11% power reflected. A poorly torqued SMA connector can have VSWR > 2.0, meaning you lose 11% of your signal before it even enters the RU. In your sensitivity tests, a VSWR of 2.0 at the cable-to-RU connection costs you about 0.5 dB sensitivity.
Return loss — how VNA shows mismatch:
Return Loss (dB) = −20·log(reflection coefficient Γ). RL = 20 dB means Γ = 0.1 = 1% power reflected = excellent. RL = 10 dB means Γ = 0.316 = 10% reflected = poor. Your VNA S11 measurement shows return loss. Target: S11 < −20 dB (RL > 20 dB) for all cables and connectors in your test setup.
Why 50 ohms?
At RF, a cable is a transmission line with characteristic impedance Z₀ set by its geometry, not its length. The industry standardised on 50Ω: coax handles maximum power near 30Ω and minimum loss near 77Ω — 50Ω is the compromise. Rule: keep the entire path 50Ω end to end.
Reflection coefficient (Gamma)
Γ = (ZL − Z0) / (ZL + Z0) Matched (ZL=50Ω): Γ = 0 Open (ZL=∞): Γ = +1 Short (ZL=0): Γ = −1
Return loss and VSWR — the two numbers you live by
Return Loss (dB) = −20 × log₁₀|Γ| ← bigger is better VSWR = (1 + |Γ|) / (1 − |Γ|) ← near 1 is better
VSWRReturn Loss% reflectedVerdict
1.0:1∞0%Perfect
1.5:114 dB4%Good — typical spec
2.0:19.5 dB11%Marginal
3.0:16 dB25%Bad
∞0 dB100%Open or short
Keying a PA into an open port (Γ = +1, 100% reflected) returns all power into the PA — can permanently damage it. This is why VSWR-trip protection exists and why you NEVER connect a PA to an unterminated port.
VNA calibration standards: Load = perfect 50Ω (Γ=0), Open/Short = perfect reflectors (Γ=±1). The SOLT cal removes systematic errors so what you measure is the DUT, not your cables.

M03 The RF Chain — TX/RX flow, gain cascade, noise figure, sensitivity Beginner–Intermediate click to expand▾

RF chain gain cascade — how gains and losses combine

Gain cascade in dB — just add:
The beauty of dB: total chain gain = sum of all individual gains and losses. Example DL chain: DAC output 0 dBm → PA gain +43 dB → duplexer loss −0.5 dB → coupler loss −30 dB → BOB SMA = +12.5 dBm. For UL: antenna receives −97.5 dBm → duplexer −0.5 dB → LNA +20 dB → mixer −7 dB → ADC input = +15 dBm... wait, that cannot be right — AGC reduces gain to keep ADC safe. Real chain includes AGC which maintains ADC at −12 dBFS regardless of input.
Noise Figure in a cascade — Friis:
Unlike gain, noise figures do NOT simply add. First stage NF dominates. NF_total = NF1 + (NF2−1)/G1 + (NF3−1)/(G1×G2) + ... This is why LNA is first active component and why cable before LNA directly adds to NF. See NCH card for full numerical calculation showing your 5.75 dB system NF.
P1dB — compression point:
At high input powers, the PA gain compresses — output power no longer tracks input linearly. P1dB is the input power where gain drops by 1 dB from its small-signal value. Operating near P1dB causes ACLR failures. Your PA is backed off from P1dB to operate in its linear region — this is why DPD is needed, it allows operating closer to P1dB while maintaining linearity.
The transmit chain (left to right)
StageWhat it does
Digital IQWaveform as numbers (baseband), measured in dBFS. IQ playback injects here.
DACDigital → analog: turns IQ samples into analog baseband voltage.
Mixer + LOUp-conversion: f_RF = f_LO + f_baseband. Puts signal on carrier frequency.
FilterRemoves mixer images and out-of-band products. Leaves clean band.
PAPower amplifier: lifts milliwatt signal to tens of watts. Hottest, most non-linear block — reason DPD exists.
Duplexer / T/R switchRoutes TX to the shared antenna. FDD: frequency-split duplexer. TDD: time switch.
The receive chain (right to left)
StageWhat it does
LNAFIRST thing the weak (~−100 dBm) signal hits. High gain, very low noise — sets the whole receiver noise figure.
FilterSelects the wanted channel, rejects blockers and adjacent channels.
Mixer + LODown-conversion to baseband: f_baseband = f_RF − f_LO.
ADCAnalog → digital: samples the IQ signal for the modem.
Gain cascades — just addition
Total chain gain = sum of every stage gain and loss Example: DAC drive +5 dB + filter loss −2 dB + PA gain +40 dB = net +43 dBm output
Noise figure cascade — Friis formula
NF_total = NF₁ + (NF₂−1)/G₁ + (NF₃−1)/(G₁×G₂) + ... The FIRST stage dominates. High-gain, low-NF LNA first swamps everything downstream.
Noise floor = −174 + 10×log₁₀(BW_Hz) + NF Sensitivity = −174 + 10×log₁₀(BW_Hz) + NF + required_SNR
A bad LNA → worse NF → higher noise floor → worse sensitivity → FAILED test 7.2. When a radio hears down to −100.8 dBm, Friis decided that number. Nothing abstract — it decides whether the unit ships.
M04 Key Radio Metrics — RSSI, sensitivity, dynamic range, EIRP, TRP Intermediate click to expand▾

Key radio metrics — RSSI, RSRP, RSRQ, SINR explained

RSSI vs RSRP vs RSRQ — what each measures:
RSSI (Received Signal Strength Indicator): total wideband power received — signal + interference + noise. Measured in dBm. Your CLI get_rssi reads this.
RSRP (Reference Signal Received Power): power of LTE reference signals (CRS) per resource element. More precise than RSSI. Used for handover decisions. Range: −44 to −140 dBm.
RSRQ (Reference Signal Received Quality): RSRP / RSSI × N_RB. Includes interference quality. Range: −3 to −19.5 dB.
SINR (Signal to Interference+Noise Ratio): signal power / (interference + noise). The quality metric the scheduler uses.
Dynamic range — why it matters for your tests:
Dynamic range = max receivable signal − sensitivity floor = ~0 dBm − (−99 dBm) = 99 dB. Your ADC has 74 dB of instantaneous dynamic range. The AGC extends this by adjusting gain — a close UE at −40 dBm and a far UE at −99 dBm both need to be handled cleanly. If AGC saturates, all RSSI measurements are wrong.
EVM — Error Vector Magnitude (TX quality metric):
EVM measures how far each received IQ symbol is from its ideal constellation point, as a percentage of the ideal signal amplitude. EVM = |error vector| / |reference vector| × 100%. Limits: QPSK < 17.5%, 16QAM < 12.5%, 64QAM < 8%, 256QAM < 3.5%. EVM failures caused by: phase noise (LO quality), IQ imbalance, nonlinearity (DPD failure), clipping (CFR too aggressive).
RSSI
Total power in the receive band at the radio input, in dBm. Wideband: it sums wanted signal + noise + interference. High RSSI alone does NOT mean good signal — it could be mostly interference. Used for coverage monitoring and AGC control.
Sensitivity
Sensitivity = −174 + 10×log₁₀(BW_Hz) + NF + required_SNR Example: BW=10 MHz → −174+70+NF4+SNR1 = −99 dBm
Minimum input power still meeting BLER ≤ 5% (RCT test 7.2). Set by the chain's noise figure. 3GPP Wide Area BS REFSENS limit: −69 dBm (you should easily achieve −97 to −100 dBm).
Dynamic range and receiver test family
TestWhat it proves3GPP clause
Reference sensitivityMin input power meeting BLER ≤ 5%7.2
Dynamic rangeDecode wanted signal with in-band AWGN present7.3
Adjacent channel selectivity (ACS)Reject interferer just outside the channel7.5
In-channel selectivity (ICS)Decode beside a stronger in-band signal7.4
Narrowband blockingReject 1-RB interferer near band edge7.5
Wideband / out-of-band blockingReject strong in-band LTE / OOB CW interferers7.6
Receiver intermodulationReject IM products of two interferers7.8
RSSI readback calibrationRadio's reported RSSI matches true input powerRuAuto
EIRP and TRP
EIRP = TX power (dBm) + Antenna gain (dBi) − Losses TRP = EIRP integrated over the full sphere
Your AAU beamforming gain: ~+12 dB for B1/B3/B41 (12-element arrays) · ~+6 dB for B8/B28 (6-element arrays). So per-PA output 38.4 dBm → TRP 44.4 dBm → with beamforming 50.4 dBm. Three different power numbers — don't confuse them.
M05 Modulation & IQ — constellations, OFDM, EVM, IQ playback Intermediate click to expand▾

IQ modulation, OFDM, constellations — how radio carries data

IQ — In-phase and Quadrature:
A single RF carrier can carry two independent data streams: I (in-phase, cosine) and Q (quadrature, sine). They are orthogonal — they do not interfere with each other. A QAM constellation is a grid of I/Q amplitude combinations. QPSK uses 4 points (±1, ±1 for I and Q). 16QAM uses 16 points. 64QAM uses 64 points. More points = more bits per symbol = higher throughput = but needs higher SNR to distinguish points.
OFDM — how LTE uses it:
OFDM (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing) divides the channel into many narrow subcarriers (15 kHz each in LTE). Each subcarrier carries its own QAM symbol. 1 Resource Block = 12 subcarriers × 180 kHz. 10 MHz channel = 50 RBs = 600 subcarriers. OFDM is robust against multipath because the cyclic prefix (4.69 μs) is longer than most delay spreads. The IFFT in the FHGW converts your frequency-domain subcarrier assignments into the time-domain OFDM signal.
IQ imbalance — what goes wrong:
If the I and Q paths have amplitude or phase mismatch, the constellation rotates and the points blur. Amplitude imbalance: all points shift toward I or Q axis. Phase imbalance: constellation rotates. Both increase EVM and cause ACLR to worsen. In your RU: IQ imbalance manifests as asymmetric constellation in the EXA modulation analysis view — left/right clusters at different sizes, or constellation tilted off axis.
IQ — why two numbers?
A signal has both amplitude and phase. The clean way to carry both is two numbers: I (in-phase) and Q (quadrature, 90° offset). Any modulated signal is I + jQ — a point on a 2D plane. The DAC, ADC, and all digital processing work in IQ.
Constellations and modulation orders
ModulationBits/symbolPointsEVM limit (3GPP)
QPSK24≤ 17.5%
16QAM416≤ 12.5%
64QAM664≤ 8%
256QAM8256≤ 3.5%
Higher order = more data per symbol, but points sit closer together, demanding a cleaner signal. 256QAM needs EVM ≤ 3.5% — four times tighter than QPSK. This is why DPD and CFR matter so much.
OFDM and the resource grid
LTE/5G split the channel into many narrow 15 kHz subcarriers, each a low-rate QAM symbol. One subcarrier × one symbol = one Resource Element (RE). 12 subcarriers × 7 symbols = one Resource Block (RB). The test "prb: 273" means 273 RBs are allocated (= 100 MHz 5G NR channel).
EVM — test 6.5.2
Error Vector Magnitude = distance from where a symbol SHOULD be to where it LANDED, as % of ideal magnitude. A PA driven too hard (Module 6) raises EVM. The EXM measures this via the modulation analysis mode (sa_set_modulation_analysis_mode).
IQ playback — how Rx tests work
Receiver tests need a known, repeatable uplink signal. A waveform is pre-computed as an IQ file (.bin / .wfm) and a signal generator plays it into the radio. In RuAuto: PRACH_idx158_100MHZ.wfm for PRACH tests, PUCCH format waveforms for PUCCH tests. The EXM does double duty — generator for Rx tests, analyzer for Tx tests.
🎯 Analogy: constellation is like reading handwriting

A perfect constellation = neat, crisp handwriting — every letter exactly where it should be. Phase noise = someone writing on a vibrating bus — the letters are in the right place but wobbly. IQ imbalance = writing with the paper tilted — everything is skewed in one direction. PA compression = writing with a blunt pencil — all the letters are squished together toward the centre. The EXA shows you the handwriting and you diagnose what is wrong with the pen.

M06 DL TX Chain — Power scaling, CFR, DPD, DAC scale Intermediate click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRSTDL TX chain in one sentence: CFR clips the signal peaks so the PA does not have to handle massive spikes, then DPD pre-distorts the signal so the PA's natural nonlinearity is cancelled out — together they let you run the PA close to full power while still meeting the ACLR limit.

DL TX chain — CFR, DPD, power scaling, common failures

CFR — why PAPR must be reduced before PA:
OFDM signals have high PAPR (Peak to Average Power Ratio) — typically 10–12 dB. This means the PA must handle peaks 10–12 dB above the average power. To handle the peaks without clipping, the PA would need to be backed off by 10–12 dB from its P1dB — operating at only 1/10th to 1/100th of its capacity. CFR clips these rare high peaks and smooths them, reducing PAPR to ~8 dB. This lets the PA operate 3–4 dB closer to P1dB, dramatically improving efficiency.
DPD convergence — the 60-second rule:
DPD adapts its pre-distortion polynomial coefficients by comparing the PA output (via observation path) to the ideal signal. This adaptation takes 30–60 seconds after power-on. During convergence: ACLR may be 5–10 dB worse than final value, EVM is elevated, power may fluctuate ±0.5 dB. Always wait for DPD to converge before measuring ACLR, EVM, or doing TX gain calibration. Check DPD status register or simply wait 60 seconds after enabling TX.
Common TX failures and root causes:
ACLR fail: DPD not converged (wait 60s), DPD model mismatch after hardware change, PA operating beyond P1dB (check rated power), CFR not working.
EVM fail: IQ imbalance, LO phase noise, clipping from over-driven input, DPD coefficients diverged.
Power low: tx_calibration_eeprom.json missing (fault 12), wrong TX_GAIN register, PA bias wrong, damaged PA.
The real FHGW DL chain order
Digital 2CC → DL Power Scaling → Gain → CFR → Gain → DPD → Per-channel Gain → DAC
The power_monitor reads dBFS at taps along the way. DPD is ONE link in this chain — not a standalone box.
PA compression and P1dB
Amplifiers are linear only up to a point. P1dB marks where gain has dropped 1 dB from linear. Past P1dB: compression, distortion, spectral regrowth (= ACLR fails), constellation smearing (= EVM fails).
PAPR — why OFDM is hard on PAs
OFDM sums hundreds of subcarriers. When they momentarily align in phase, the instantaneous power peaks ~10 dB above average (PAPR ≈ 10 dB). To prevent clipping, the average must run far below P1dB — hurting efficiency. This is why power_monitor shows DL around −21 dBFS, leaving headroom for peaks.
CFR — Crest Factor Reduction
CFR deliberately clips signal peaks (then applies a filter so it doesn't splatter) to reduce PAPR before the PA. On your FHGW: register 0xb0290000, filter_length 511, threshold 8.3. Two working points: 0xD7 (occupancy > 50%) and 0x128 (occupancy ≤ 50%). Less PAPR = PA can run with less back-off = more efficient.
DPD — Digital Pre-Distortion
DPD pre-warps the signal with the mathematical inverse of the PA's nonlinearity. The PA then "undoes" the pre-distortion → the cascade behaves linearly even though the PA itself is nonlinear. A feedback (observation) path adapts the model. CFR + DPD together let you run the PA hot (efficient) while still passing ACLR/EVM conformance tests.
If DPD fails or is miscalibrated: sudden ACLR degradation of 10–20 dB. PreCheck: DPD Gain Register and DPD Input Power + PAPR must both pass before any RF test begins.
RuAuto PreChecks for the DL chain
PreCheckWhat it confirms
Power Monitor DLDL digital power (dBFS) is in range (not clipping, not too low)
CFR Input PowerCFR input level is correct for its working point
DPD Gain RegisterDPD is configured with correct register values
DPD Input Power + PAPRDPD is being fed the right level and seeing expected PAPR
M07 ACLR & Spectrum Analysis — RBW, cable loss, TDD gating, SEM Intermediate click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST ACLR in one sentence: When you transmit, your signal should stay neatly inside your assigned frequency channel. ACLR measures how much leaks into the neighbouring channel. Think of it as "staying in your lane" — the 3GPP limit says your leakage must be 45 dB weaker than your main signal. Failure means your PA is nonlinear and DPD is not fixing it properly.

ACLR — Adjacent Channel Leakage Ratio measurement setup

What ACLR measures and the limit:
ACLR = power in adjacent channel / power in wanted channel, in dBc. 3GPP limit for LTE base station: −45 dBc for adjacent channel (offset = channel BW), −50 dBc for alternate channel (offset = 2× channel BW). Measured on EXA using the ACLR/ACP measurement mode. A value of −42 dBc = FAIL (limit is −45 dBc). This means the PA is leaking 3 dB too much power into adjacent spectrum.
EXA setup for ACLR measurement:
Center freq = band center (B1 = 2140 MHz). Span = 5× channel BW minimum. RBW = 100 kHz. Atten = 20–30 dB (preamp OFF — signal is strong). Input = BOB SMA + 30 dB pad. Trigger = frame trigger or free-run. Use EXA ACLR function (not manual integration). Important: EXA automatically integrates power in each channel using the correct LTE RRC filter — do not try to measure ACLR manually from the spectrum trace.
TDD gating for B41 ACLR:
B41 is TDD — the PA transmits only during DL subframes. EXA must be gated to measure only during TX active periods. Without gating, the ACLR measurement includes the noise floor during UL periods, making ACLR appear 5–10 dB better than it actually is. Set EXA gate delay = DL subframe start offset, gate length = DL subframe duration. Use the TDD frame structure from tc_cadence.json to find the correct timing.
ACLR — test 6.6.2
Adjacent Channel Leakage Ratio = wanted-channel power / adjacent-channel leakage power, in dBc. The direct measure of spectral regrowth from PA nonlinearity and DPD performance. In RuAuto: sa_set_ACP_mode. Higher dBc = better (less leakage).
VerdictCondition
Passmeasured_ACLR ≥ aclr_kpi (e.g. 54 dBc)
Pass(Tolerance)aclr_kpi − tolerance ≤ measured < aclr_kpi
Failmeasured < aclr_kpi − tolerance
3GPP minimum ACLR for Wide Area BS: Offset A (±1 BW) ≥ 45 dBc, Offset B (±2 BW) ≥ 50 dBc. RuAuto typically applies tighter limits (54–55 dBc).
Spectrum emission mask (SEM) — test 6.6.3
The whole transmitted spectrum must sit under a stepped emission ceiling. ACLR checks ±1 and ±2 channel offsets. SEM checks the full spectrum out to ±30 MHz and beyond. Spurious (6.6.4) checks at specific far-field frequencies.
Cable-loss de-embedding — critical
Every cable and connector steals power. RuAuto stores per-frequency losses in cable_loss.json and applies them: extract_cable_loss() / :CORR:BTS:GAIN command to the EXM. Without de-embedding every power reading is wrong by the path loss amount.
TDD gating — mandatory for B41
On B41, the radio transmits only in downlink slots. The analyzer MUST be gated to measure only the TX slot. Without gating you average in the silent UL slots and read too low.
RuAuto TDD gate settings: standard preset config 3, special-subframe config 8 (SSFR 8), gate delay ~3.1 ms, gate length ~2.8 ms. EXM commands: sa_set_gate_view_state('ON'), sa_set_trigger_gate_length(0.001).
Rookie-error checklist: (1) Forgot cable-loss correction. (2) Wrong RBW. (3) No TDD gating on B41. (4) Reference level too low → analyzer compresses → false low reading. (5) Too little averaging. All five produce wrong results that look real.
M08 PRACH — Zadoff-Chu, Ncs/ZCZ/K, detector, timing advance Advanced click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRSTPRACH in one sentence: When a phone wants to join the network, it shouts a special code (Zadoff-Chu preamble) — the base station must hear this code even when the phone is at the cell edge, which is exactly what your sensitivity test verifies.

PRACH — Zadoff-Chu preambles, detection threshold, timing advance

What PRACH is and when it is sent:
PRACH (Physical Random Access Channel) is the UE's first transmission when connecting to the network. The UE sends a PRACH preamble to request access. The gNB must detect this preamble even at very low power — this is your sensitivity test. PRACH uses Zadoff-Chu sequences (length 839 for long preamble, 139 for short) chosen for their perfect correlation properties — a Zadoff-Chu sequence correlated with itself gives a sharp peak, making it easy to detect.
PRACH detector — how detection works:
The RU receives the wideband UL signal and runs a correlator against each of the 64 possible Zadoff-Chu root sequences. If the correlation peak exceeds a threshold (noise floor × peak_multiplier α), a PRACH is declared detected. The threshold α trades off: low α = sensitive (detect weak UEs, but more false alarms), high α = robust (few false alarms, but misses weak UEs). Your DSA sensitivity test verifies that at the stated threshold power, the detection rate exceeds 99%.
Timing Advance — what PRACH timing measures:
When a PRACH is detected, the RU measures the arrival time of the correlation peak. The offset from the expected time = propagation delay from the UE. The gNB sends a Timing Advance command telling the UE to advance its transmission timing by this amount. This ensures UL signals from all UEs arrive at the RU synchronised to within the cyclic prefix window (4.69 μs). TA range: 0 to 667 μs = ~100 km cell radius.
What PRACH is for
PRACH (Physical Random Access Channel) is how a UE first reaches the network with no uplink timing. At power-on, or to re-sync, the UE sends a random-access preamble (a "signature"). The base station detects it and replies with a timing-advance (TA) command — telling the UE how early to transmit so data arrives at exactly the right time.
Preamble structure
Preamble = Cyclic Prefix (CP) + Zadoff-Chu (ZC) sequence + Guard interval
Preamble formats 0–3 differ in CP/sequence/guard lengths — for different cell radii. Format 4 is TDD-only (rides in the UpPTS field of the special subframe). FHGW limitation: only PRACH config index 4, Frame Config 2 / SSF 6.
Zadoff-Chu sequences
ZC sequences have constant amplitude (important — not all amplitude variation means signal content), a single sharp autocorrelation peak, and low cross-correlation. 64 preamble signatures are made from one root by choosing a cyclic shift. The shift granularity is set by Ncs (defines the Zero-Correlation Zone).
Ncs / ZCZ / K trade-off
SettingEffect
ZCZ=1 → K=64, 1 rootSmall allowable delay, no inter-root noise
ZCZ=12 → K=6–7, ~10 rootsLarger allowable delay, higher inter-root noise
Allowable delay per UE = Ncs × FFT_size / 839. Bigger cells need larger allowable delay → more roots → more inter-root noise. This is a fundamental cell-size vs. capacity trade-off.
The PRACH detector (FlexRAN-style)
1. Remove CP → FFT → extract PRACH subcarriers 2. Multiply by conjugate of root ZC (correlation) 3. IFFT → power-delay profile 4. Noise estimator: Noise_est = mean(noise vector from correlation) 5. Peak multiplier: detected if peak / Noise_est exceeds threshold 6. Peak position → timing advance
In RuAuto — test_Rx_PRACH
EXM plays a PRACH IQ waveform (e.g. PRACH_idx158_100MHZ.wfm) into the RU UL port. The test sweeps input power down using binary search or sensitivity (stepped coarse→fine) to find the detection threshold against PRACH_KPI. Output: miss-detection %, false-alarm %, timing advance avg/std, SNR. FHGW KPI: base_dbm (e.g. −87 dBm) + DSA per-band offset.

M09 AAU Architecture — board split, single DPD observation loop, beamforming Advanced click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRSTAAU architecture in one sentence: Your Metro AAU has two boards — a digital board (midBRD) that processes the signal and a radio board (RFFE) that amplifies and transmits it — and four columns (A/B/C/D) each doing this independently so they can steer the beam.

AAU architecture — midBRD, RFFE, board split, 5-band design

5-Band AAU board structure:
Your Metro AAU has two main boards: midBRD (mid-band board) handles B1 (2140 MHz) and B3 (1843 MHz) digital processing, DAC/ADC, and digital beamforming. RFFE boards (RF Front-End) handle the analog RF — PA, LNA, duplexer, BPF — for each column. B8 (900 MHz), B28 (758 MHz) are low-band and handled by a separate LB RFFE. B41 (2545 MHz TDD) shares the mid-band RFFE with B1/B3. The midBRD connects to RFFE via JESD204B high-speed serial interface.
Single DPD observation path — shared between bands:
DPD needs to observe the PA output to adapt. A single observation receiver (ORX) path is shared between B1, B3, and B41 — it cannot observe all bands simultaneously. The DPD engine time-shares the ORX, adapting one band at a time. When you change power on one band, the DPD for that band re-adapts while others hold their last coefficients. This is why individual band power changes take 60s for DPD to re-converge.
4T4R vs 4T2R vs 2T2R — flavour impact:
4T4R: all 4 columns (A/B/C/D) active for TX and RX — full beamforming, best capacity. 4T2R: 4 TX columns but only 2 RX — used for LB (B8/B28) where 2 RX paths are sufficient. 2T2R: reduced mode for lower power operation. The flavour (b1b3, b1b3b41, b1b3b8b28b41) determines which bands are active simultaneously and which columns are used — directly affecting DSA values and RX path counts in the test table.
The board split
BoardRole
FHGW (Xilinx ZU67 RFSoC)Digital: DUC/DDC, power scaling, CFR, DPD, DAC/ADC — the brains. 8 TX + 8 RX.
Mid-boardFiltering, splitting/combining, calibration coupling between FHGW and RFFE.
RFFE (RF Front End)The high-power analog: PAs, LNAs, switches, circulators, antenna feed.
Antenna arrays and beamforming gain
B1/B3/B41: 4-2-2-4 element arrangement (12 elements, 4 columns) → beamforming gain ~+12 dB. B8/B20/B28: 3-3 (6 elements, 2 columns) → beamforming gain ~+6 dB. This is why TRP is 6–12 dB higher than per-PA output power.
Single shared DPD — the calibration observation loop
One shared DPD cannot watch every PA simultaneously. The solution: directional couplers tap each branch, and a switch matrix (SW1…SW25) routes ONE branch at a time to a shared observation receiver (OBS). That OBS feeds the DPD/calibration engine. The same loop runs TX CAL, RX CAL, and OB CAL.
The calibration switches must be absorptive (50Ω at all ports) with isolation >40 dB at 2.7 GHz. If they're not — unused paths leak into the observation path, corrupting the DPD model → ACLR degrades.
Front-end components (from schematics)
ComponentFunction
Doherty PA (carrier + peaking)High-efficiency: main amp + peaking amp that engages on peaks. RENESAS F8410/F84012.
Phase shifter (PE44820DS)0–360° phase control per element — the beamforming knob.
PIN-diode switches (SP4T)Route paths. Must be absorptive, >40 dB isolation.
Directional couplers (10/20/25 dB)Tap power sample for DPD observation and power monitoring.
SAW / BPF filtersBand selection. Your E5071C S21 traces show these.
LT5581 RF power detectorPower monitoring at RF level for levelling/protection.
M09b RFFE TX Block Diagram — B7/B1/B3 three-band TX_A path decoded stage by stage Advanced click to expand▾

RFFE TX path — what each block does and common faults

midBRD to RFFE interface — JESD204B:
The midBRD (digital board) sends IQ samples to the RFFE (analog board) via JESD204B — a high-speed differential serial interface running at 122.88 MSPS per lane. Each band has its own lane pair. If the JESD204B link goes down (clock drift, cable fault on the board-to-board connector), that band loses its TX signal entirely. Symptom: TX power = 0, no ACLR error, just silence. Debug: check JESD lock status register on midBRD.
PA — the highest-risk component on the RFFE:
Each PA is a separate GaN device per band per column. 12 PAs total (3 bands × 4 columns). Common failure modes: (1) Over-temperature: ambient > 55°C causes thermal derating, > 85°C junction causes shutdown. (2) VSWR: bad antenna connection reflects power back into PA — VSWR > 3 triggers protection. (3) Over-current: wrong OVERCURRENT register (default 0xFF = disabled protection — always set correct value). (4) ESD damage from careless connector handling. PA failure = that band/column TX dead, other bands/columns unaffected.
BOB SMA coupler — why −30 dB:
The directional coupler taps a fixed fraction of the main TX signal (−30 dB = 1/1000th of power) and routes it to the BOB SMA port for measurement. The main path continues to the antenna unaffected. At B1 rated power (+43 dBm antenna), BOB SMA = +13 dBm. Add 30 dB attenuator pad: EXA input = −17 dBm. Your rated target at BOB SMA (−16.7 dBm for B1) already accounts for the coupler ratio — so comparing EXA reading to −16.7 dBm target directly gives you the pass/fail without any manual correction.
What the diagram is showing — the big picture
This is the RFFE1_TX_A block diagram — the transmit signal path inside one RFFE (RF Front End) module of your 6-band AAU. The image shows THREE parallel TX chains — one for B7 (blue, top), one for B1 (red, middle), and one for B3 (orange/pink, bottom) — that all combine into a SINGLE antenna port called TX_A. This is multi-band operation on one shared antenna: B7, B1, and B3 TX signals all go out through the same physical antenna connector.
Stage-by-stage explanation — every block in the diagram
StageSymbol in diagramWhat it doesWhy it matters to your testing
TX_B7_A / TX_B1_A / TX_B3_ABlue circle (input)Digital IQ signal from FHGW DAC output, upconverted to RF. This is the starting point — the signal coming FROM the Xilinx RFSoC DAC at the correct carrier frequency.The rated power at the BOB SMA connector is measured HERE (before the RFFE). This is the P_rated in your 4G test plan (e.g. B1 = −16.7 dBm, B3 = −15.7 dBm).
Phase shifter ⊘Circle with diagonal line (⊘)A digitally-controlled phase shifter (e.g. PE44820DS) that sets the transmit phase of this antenna element relative to the others. This is THE beamforming control. By setting different phases across all RFFE elements, the array steers the beam in a chosen direction.When phase is equal across all elements → beam goes straight ahead. When phase is swept across elements → beam tilts. Phase calibration is what the OB_CAL (observation calibration) measures. If phase is wrong → no beamforming gain → TRP fails.
BPF 5×BW ≋Wavy box labeled 5×BWBandpass filter with bandwidth = 5 times the channel bandwidth. For 10 MHz LTE: BPF BW ≈ 50 MHz. This removes DAC images (mirror signals at harmonics of the sampling rate), out-of-band noise, and LO harmonics BEFORE they are amplified by the PA. Much cheaper to filter here at low power than after the PA.If this filter is degraded (insertion loss too high → output power drops). VNA S21 measurement of this filter should show <1 dB IL in passband, >30 dB rejection at image frequency. This is what your E5071C S21 traces show for these filters.
V ATT (Variable Attenuator) ∿Box with waveform symbolA voltage-controlled (PIN diode or GaAs) attenuator that provides adjustable gain/loss BEFORE the driver amplifier. This is the fine power control: sets the exact output power level by controlling how much signal reaches the PA. Also used for dynamic Vdd power optimization — at low load, reduce drive level AND reduce Vdd.The V ATT is what the DL power_monitor sees changes when you modify DAC current or gain registers. If V ATT is stuck at maximum attenuation → no TX output. At minimum attenuation → risk of PA overdrive → ACLR fails.
Pre-driver ▷Triangle (amplifier symbol)A driver amplifier (small-signal linear amp, Class A) that boosts the signal from the V ATT to the input level required by the main PA. Provides ~15–20 dB gain. Must be very linear — any distortion here is further amplified by the PA and corrupts EVM/ACLR.Pre-driver NF is not critical (signal is already strong). Pre-driver linearity IS critical — its IIP3 must be high enough that it stays linear even at peak PAPR moments. If pre-driver compresses → EVM fails even with perfect DPD on the PA.
PA (Power Amplifier) ▷▷Large double triangle (green border)The GaN Doherty PA (RENESAS F8410/F84012). Carrier amp + peaking amp. Amplifies the signal from pre-driver output (~+5 dBm) to the final output power (+40+ dBm). This is where 95% of the DC power is consumed. DPD corrects its nonlinearity.This is the most tested block. Your PA efficiency test plan (PPT2) measures drain efficiency here. ACLR test (6.6.2) verifies DPD is correcting its nonlinearity. Temperature sensor monitors its junction temperature. Dynamic Vdd (40→32→25V) is applied to this block.
Directional coupler □Rectangular box after PAA 4-port device that taps a small fraction (e.g. −20 dB) of the PA output power into the observation path, while passing the main signal through with minimal loss (~0.1–0.3 dB). The tapped signal goes to the DPD observation receiver (OBS) to update the DPD model.If the coupler is lossy → DPD observation power is wrong → DPD model diverges → ACLR suddenly degrades. If the observation switch matrix (SW1–SW25) selects the wrong coupler → DPD is modeling the wrong PA → all ACLR measurements degrade on that branch.
Circulator ◎Circle with arrowA 3-port passive ferrite device that routes RF power in ONE direction only: PA output → antenna (forward), antenna → load/RX path (reverse). It provides ~20 dB of TX-to-RX isolation AND protects the PA from reflected power. If the antenna has poor VSWR (cable disconnect, damaged connector), the reflected power goes to the circulator dump port, NOT back into the PA.CRITICAL for PA protection. If the circulator fails or is removed → any cable disconnect sends 100% reflected power back into the PA → PA damage. The VSWR trip protection works WITH the circulator. When you see PA protection events during testing → check circulators first.
Band-specific TX filter ≋ (B7/B1/B3)Wavy box after circulatorEach band has its own post-PA bandpass filter. B7 filter passes 2500–2570 MHz, rejects everything else. B1 filter passes 2110–2170 MHz, rejects everything. B3 filter passes 1805–1880 MHz, rejects everything. These suppress PA harmonics and intermodulation products that would otherwise appear in the SEM measurement.SEM test (6.6.3) directly measures what comes through here. If a TX filter is degraded → spurious emissions appear in the SEM → test fails. Your VNA E5071C S21 measurements characterise these filters. The S21 passband loss is what you de-embed in your cable_loss.json corrections.
Diplexer / Triplexer ┤├Double vertical bars (purple border)Combines the three filtered TX signals (B7 + B1 + B3) from separate paths into a SINGLE wideband output. A diplexer combines 2 bands; a triplexer combines 3. Uses reactive (LC/ceramic) filtering to pass each band on its path while blocking the other bands.Insertion loss here is in the TX path — affects output power. Cross-band isolation determines whether B7 TX power leaks into the B1 or B3 path (and vice versa). If isolation is poor → inter-band intermodulation → new spurious emissions at f_B7 ± f_B1 frequencies → fails spurious test.
Final filter + TX_A outputFilter box → green circleA final cleanup filter and the physical antenna port TX_A. This is the antenna connector where all three band signals emerge combined. The TX_A label corresponds to Antenna A — your RFFE has multiple antenna ports (A, B, C, D) for the full beamforming array.THIS is where your VNA measures cable loss (S11 return loss at this port). And where the EXM or EXA connects via attenuator pad for ACLR and power measurements. All power readings must be de-embedded back to this port.
The dashed vertical lines in the diagram — what they mark
The green and red dashed vertical lines mark functional boundaries within the RFFE board. The green dashed line separates the low-power section (phase shifter, BPF, V ATT, pre-driver) from the high-power section (PA, coupler, circulator). The red dashed line marks where the DPD observation tap exits. These boundaries matter for troubleshooting — a fault on the left of green = digital/control issue, fault between green and red = PA drive level issue, fault on the right of red = filtering/combining issue.
Single DPD architecture — one observer for three PAs
Notice the diagram shows THREE separate PAs (one per band) but the coupler taps all three. The single DPD block on the FHGW cannot observe all three simultaneously — the switch matrix (SW1–SW25) routes one band at a time to the shared observation receiver. DPD adapts the model for B7 PA, then switches to B1 PA, then B3 PA, cycling through them. This is the "single DPD" architecture referenced in the original AAU block diagram document (1.6m 6 AAU Block Diagram_B1B3 single DPD V0.2.vsdx).
What a power measurement failure tells you about which stage is faulty
Measurement failureLikely faulty stageHow to confirm
Output power low on all 3 bands on this antennaDiplexer/triplexer or final filter — common to all three pathsCheck each band individually. If all three are equally low → common path fault.
Output power low on B1 only, B7 and B3 OKB1 TX chain specific: V ATT, pre-driver, PA, circulator, or B1 band filterCheck power_monitor DL for B1 specifically. If digital power OK → analog fault between DAC output and antenna.
ACLR fails on B3 onlyB3 DPD model diverged, or B3 PA compression, or B3 coupler not routing to observationCheck DPD Gain Register PreCheck for B3. Force DPD re-adaptation. Check switch matrix routing.
All bands fail ACLR suddenlyObservation path fault — DPD cannot adapt any PACheck coupler observation output. Check switch matrix for stuck position. Check OBS receiver path in FHGW.
SEM fails — spur at B1+B3 frequencyDiplexer cross-isolation degraded → inter-band IM productCheck diplexer isolation with VNA. Replace if isolation <40 dB.
PA protection trips on B1High VSWR on B1 path — circulator seeing reflected powerCheck antenna connector and cable. Measure S11 at TX_A port with VNA. Should be <−10 dB.
Connection to your real test work
When you run test_Tx_BS_Output_Power on the B1 port — you are measuring the signal at TX_A after it has passed through ALL the stages above: Phase shifter → BPF → V ATT → Pre-driver → PA → Coupler → Circulator → B1 filter → Diplexer → Final filter → TX_A. Any one of those stages can cause the test to fail. The block diagram is your fault-isolation roadmap.
The power budget through the RFFE: enter at ~−16.7 dBm (FHGW BOB) → phase shifter ~0 dB → BPF ~−0.5 dB → V ATT ~−3 dB (variable) → pre-driver ~+18 dB → PA ~+40 dB → coupler ~−0.2 dB → circulator ~−0.3 dB → TX filter ~−0.5 dB → diplexer ~−0.5 dB → TX_A ≈ +37 to +42 dBm. That is your TRP/EIRP starting point before beamforming gain.
M09c FHGW DL Chain — LowPHY → DFE → DAC with real register values and power taps Advanced click to expand▾

FHGW DL processing chain — what each block does

BFP decompression — restoring full IQ precision:
The DU compresses IQ samples before sending over eCPRI: 16-bit samples → 9-bit mantissa + 4-bit shared exponent per resource block. The FHGW must exactly reverse this. BFP expansion error corrupts IQ amplitudes by powers of 2 → RSSI steps of 6 dB, EVM degradation, PRACH detection failures. If you see unexplained 6 dB RSSI jumps between columns, suspect BFP — check FHGW firmware version and eCPRI error counters.
CFR and DPD — the two linearisation stages:
CFR (Crest Factor Reduction) clips signal peaks above a threshold, then filters to restore spectral shape. Reduces PAPR from 12 dB to ~8 dB. Aggressive CFR improves PA efficiency but degrades EVM. Too much clipping = EVM failure even before the PA.

DPD (Digital Pre-Distortion) applies the inverse of the PA's nonlinearity. The PA then "un-distorts" back to linear. DPD learns the PA's behaviour via the ORX observation path. If DPD diverges (coefficients go unstable): ACLR suddenly worsens by 10–15 dB. Check DPD_STATUS register. Re-enable to force re-convergence.
DFE — Digital Front End:
DFE performs interpolation (upsampling from symbol rate to DAC rate) and frequency shifting (moving the baseband signal to the correct IF frequency before DAC). A DFE configuration error puts the signal at the wrong frequency → TX power at correct band is zero, but a spurious signal appears elsewhere. Check DFE_FREQ_OFFSET register if TX power is missing but no fault is logged.
What this diagram shows — the complete FHGW DL signal path
This is the most important internal diagram of your FHGW. It shows the complete digital downlink chain from the DU IQ input all the way to the DAC output, with REAL power level readings at every measurement tap and REAL register values for every gain/CFR stage. This is what David Bekker uses to explain where power goes and why ACLR passes or fails.
The two sections — LowPHY and DFE

DFE (blue background)Gain → CFR → Gain → DPD → Gain Per Channel → DAC. This is the Digital Front End — linearisation and scaling before the analog domain.FHGW firmware registers. Controlled via SSH CLI or NETCONF. Your PreChecks verify these.

DPDRegister: 0xb02900XX
Value: 0x161		Digital Pre-Distortion applies the inverse of the PA nonlinearity. The model is a look-up table (LUT) or polynomial indexed by instantaneous IQ amplitude. DPD is adaptive — it continuously updates its model via the observation (coupler → OBS receiver) path.After DPD: power = −12 dBFs. CFR and PAPR — the most misunderstood part of this diagram
People expect power to DROP through every stage (gain < 0). But notice: power RISES from −15.2 dBFs to −8.8 dBFs across the CFR block (+6.4 dB). This seems impossible — the CFR is supposed to clip peaks, not add power. Here is what actually happens:
An OFDM signal has high PAPR. The average power is low but the peaks are high. When you clip the peaks, you remove the energy in those peaks — but the average power calculation is dominated by how often each amplitude occurs. CFR clips just the rare high peaks, but their removal means the waveform can now run at a higher average power without clipping the ADC/DAC. In practice: after CFR, the entire waveform is scaled UP so the clipped peaks sit at the DAC full-scale limit. The average power rises because the distribution is now less peak-heavy. The PAPR goes from ~11 dB to 8.3 dB — meaning the signal is now 8.3 dB more "compact" — and this compactness is the gain.
The CFR threshold = 8.3 means clip everything above 8.3/10 = 83% of full scale. wcfr_threshold = 8.5 is the wide-CFR threshold — a second pass that clips wider peaks. filter_length = 511 is the FIR smoother length — longer = better spectral containment but more latency. These values are tuned so EVM stays within 3GPP limits (clipping adds EVM) while ACLR also passes (too little clipping = PA runs too backed-off = inefficient, too much = spectral splatter).
