The B28 power deficit — exactly what happened
Your open investigation: B28 shows ~3 dB output power deficit between firmware builds. Looking at this diagram: the most likely cause is a change to the DAC Output Scale register (DAC Current value). The diagram shows DAC Current [28318] = −2.87 dB. If a firmware update accidentally changed [28318] to a lower value (e.g. 20000 → different dB offset), the output power drops by exactly that difference. PWK confirmed it was a DAC setting change between builds. The fix: restore the correct DAC current register value for B28 on the affected firmware build.
Never change DAC current registers without first noting the current value and verifying output power against P_rated. A 1-register change here affects every test: Tx power, ACLR, EVM, SEM — all measured relative to the expected output power level.

Reading real lab screenshots — EXM ACP and Modulation Analysis

EXA ACP display — field by field:
The ACP (Adjacent Channel Power) screen shows: Main channel power = your TX output (should match rated target ±1 dB). Adj channel = power at ±1 channel offset — this is ACLR. Alt channel = power at ±2 channels — stricter limit. Channel bars = blue = main, orange = adjacent, red = limit exceeded. If any bar is red: FAIL. Most common cause: DPD not converged (measured too soon after TX enable). Wait 60 seconds and re-measure.
Modulation Analysis constellation — what each shape means:
Tight grid of clusters: excellent — all symbols hitting their targets. Fuzzy/spread clusters: phase noise (LO) or SNR too low. Clusters offset from origin: DC offset / LO leakage. Clusters compressed along one axis: IQ amplitude imbalance. Grid rotated: IQ phase imbalance. All clusters compressed inward: PA compression — DPD not working. Asymmetric spread on one side: memory effect in PA (DPD model order too low).
EVM percentage — reading the number:
EVM is shown as a percentage. Lower = better. Limits: QPSK < 17.5%, 16QAM < 12.5%, 64QAM < 8%, 256QAM < 3.5%. An EVM of 2.5% on 64QAM is excellent. An EVM of 9% on 64QAM is a fail. If EVM is near the limit: first check DPD convergence. Then check LO phase noise spec on EXA (set IF bandwidth appropriately — too wide IFBW degrades EVM measurement accuracy).

What the spectrum display shows
The blue filled shape in the centre is the 10 MHz LTE B28 DL carrier at 780.5 MHz. The yellow trace is the noise floor of the measurement. The green trace is the averaged spectrum. The red horizontal lines are the limit lines. The four ACP channel windows (Lower B, Lower A, Carrier, Upper A, Upper B) are marked by the vertical dashed lines. The dBc labels (0.0 dBc, 0.1 dBc, 0.0 dBc, 0.0 dBc) at the top of each window confirm that every adjacent channel is at essentially 0 dBc — pure noise floor, no real PA distortion products. This is expected at −35 dBm (very low power — well below where PA nonlinearity matters).
Key learning: ACLR is only meaningful when the PA is operating near its normal output power. At −35 dBm (7.9 dB below B28 P_rated of −27.3 dBm), the PA is deeply backed off and perfectly linear — no DPD even needed. For a real ACLR conformance test, you would run this at full P_rated and expect to see −45 to −60 dBc in the adjacent windows, NOT 0 dBc.

Constellation diagram — what you are seeing
The top-left quadrant shows the OFDM constellation (Layer 0, CC0). You can see 4 clusters corresponding to QPSK (4 constellation points). But the clusters are very large and spread — EVM ~9.7%. Ideal QPSK at this power should have tight clusters (EVM <2%). The spread is caused by the ADC overrange in the EXM. The blue dots in the centre are pilot/reference signal symbols that have different power from data symbols. The red scattered dots are data symbols smeared by the measurement fault.
Error Vector Spectrum — what you are seeing
Top-right quadrant shows EVM per subcarrier (−300 to +300 carriers, 601 total for 10 MHz LTE). The white line is the average EVM per subcarrier. You can see EVM is roughly uniform across all subcarriers at ~10% with spikes reaching 32% on individual subcarriers. Uniform EVM across frequency = NOT a filter notch or cable multipath (those cause frequency-selective EVM). Uniform = noise source or ADC clipping — consistent with the overrange fault.
🔧 How to fix this for next time
Problem: Channel Power = 48.333 dBm, Ext Gain = −56 dB → signal at EXM input = −7.667 dBm. EXM Range = 55 dBm is the reference level but the internal attenuator setting (10 dB shown in Screenshot 1) was not correctly applied here. The EXM ADC is overranging.

Fix option 1: Increase external attenuation (add 10–20 dB pad between PA output and EXM). This is the safest — never let the EXM input exceed its rated maximum.
Fix option 2: In EXM → AMPTD → RF Range → increase to 65 or 70 dBm to tell the instrument to expect a stronger signal.
Fix option 3: EXM → AMPTD → Atten → increase internal attenuation from 10 dB to 30 dB.
Quick check: Always verify STATUS bar shows no red errors before accepting EVM results. "ADC over range" = measurement is invalid.

ACLR margin analysis — is 46.45 dBc comfortable?
The 3GPP E-UTRA ACLR limit is 45 dBc. Your measurement is 46.45 dBc — only 1.45 dB of margin. PW internal gate is typically 54 dBc (tighter). So this full-power reading is borderline for the PW gate even though it passes 3GPP. Possible causes of marginal ACLR at B28:
B28 (700 MHz band) has wider DPD bandwidth requirements — the PA nonlinearity at 780 MHz may have different memory characteristics than B1/B3 at 2 GHz
The ~3 dB B28 power deficit (your open investigation) suggests the PA may be operating at a different point than intended — if DAC current was changed, DPD model may not match current operating point
Check: was DPD re-adapted after any power or firmware change? DPD model is valid only for the operating point it was trained on
B28 PA (RENESAS or equivalent at 700 MHz) has higher memory effects due to lower frequency — longer DPD filter taps may be needed
When ACLR is borderline: reduce TX power by 1 dB and re-measure. If ACLR improves significantly (3+ dB) → PA compression. If ACLR barely changes → DPD model mismatch or memory effects. The response shape tells you the root cause.

PLAIN ENGLISH FIRSTLab practice in one sentence: Before every test session, you verify three things — that your cable loss is measured, your EXM output is accurate, and your DPD has converged — because 3 out of 4 test failures are caused by setup errors, not hardware faults.

Real lab screenshots — EXM ACP, Modulation Analysis decoded

Reading the EXM ACP screenshot:
ACP (Adjacent Channel Power) display on EXM shows: centre channel power (your rated output), adjacent channel power at ±offset frequency, alternate channel at ±2× offset. The ratios between adjacent and centre are ACLR values. Red bars exceeding the mask = FAIL. Vertical axis: power in dBm. Pass criterion: adjacent channel ≥ 45 dB below centre. Check: is DPD converged? Is measurement BW correct for your channel BW?
Reading the Modulation Analysis (constellation) display:
EVM display shows IQ constellation plot. Good result: tight clusters at each QAM point, all within the decision boundary. Problems: Spread clusters = phase noise (LO quality). Clusters offset from grid = DC offset (LO leakage). One axis compressed = IQ amplitude imbalance. Rotated grid = IQ phase imbalance. All points compressed inward = PA compression. Each fault pattern gives different constellation shape — learn to read them.
EXM screenshot — what each field means:
Carrier freq: your configured DL centre frequency. Output power: measured conducted output (before coupler loss). EVM rms: overall modulation quality (pass < 8% for 64QAM). EVM peak: worst single symbol (pass < 24% for 64QAM). Freq error: carrier offset from programmed frequency. Symbol rate: confirms correct FRC loaded. CRC: pass/fail on PBCH decode (if measuring DL reference signals).

FHGW DL chain — LowPHY, DFE, DAC, register map

FHGW DL processing chain:
eCPRI receive → BFP decompression (9-bit mantissa + 4-bit exponent → 16-bit IQ) → resource mapping → IFFT (1024/2048 point per BW) → cyclic prefix insertion → CFR (clip + filter, PAPR target 8 dB) → DPD (pre-distortion lookup + adaptation) → DFE (digital front-end: half-band filter, interpolation, frequency shift) → DAC interface (JESD204B) → DAC → analog path.
Key register map locations:
DPD coefficients: FHGW memory map 0x4000_0000 (DPD_COEF base). Read via: fhgw_read 0x40000000. CFR threshold: CFR_THRESH register. PAPR limit: CFR_CLIP_LEVEL. DPD enable: DPD_ENABLE_B1/B3/B41. DAC scale: DAC_SCALE per band → sets digital gain before DAC → directly affects output power. Incorrect DAC_SCALE causes TX power wrong by fixed offset independent of TX_GAIN calibration.
DPD observation path — how the feedback loop works:
A small portion of the PA output is tapped by the coupler and routed back to an observation ADC (ORX) on the FHGW. The ORX digitises this sample. DPD engine compares: ideal (DPD input) vs actual (ORX sample). Computes error and updates LUT (Look-Up Table) coefficients. Convergence: error < 1% = converged. Indicators: DPD_STATUS register bit, ACLR improvement from −30 dBc to < −45 dBc.

RFFE TX block diagram — B1/B3 three-band TX_A path

RFFE TX_A path structure (B1/B3/B41):
TX_A path handles Column A for all mid-band frequencies. Signal enters from FHGW DAC per band (B1 and B3 at different times or different IQ streams). Band selection switch routes to the correct PA driver and PA for each band. B1 PA and B3 PA are separate devices — different frequency response. B41 may share B1 PA hardware with band-specific matching network. RFFE board connects to midBRD via JESD204B high-speed differential interface.
Key RFFE control registers:
TX_GAIN per band per column: digital attenuator setting → sets output power. Written from tx_calibration_eeprom.json at boot. PA_BIAS per band: gate voltage setting → sets PA operating class and efficiency. PE44820DS: phase shifter per column → beamforming angle. RFFE_ENABLE per band: enables/disables RF path. All controlled via SPI bus from midBRD FPGA. CLI command: rffe_read/rffe_write for debug access.
Common RFFE faults in your work:
RFFE2 LB fault: Low-band RFFE (B8/B28) JTAG re-flash required when RFFE control firmware corrupted. Symptoms: B8/B28 fail to enable, fault code logged. Fix: 5-pin JTAG connector on RFFE2 board, flash via OpenOCD. Over-current fault: TX_OVERCURRENT register set to wrong value (default 0xFF = no protection). Correct per-band spec in register. See B3/B1 overcurrent discrepancy found by Dileep.

Lab measurement practice — bench setup, instrument connections, test checklist

Standard bench setup for RCT:
EXM (E6640A) → SMA cable → RU BOB SMA port (UL inject). EXA (N9010B) → 30dB pad → SMA cable → RU BOB SMA port (DL measure). VNA (E5071C) → calibrated cable → RU BOB SMA (phase cal). All instruments connected to lab LAN (10.62.2.x subnet). EXM IP: check front panel. EXA IP: 10.62.2.135. RU connected to FHGW via Ethernet. FHGW connected to BBU/DU. GPS/PTP sync to DU for TDD bands.
Pre-measurement checklist (do before every test session):
□ Measure cable loss with VNA → note value per cable
□ Verify EXM output power with EXA before injection
□ Check RU is fully booted and all bands enabled
□ Confirm DPD converged (wait 60s after TX enable)
□ Set EXA preamp OFF for TX measurements, ON for RX
□ Verify GPS/PTP lock for TDD (B41) tests
□ Check connector torque with torque wrench (SMA: 0.9 N·m)
□ Confirm tc_cadence.json has correct DSA values loaded
Instrument IP and SCPI port:
All Keysight instruments listen on TCP port 5025 for SCPI commands. Connect via socket: socket.connect((ip, 5025)). Send: s.send(b"*RST\n"). Query: s.send(b"*IDN?\n"); s.recv(1024). EXA centre freq: ":FREQ:CENT 2.14e9\n". EXM output power: ":POW:AMPL -95\n". EXM RF on: ":OUTP ON\n". RuAuto handles all this automatically via tc_cadence.json.
Instrument roles
InstrumentRole

VNA E5071CReturn loss / VSWR and cable-loss characterisation. S21 for filters and cables.

The pitfalls that catch every new engineer
1. Forgetting cable-loss / de-embedding — every power number is wrong without it.
2. Overloading the analyzer — reference level too low → compression → false low reading.
3. Wrong RBW, or no TDD gating on B41.
4. Loose/dirty connectors — torque to spec, inspect with magnifier, keep caps on.
5. Keying a PA into an open/short port — VSWR trip → PA damage.
6. Not waiting for DPD to converge after power change before taking measurements.
M11 PA Efficiency & Power Optimization — Dynamic Vdd, gate bias, sequencing Advanced click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRSTPA efficiency in one sentence: The PA converts DC electricity into RF — but only 35% becomes useful signal; the rest becomes heat. Dynamic Vdd reduces this heat by lowering the supply voltage when the signal is quiet, just like dimming a light when you don't need full brightness.

PA efficiency — Dynamic Vdd, class AB, gate bias, power optimisation

PA efficiency classes — why Class AB:
Class A: always on, linear, efficiency ~30% max. Class B: on for half cycle, efficient ~78% max, but nonlinear crossover distortion. Class AB: compromise — on for slightly more than half cycle, efficiency ~35–45% with DPD linearisation. Class F: resonant load, theoretical ~90% but very narrowband. Your GaN PA operates Class AB — DPD handles the nonlinearity, and ~35% efficiency is acceptable for the power levels involved.
Dynamic Vdd — what it does and why it matters:
Dynamic Vdd (supply modulation) changes the PA drain voltage in proportion to the instantaneous signal envelope. For low-amplitude OFDM symbols, Vdd drops → less power wasted as heat. For high-amplitude peaks, Vdd rises → PA stays linear. This improves average efficiency from ~35% to ~50%+ for OFDM signals with their high PAPR. Your AAU has Dynamic Vdd implemented per column — the staircase supply voltage tracks the signal envelope in steps. The step size and timing are in the PA configuration registers.
Thermal management — why temperature monitoring matters:
GaN PA junction temperature limit: typically 150–200°C. At 20W output and 35% efficiency, each PA dissipates ~37W of heat. With 4 columns = 148W of heat generation inside the AAU enclosure. The thermal protection system monitors junction temperature via diode sensors and reduces power or shuts down if temp exceeds threshold. In your RCT: PA_PROTECTION fault typically triggers at 85–95°C junction. Check ambient temp and heatsink contact if PA protection fires repeatedly.
The efficiency problem
A macro PA can burn hundreds of watts. Drain efficiency = RF power out / DC power in. A PA is MOST efficient near saturation and LEAST efficient when backed off. But OFDM PAPR forces back-off. So at low traffic the PA sits deep in back-off, wasting power.
Dynamic Vdd — the core solution
Instead of one fixed drain voltage (Vdd) for all conditions, lower Vdd as traffic (RB occupancy) falls. Less Vdd at low load = efficiency peak moves to the backed-off operating point = less wasted power.
Load (occupancy)B1/B3 VddB8/B28 VddB41 Vdd
100% (full load)40 V~48 V~45 V
50% (busy hour)32 V (Vdd_Low1)——
≤30% (medium)25 V (Vdd_Low2)——
What you must re-tune when lowering Vdd
Lowering Vdd changes PA behaviour. You must re-tune: (1) CFR working point — pre-CFR gain register 0xb0290000: 0xD7 for occupancy > 50%, 0x128 for ≤ 50%. (2) Output power via DAC current. ACLR/EVM must stay within spec throughout the transition.
Transition order is critical: when load DROPS → lower Vdd AFTER occupancy has dropped (not before — you'd clip at the new Vdd). When load RISES → raise Vdd BEFORE occupancy increases (not after — the signal would clip at the old low Vdd).
Gate bias (Vgg) — second lever
The gate bias Vgg3_p (tested at −6.5 V datasheet, −5.5 V, −4.5 V) trades quiescent current for linearity. Adjusting Vgg adds further power savings especially when Vdd is already below nominal.
Safe PA bias sequencing (RENESAS)
GaN PA (RENESAS F8410/F84012) has drain rail (VDD) and gate rails (VGG1/2/3). Enabled by AND of TX_EN and MC_EN. Bias must follow the RENESAS sequence to avoid device damage. Even fully OFF: draws ~108 mA from VDD1 + ~1 mA leakage.
M12 Reading the RCT Config — tc_cadence, Group-IDs, Test-IDs, KPI limits Advanced click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRSTtc_cadence.json in one sentence: This is the master test script — it tells RuAuto what band to test, what power to inject, what limits to check, and what to measure, so every test runs the same way every time without manual setup.

tc_cadence.json — how the RCT config drives all tests

tc_cadence.json structure:
tc_cadence.json is the master config that tells RuAuto exactly what to test and what limits to apply. Structure: Group-IDs group related tests (e.g. TX_POWER, ACLR, RSSI_CAL). Each group contains Test-IDs (individual test cases). Each test has: band, BW, FRC/modulation, injection power (= base + DSA), pass/fail limits, measurement instrument, number of averages. RuAuto reads this file at startup and executes all enabled tests in order.
How DSA appears in tc_cadence.json:
For sensitivity tests: injection_power = base_power + DSA_offset. Example B1 entry: {"band":"B1","BW":"10M","FRC":"A1","injection_dBm":-87.0,"DSA_offset":5.0,"limit_BLER":0.05}. RuAuto computes: EXM_power = injection_dBm + DSA_offset = −87 + 5 = −82 dBm. This is sent to EXM. The test waits for PRACH detection rate and compares to the BLER limit.
Group-IDs and Test-IDs — how to navigate failures:
When RuAuto reports a failure, it includes Group-ID and Test-ID. Group_TX_POWER > Test_B1_10M = TX power test for B1 at 10 MHz failed. Group_RSSI > Test_B3_Ch2 = RSSI calibration failed on B3 ADC channel 2. This tells you exactly which band, which BW, which measurement, and which column/ADC channel to investigate. The log file (rct_results.json) stores all results with timestamps for post-analysis.
Tests are DATA, not code
In RuAuto you almost never write a new test in Python. A test is a generic method driven by JSON. To "write" or change a test you edit the config. Reading the config IS reading the test.
The 4-layer lookup chain
LayerFileContains
1. Entry INIsetup.ini / setup_conf.iniLists which JSON files to load for each section
2. tc_cadence.jsonTest-IDs + Group-IDs + Cadence-IDsPer-test parameters, scheduling, P0/P1/P2 selection
3. fdd/tdd_test_setup.jsonDUT configurationIPs, bands, antenna-to-RFIO mapping
4. FHGW_Box_kpi_thresholds.jsonPass/fail limitsKPI numbers with 3GPP references
Real ACLR Test-ID (from your tc_cadence.json)
"test_Tx_ACLR": { "tm": "1.1", // E-TM test model 1.1 (QPSK, all RBs) "test_type": "ACP", // → SCPI sa_set_ACP_mode "prb": "273", // full carrier loaded "trb": "1", // transceiver index "test_duration": "960000", // microseconds — long for ACLR dwell "sample_time": "3", // average 3 samples "KPIs": { "aclr_kpi": 54, "aclr_kpi_tolerance": 1 } }
Real Group-ID and Cadence-ID
"TS_DL_CI": { "IsDL": true, "band": "n78", "frequency": ["M"], "BW": ["40"], "SCS": "30", "tm": ["1.1"], "ext_trig_delay": "0.00998675", "Tests": ["test_Tx_BS_Output_Power", "test_Tx_modulation_analysis", "test_Tx_ACLR"] } "P0": ["TS_DL_CI", "TS_UL_CI"]
4G vs 5G structural difference
4G Test-IDs are THIN — just a filter (e.g. frequency: [fm], etm: [1.1]) and the KPI number lives in the threshold file.
5G Test-IDs are FAT — each carries test_type, prb, test_duration, AND an inline KPIs block. For 4G: read the threshold file for limits. For 5G: read tc_cadence.json.
M13 RU Features & Operations — uSleep, PA protection, RSSI accuracy, IQ playback Advanced click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRSTRU features in one sentence: uSleep turns the PA off when no users are connected (saves 70% power), PA protection shuts it down if it gets too hot, and IQ playback records what the RU received so you can replay it later for debugging.
1. uSleep (Micro-Sleep)

RU features — uSleep, PA protection, RSSI, IQ playback, DPD

uSleep — low power idle mode:
uSleep suspends RF chain when no UEs are scheduled. PA bias switches off → power consumption drops ~70%. Wakeup latency: <1 ms (fast enough for any LTE subframe). Trigger: scheduler indicates no DL allocations for N consecutive subframes. Config: USLEEP_THRESHOLD_N in RU config. During RCT: uSleep must be disabled or the EXM injection during "idle" subframes will not be received. Check: USLEEP_ENABLE = 0 in test mode.
PA protection — thermal, VSWR, over-current:
Thermal: TJ sensor monitors PA junction temp. Warning at 80°C, shutdown at 95°C. Recovery: auto when temp drops 10°C below threshold. VSWR: reflected power detector triggers if VSWR > 3.0 (10% reflected). Reduces power to protect PA from load mismatch. Over-current: PA drain current monitored. If > OVERCURRENT_THRESHOLD register: immediate PA disable. Default register 0xFF = no protection — set correct value per band per PA spec.
IQ playback — what it is and when to use:
IQ playback captures raw ADC samples (IQ data) from the RX chain and stores them in memory. Used to: replay a received signal for offline processing, debug PRACH detection algorithm without live UE, verify RX chain IQ integrity. CLI: iq_capture --band B1 --duration 10ms → saves IQ.bin. Replay with iq_playback command. Useful for debugging intermittent PRACH detection failures — capture the signal around the failure event and replay at leisure.
What uSleep is: PA (biggest power consumer, 40–200W) switches OFF during empty OFDM symbols. At low traffic, 60–80% of symbols may be empty → proportional power saving. Finer-grained than Dynamic Vdd (per-symbol vs per-subframe).
Failure: EVM spikes on symbol 0 after sleep but OK on symbol 1+ → PA bias slow to ramp. Check RENESAS gate bias sequencing registers.
2. Reduced Carrier Output Power
How it works: Lower the DAC current register or V ATT in RFFE. PA backs off → naturally more linear → ACLR/EVM improve. But efficiency drops (PA wastes more power as heat per useful watt out). Always wait 60s after power change for DPD to re-adapt before measuring ACLR.
3. RU Capabilities
4. Tilt (Electrical Beam Tilt)
5. RSSI Accuracy
6. IQ Playback and Recording
7. Variable Load Tests (DPD)
8. Dynamic Range
9. PA Protection
10. PA Shutdown Process
Key rule: Startup and shutdown are mirror images. Startup: Vdd ON first → then Vgg ON. Shutdown: Vgg OFF first → then Vdd OFF. Always check get_faults after shutdown — should return empty for a clean sequence.

M14 RSSI & Receive Chain — dBFS vs dBm, ADC calibration, dynamic range results Advanced click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRSTRSSI in one sentence: RSSI is the radio's report of how strong a signal it received — but the raw number is in ADC counts (dBFS), and you need a calibration constant (ADC_ADJUST) to convert it to the real-world power in dBm that you can compare to your EXM injection.

RSSI and receive chain — dBFS to dBm, ADC calibration, dynamic range

dBFS to dBm conversion — the complete path:
get_rssi N → returns value in dBFS (e.g. −12.5 dBFS). ADC_ADJUST stored in hardware.json per band per ADC channel. Conversion: P_dBm = dBFS + ADC_ADJUST. If ADC_ADJUST_B1_ADC0 = −85: P_dBm = −12.5 + (−85) = −97.5 dBm at RU antenna port. This matches EXM injected −95 dBm minus cable loss −2.5 dB = −97.5 dBm. Agreement within ±1 dB = calibration good.
ADC channel mapping — which command reads which path:
B1 Column A → ADC channel 0 → get_rssi 0
B1 Column B → ADC channel 1 → get_rssi 1
B1 Column C → ADC channel 4 → get_rssi 4
B1 Column D → ADC channel 5 → get_rssi 5
B3 Column A → ADC channel 2 → get_rssi 2
B3 Column B → ADC channel 3 → get_rssi 3
B3 Column C → ADC channel 6 → get_rssi 6
B3 Column D → ADC channel 7 → get_rssi 7
B8/B28 use 2 paths (A and B only) with separate ADC_ADJUST values.
RSSI failures — diagnosis by which number is wrong:
All three (EXM, CLI, DU) off → EXM not calibrated, or cable loss not subtracted.
CLI wrong, DU correct → ADC_ADJUST wrong for that channel.
CLI correct, DU wrong → FHGW processing chain issue.
One column CLI wrong, others correct → hardware fault on that column (LNA, cable, connector).
All columns drift same direction as unit warms → temperature compensation not configured.
The real RSSI calibration method
Inject a CW tone at band centre at 3 known power levels (e.g. −40.5, −60.5, −70.5 dBm). Read RSSI at each. Fit an approximate straight line. Compute the average offset. Write that offset per-ADC into /etc/configs/hardware.json (the ADC_ADJUST vector — one entry per ADC 0–7). Then automation sweeps the input over [−40 dBm : 1 dB : −120 dBm] and records corrected RSSI.
Band-to-ADC mapping (real hardware)
B1 uses ADCs 0, 1, 4, 5. B3 uses ADCs 2, 3, 6, 7. Each ADC is calibrated separately with its own ADC_ADJUST offset. This is why get_rssi returns 8 values — one per ADC, and which one matters depends on your band and flavor.
Real RSSI accuracy results
ADCBandADC RMS at sensitivity point (dBFS)2 dB error margin (dBm)
0B1−44.9−95.5
2B3−43.3−93.5
Per-antenna results ranged ~−76 to −90 dBm for the 2 dB error margin. The spread across ADCs/antennas is exactly why each ADC gets its own offset — a single global offset would be wrong for some.

M15 UL RCT Embedded & Dynamic Test — ul-rct-test, 4-stage pipeline, real results Expert click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRSTUL RCT in one sentence: The uplink RCT test injects a known signal from the EXM into the RU receive port and checks that the RU correctly reports the signal power — if it reports wrong, something is wrong with the receive chain or calibration.

UL RCT test — ul-rct-test pipeline, 4-stage process, what it verifies

What the UL embedded RCT tests:
The UL RCT (uplink Radio Conformance Test) verifies that the RU's receive chain is performing correctly end-to-end — from RF input at the antenna port to decoded data at the DU. It uses EXM to inject a known uplink signal and measures: (1) PRACH detection rate (sensitivity), (2) RSSI accuracy (calibration), (3) SINR under various conditions, (4) multi-path robustness (EPA/ETU if PropSim connected).
4-stage UL test pipeline:
Stage 1 — Sync: RU acquires timing from DU. GPS/PTP lock verified for TDD.
Stage 2 — RSSI calibration: EXM injects known power, CLI and DU readings verified vs EXM.
Stage 3 — Sensitivity: EXM injects at DSA-corrected threshold per band/BW/FRC. PRACH detection rate measured. Must exceed 99% in 100 attempts.
Stage 4 — Dynamic range: EXM sweeps from −60 to −110 dBm. Verifies RSSI tracks linearly across the dynamic range window.
ul-rct-test command and parameters:
ul-rct-test --band B1 --bw 10M --frc A1 --iterations 100 --dsafile tc_cadence.json
Key parameters: band (B1/B3/B8/B28/B41), BW (5M/10M/15M/20M), FRC (A1/A2/A3/A5), iterations (100 minimum for statistical validity), dsafile (points to your calibrated DSA table). Results saved to rct_results_YYYYMMDD.json with per-column pass/fail, RSSI error, and detection count.
What UL RCT embedded is
Validates the entire uplink receive path — antenna to BLER — against 3GPP FRCs. "Embedded" means it runs entirely on the FHGW: no DU, no external test PC, one CLI command. A signal generator still injects the FRC waveform; everything else is on-RU. Catches receive-chain regressions at box level, fast, before DU integration.
The 4-stage pipeline
StageWhat it doesResource
1. IQ RecordCaptures raw IQ from FPGA channel-filter tap into tmpfs~2.5 MB/frame at 61.44 Msps
2. DownsampleConverts FHGW rate down to PHY decoder input rate (lte_downsample)~24% of processing time
3. PHY DecodeO-RAN 7.2x low-PHY: FFT, channel estimation, demap, decode, CRC (test_ulsim)~49% of time
4. ResultsBLER, SNR, RSSI to shell and log files—
CLI commands
ul-rct-test 35 a13 10 0 100 --debug # full run, all params ul-rct-test -sc 4 2 # shortcut, positional ul-rct-test -l # list supported scenarios ul-rct-test 10 a34 0 # → BLER 0.00% SNR 24.6 dB

M16 TDD LTE & PHY DU Impact — frame structure, special subframe, HARQ, PSS/SSS Advanced click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRSTTDD in one sentence: Band 41 cannot transmit and receive at the same time — it takes turns, transmitting in some time slots and receiving in others, which means your EXA measurements must be gated to only the transmit slots, otherwise the results will be wrong.

TDD frame structure — special subframes, DL/UL ratio, B41 timing

TDD vs FDD — the fundamental difference:
FDD (B1/B3/B8/B28): separate frequencies for DL and UL. They can transmit simultaneously. Duplexer separates them at the antenna. TDD (B41): DL and UL share the same frequency, separated in time. A T/R switch connects either the PA (during DL) or LNA (during UL) to the antenna. PA and LNA never operate simultaneously — no duplexer needed. This is why B41 has better NF (2.0 dB) — the T/R switch has lower loss than a duplexer.
TDD frame structure — subframe types:
LTE TDD uses 10ms radio frames divided into 10 subframes (1ms each). Subframe types: D=Downlink, U=Uplink, S=Special. Special subframe has 3 parts: DwPTS (DL pilot), GP (guard period for switching), UpPTS (UL pilot). Common config 2: DSUDD DSUDD = repeating pattern. Config 5: DSUUU DSUUU = more UL. Your B41 config is set in the DU — check which TDD config is active before EXA gating setup.
Timing impact on measurements:
B41 ACLR must be measured with EXA gating on DL subframes only. PRACH arrives in UL subframes only. The guard period (GP) must be large enough for signal propagation delay plus switching transient — typically 3–14 OFDM symbols. PTP synchronisation accuracy must be ±1.5 μs for TDD — a drift > 1.5 μs causes DL/UL collision (TX and RX active simultaneously) which can damage the T/R switch and the LNA.
TDD vs FDD — the key difference
FDD (B1/B3/B8/B28): separate paired UL/DL frequencies, transmit and receive simultaneously. TDD (B41): UL and DL share the same frequency, alternating in time slots. TDD works in unpaired spectrum. The price: more complex scheduling, more stringent timing requirements.
TDD frame structure — what you must know for B41
PW products use two combinations: (UL/DL config 2, SSF config 7) and (UL/DL config 3, SSF config 8). The special subframe splits into: DwPTS (downlink data) + Guard Period (propagation delay protection) + UpPTS (SRS/PRACH or extra guard).
ConfigDwPTS symbolsGP symbolsUpPTS symbols
SSF config 71022
SSF config 81112
PSS/SSS position changes in TDD
SignalFDD positionTDD position
PSSLast symbol of slots 0, 103rd symbol of special subframes (sf 1, 6)
SSS2nd-last symbol of slots 0, 10Last symbol of slot 1 (sf 0) and slot 11 (sf 5)
PDCCHUp to 3 OFDM symbols≤2 symbols in sf 1 and 6
TDD advantages and challenges
Advantage — Reciprocity: UL and DL share the same frequency, so SRS measurements from UEs directly drive DL beamforming weights. No CSI feedback needed. This is the massive MIMO advantage for B41.
Challenge — Timing: Cross-slot interference between neighbouring cells if their DL/UL configurations don't align. Requires stringent PTP timing (grandmaster Falcon, IEEE-1588v2, <1 µs accuracy).
FHGW TDD constraint: Only PRACH config index 4 supported, Frame Config 2 / SSF Config 6. This limits which cell sizes and PRACH formats can be used on B41.
A01 RF fundamentals — signals, power, frequency, wavelength Beginner click to expand▾

RF fundamentals — signals, power, frequency, wavelength

Frequency, wavelength, and why band choice matters:
f = 1/T (Hz). λ = c/f where c = 3×10⁸ m/s. B1 at 2140 MHz: λ = 14 cm. B28 at 758 MHz: λ = 40 cm. Lower frequency = longer wavelength = better building penetration = wider coverage. Higher frequency = shorter wavelength = more bandwidth available = higher capacity. This is why B28 (700 MHz) is used for coverage (rural, indoors) and B41 (2545 MHz) for capacity (dense urban).
Power — amplitude, dBm, and what numbers mean in RF:
Signal power in RF is always in dBm (decibels relative to 1 mW). 0 dBm = 1 mW. +30 dBm = 1 W. +43 dBm = 20 W (your PA). −99 dBm = your RX sensitivity. The 142 dB difference between PA output and sensitivity threshold is the dynamic range challenge that every part of the RF chain must handle.
Sine wave parameters — amplitude, phase, frequency:
A sine wave is fully described by: amplitude (power level in dBm), frequency (carrier), and phase (timing offset vs reference). Beamforming works by controlling phase per column. ACLR measures spectral purity. EVM measures how accurately amplitude and phase are reproduced for each symbol. All three physical parameters appear as measurement metrics in your RCT.
1.1 What is RF?
RF stands for Radio Frequency — electromagnetic waves that carry energy and information through space without any physical conductor. The RF spectrum spans from roughly 3 Hz to 300 GHz. Below 20 kHz is audio; above 300 GHz is infrared/optical. Everything in between is RF.
An electromagnetic wave has two components oscillating perpendicular to each other and perpendicular to the direction of travel: the electric field (E) and the magnetic field (H). These cannot exist independently — changing E creates H and vice versa (Maxwell's equations). The wave travels at the speed of light c = 3×10⁸ m/s in free space.
Key bands you work with:
BandFrequencyWavelength (λ)Use case
B28700 MHz42.9 cmRural coverage — penetrates buildings, long range
B8900 MHz33.3 cmWide area coverage, voice fallback
B31800 MHz16.7 cmUrban capacity + coverage balance
B12100 MHz14.3 cmUMTS/LTE urban capacity
B412500 MHz12.0 cmTDD, high capacity in dense areas
Why B28 gives better range than B1: Lower frequency → longer wavelength → lower path loss exponent in the Friis equation. At 700 MHz, a signal travels ~10 dB further for the same power compared to 2100 MHz. That's why B28 is used for rural/coverage layers and B1/B3/B41 for urban capacity.
1.2 dB — The most important unit in RF
Almost everything in RF is expressed in decibels (dB). The reason: RF engineers deal with power ranges spanning 12 orders of magnitude — from 100 W transmitters to −120 dBm received signals. Logarithmic scale makes this manageable.
Power ratio in dB: dB = 10 · log₁₀(P₂/P₁)
Voltage ratio in dB: dB = 20 · log₁₀(V₂/V₁)
Power ratiodB valueMemory trick
2×+3 dB"Double = 3 dB"
10×+10 dB"10× = 10 dB"
100×+20 dB10 dB + 10 dB
1000×+30 dB1 W when P₁ = 1 mW
0.5×−3 dB"Half power = −3 dB"
0.1×−10 dBOne tenth
dBm = power in dB relative to 1 milliwatt. Absolute power unit. 0 dBm = 1 mW.
dBmActual powerContext

Rules for dB arithmetic:
Multiply power ratios → ADD their dB values. A 3 dB attenuator followed by a 10 dB amplifier = net +7 dB gain.
dBm + dB = dBm. Input power 0 dBm + 20 dB gain amp = +20 dBm output. ✓
dBm + dBm is MEANINGLESS. You cannot add absolute power levels in dB. (Two 0 dBm sources combined = +3 dBm, not 0 dBm.)
dBm − dBm = dB. Output (−10 dBm) − input (−30 dBm) = gain of 20 dB. ✓
1.3 Impedance — why everything is 50 Ω
All RF equipment uses 50 Ω impedance as the standard interface. This is a compromise: 30 Ω gives minimum loss in a coaxial cable, 77 Ω gives maximum power handling. 50 Ω is the geometric mean — chosen by military in the 1940s and it stuck. Every connector, cable, port on your EXA, EXM, and VNA is 50 Ω.
When the impedance of connected devices doesn't match (source impedance ≠ load impedance), some power is reflected back rather than transmitted. This is the cause of return loss, VSWR, and all the reflections you see in VNA measurements.
Reflection coefficient: Γ = (ZL − Z0) / (ZL + Z0). If ZL = Z0 = 50 Ω: Γ = 0 (no reflection). If ZL = open (∞): Γ = +1 (all reflected). If ZL = short (0): Γ = −1 (all reflected, 180° phase shift).
Return loss: RL = −20·log₁₀|Γ| dB. Higher return loss = better match. Target: >10 dB for antennas, >20 dB for connectors and cables.
A02 Noise, noise figure, sensitivity, dynamic range Beginner–Intermediate click to expand▾
2.1 Thermal noise — the fundamental floor
Every resistor at temperature T generates random voltage fluctuations due to thermal agitation of electrons. This is Johnson-Nyquist noise. The available noise power is:
P_noise = k · T · B
Where k = Boltzmann's constant = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K, T = temperature in Kelvin (290 K = 17°C = room temp), B = bandwidth in Hz.
At 290 K: P_noise = kTB = −174 dBm/Hz (the "kTB" number every RF engineer memorizes).
Channel BWNoise powerCalculation
1 MHz−114 dBm−174 + 60 (10·log10(10⁶))
10 MHz−104 dBm−174 + 70
20 MHz−101 dBm−174 + 73
100 MHz (NR)−94 dBm−174 + 80
This is why your EXA's noise floor changes when you change RBW. RBW 100 kHz → noise floor ≈ −114 dBm. RBW 1 MHz → noise floor rises to −104 dBm. Same physics.
2.2 Noise figure (NF)
A real amplifier or receiver adds noise on top of the input thermal noise. Noise Figure (NF) quantifies how much worse the SNR gets as the signal passes through a component.
NF = SNR_in (dB) − SNR_out (dB)
NF = 0 dB would be a perfect, noiseless component. Real LNAs: NF = 1–3 dB. Mixers: 5–8 dB. Long cables at high frequency: significant NF contribution.
Effective noise figure (Friis formula for cascaded stages):
NF_total = NF₁ + (NF₂−1)/G₁ + (NF₃−1)/(G₁·G₂) + ...
Where NF values are linear (not dB) and G is gain (linear). The first stage (LNA) dominates. This is why the LNA quality matters most for receiver sensitivity — everything after it is "noise that follows the first gain stage."
Practical example for your RU receiver (B3, 10 MHz):
Thermal noise floor: −174 + 70 = −104 dBm
LNA NF = 3 dB → receiver noise floor = −104 + 3 = −101 dBm
Required SNR for LTE QPSK (1 RB): ~−1 dB
Implementation margin (filter losses, ADC, etc.): ~3 dB
REFSENS ≈ −101 − 1 + 3 = −99 dBm → 3GPP specifies −69 dBm (30 dB margin for real deployments)
2.3 Dynamic range
Dynamic range is the ratio between the strongest signal a receiver can handle and the weakest it can detect. It is limited at the bottom by the noise floor and at the top by non-linearity (compression or clipping).
For a spectrum analyzer (your EXA):
Bottom limit: Noise floor = kTB + NF of analyzer front end. Set by thermal noise and RBW.
Top limit: Mixer 1 dB compression point (P1dB). Above this, gain compresses, measurements are invalid.
Spurious-free dynamic range (SFDR): Range where the fundamental signal is visible above noise AND no third-order intermodulation products exceed the noise floor. SFDR = (2/3) · (IIP3 − kTBF).
For your RU receiver: Must handle UL signals from −120 dBm (cell edge UE) to −30 dBm (nearby UE at full power) — a 90 dB range. The AGC system adjusts LNA gain and attenuators to keep the ADC input within its linear range across this entire range.
When you do ACS/blocking tests, you're deliberately testing the edge of this dynamic range. A strong blocking signal in the adjacent channel partially saturates the front end, raising the effective noise floor and reducing the wanted signal's SNR below the required level.
A03 Filters, S-parameters, VNA measurements in depth Beginner–Intermediate click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRSTS-parameters in one sentence: S-parameters are the VNA's way of measuring how a component handles RF — S11 tells you how much signal bounces back (is the impedance matched?), and S21 tells you how much gets through (what is the gain or loss?).

S-parameters, filters, VNA — advanced RF measurements

S-parameters — what S11/S21/S12/S22 measure:
A 2-port network has 4 S-parameters. S11: input reflection (VSWR at Port 1). S21: forward transmission (gain or loss from Port 1 to Port 2). S12: reverse transmission (isolation). S22: output reflection. For a cable: S11 < −20 dB (good match), S21 = −loss dB (e.g. −2.5 dB). For your duplexer: S21_TX = −0.5 dB (TX insertion loss), S21_RX = −0.5 dB (RX insertion loss), S12_TX_to_RX < −50 dB (TX-to-RX isolation).
Filter specs — what each number means:
Insertion loss: how much the filter attenuates in the passband (bad, adds NF). Rejection: how much it attenuates out-of-band (good, blocks blockers). Passband ripple: variation of insertion loss across the passband. Group delay variation: frequency-dependent delay causing phase distortion. Your B1 pre-BPF: insertion loss 0.3 dB (passband 2110–2170 MHz), rejection > 60 dB (at B3 and B41 frequencies).
VNA usage in your lab:
S11 (cable/connector quality): both ports, check S11 < −20 dB at band frequencies. S21 (cable loss): Port 1 → cable → Port 2, magnitude gives loss, phase gives electrical length. S21 (column phase cal): Port 1 → BOB SMA → RFFE → Port 2, phase difference between columns = beamforming correction needed. Always SOLT cal first. See VNA2-7 cards for detailed procedures.
3.1 S-parameters — the language of VNA measurements
S-parameters (Scattering parameters) describe how RF signals are transmitted and reflected at the ports of a device. For a 2-port device (like a filter or cable), there are 4 S-parameters organized in a 2×2 matrix:
ParameterMeaningWhat you measureGood value
S11Input reflection (Port 1)Return loss / input match< −10 dB (VSWR < 2:1)
S21Forward transmission (Port 1→2)Insertion loss / gainNear 0 dB for cable; depends on filter
S12Reverse transmission (Port 2→1)Reverse isolation= S21 for passive, <−40 dB for amplifier
S22Output reflection (Port 2)Output match< −10 dB
S-parameters are complex numbers — they have both magnitude AND phase. Your E5071C measures both simultaneously. Log Magnitude format shows just the magnitude in dB. Phase format shows the angle. Smith chart shows both on one plot.
3.2 What the E5071C screen is showing (your filter)
Your E5071C screen throughout the videos shows S21 of what appears to be a bandpass filter or duplexer. Let's decode what you're looking at:
The passband (left side, wiggly trace): The frequency range where the filter lets signals through. The ripple you see is intentional — it's the equiripple characteristic of a Chebyshev filter design. The amplitude varies between the ripple peaks and dips (typically 0.1 to 1 dB ripple). Insertion loss at the center of the passband tells you how much signal you lose just from passing through the filter (typically 0.5–2 dB for a good diplexer).
The rolloff (middle, sharp drop): The filter transition band — where it goes from passing to blocking. A steep rolloff means better selectivity — the filter can separate closely-spaced signals. Chebyshev designs sacrifice passband flatness for steeper rolloff. Elliptic (Cauer) filters add transmission zeros in the stopband for even sharper rolloff.
The stopband (right side, flat floor): How much the filter blocks unwanted signals. Your trace shows ~50–60 dB rejection. This is how much isolation the duplexer provides between TX and RX bands — absolutely critical. If the TX signal at +43 dBm gets −50 dB isolation → only −7 dBm reaches the RX input — still easily detectable but the duplexer filter would reject it further. A real duplexer needs >50 dB between TX and RX port.
3.3 Filter types — your practical guide
Filter typePassbandRolloffBest for
ButterworthMaximally flat (no ripple)Gentle (−20 dB/decade per pole)Wideband systems where flatness matters
ChebyshevEquiripple (your E5071C trace!)Steeper than ButterworthMost bandpass/duplexer filters in cellular
Elliptic (Cauer)Equiripple in pass AND stopSteepest possible for given orderDuplexers needing extreme TX/RX isolation
BesselFlat, linear phaseGentlePulse/wideband signals where group delay flatness matters
3.4 VNA calibration in detail — why and how
A VNA works by sweeping a source signal across a frequency range, injecting it into the DUT, and measuring what comes back (S11) and what comes out (S21). The problem: the cables, connectors, and adapters between the VNA port and your DUT have their own S-parameters (loss, reflections). These systematic errors contaminate your measurement.
The three systematic errors the SOLT cal corrects:
Directivity error: The VNA's directional coupler isn't perfect — some of the incident signal leaks into the reflected wave measurement even with a perfect match at the DUT.
Source match error: The VNA source isn't perfectly matched to 50 Ω — some reflected signal from the DUT bounces back off the source and re-enters the DUT.
Frequency response error: The test cables, connectors, and adapters have their own insertion loss and phase shift which varies with frequency.
SOLT procedure step by step:
Short: Connect a short circuit (0 Ω) to Port 1 at the calibration reference plane. The VNA measures: all power should reflect back with 180° phase shift (Γ = −1). Any deviation = directivity and source match errors at that frequency.
Open: Connect an open circuit (no connection). All power reflects, 0° phase shift (Γ = +1). The known parasitic capacitance of the open is stored in the cal kit — the VNA uses it to distinguish directivity from source match.
Load: Connect a precision 50 Ω termination. Should produce Γ = 0 (perfect match, no reflection). Any measured signal = raw directivity error of the coupler. This establishes the error floor.
Thru (2-port cal only): Connect Port 1 directly to Port 2. Now the VNA can measure transmission errors — cable loss, adapter insertion loss, phase delay.
After these four measurements the VNA solves 12 error terms (for full 2-port cal) and removes them from subsequent DUT measurements. Your calibration reference plane is now at the tip of the cable/connector where you connected the Short/Open/Load — everything between VNA port and that tip is removed from the measurement.
If you move or flex the cable after calibration, the cal is invalidated. The cable's S-parameters change with flex. Always recalibrate if the setup changes. Check the cal status indicator — 'C' = active, 'Cc' = interpolated (acceptable but not ideal), no 'C' = no cal, results are uncorrected and unreliable.
3.5 Time domain analysis on the E5071C
One of the most powerful E5071C features is converting the frequency sweep into a time-domain response. The math is an inverse FFT (IFFT) of the swept S-parameter data. The result shows when reflections arrive at the measurement port — which tells you where they come from.
A signal travels at roughly 2×10⁸ m/s in typical coaxial cable (velocity factor ~0.67). So a reflection arriving at t = 5 ns came from a point 5 ns × 2×10⁸ m/s / 2 = 50 cm away from the calibration plane (divide by 2 because signal makes a round trip).
Spike at t=0: Reflection at the calibration plane itself — connector interface, impedance step at the DUT port.
Spike at t=2 ns: Reflection 20 cm down the cable — could be a kinked cable, damaged connector, or moisture ingress.
Spike at t=10 ns: Reflection 1 m from the port — cable end, unterminated stub, or mismatch at the antenna.
For your RU antenna port verification: do a 1-port S11 measurement in time domain. You should see a small reflection at t=0 (connector), then ideally nothing else. Any additional spike between the connector and the antenna location = impedance discontinuity in the feed path that's causing reflections and reducing radiated power.
A04 LTE/NR air interface — OFDM, resource blocks, FDD/TDD, physical channels Intermediate click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRSTLTE air interface in one sentence: LTE divides the channel into thousands of tiny 15 kHz subcarriers (OFDM), assigns groups of them to each user (resource blocks), and switches between FDD (separate frequencies for up/down) or TDD (same frequency, different time slots) depending on the band.

LTE air interface — OFDM, resource blocks, FDD, TDD

Resource block structure — from subcarrier to throughput:
1 subcarrier = 15 kHz. 1 Resource Block (RB) = 12 subcarriers = 180 kHz. 1 slot = 7 symbols (normal CP) = 0.5 ms. 1 subframe = 2 slots = 1 ms. Channel bandwidth to RBs: 5 MHz→25RB, 10 MHz→50RB, 15 MHz→75RB, 20 MHz→100RB. Peak throughput (100RB, 64QAM, MIMO 4×4): ~300 Mbps. Your sensitivity test uses all RBs at QPSK 1/3 — lowest throughput, best coverage.
FDD bands (B1/B3/B8/B28) vs TDD band (B41):
FDD: separate DL and UL frequencies. B1: DL 2110–2170 MHz, UL 1920–1980 MHz (190 MHz duplex gap). Duplexer separates TX and RX. Can transmit and receive simultaneously. TDD B41: DL and UL share 2496–2690 MHz. T/R switch alternates TX and RX. DL/UL ratio configurable (e.g. 3DL:1UL). Needs PTP timing synchronisation (±1.5 μs). Asymmetric — can give more DL capacity on demand.
OFDM benefits and the PAPR cost:
Benefits: flat fading per subcarrier (simple equalisation), flexible resource allocation (schedule per RB per UE), robust against multipath (cyclic prefix). PAPR cost: OFDM sum of many subcarriers creates random peaks 10–12 dB above average. PA must handle these peaks without clipping → either back off PA (lower efficiency) or use CFR+DPD (maintain efficiency). Your AAU uses CFR+DPD to enable PA operation near P1dB without ACLR violations.
4.1 Why OFDM?
A wideband channel (20 MHz of LTE) has frequency-selective fading — some frequencies fade more than others depending on the multipath environment. In a single-carrier system, a deep fade at one frequency wipes out a chunk of your data. OFDM (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing) slices the wideband channel into N narrow subcarriers, each so narrow (15 kHz in LTE) that it experiences flat fading. A fade at one subcarrier only kills data on that one subcarrier — easy to correct with FEC coding.
OFDM mechanics: N subcarriers spaced Δf = 15 kHz apart. Each subcarrier carries one OFDM symbol over duration T_symbol = 1/Δf = 66.7 µs (plus cyclic prefix). All subcarriers transmitted simultaneously — their orthogonality ensures zero ICI (inter-carrier interference) at the exact sampling points.
LTE OFDM structure:
Subcarrier spacing: 15 kHz (also 7.5 kHz for MBSFN)
Symbol duration: 66.7 µs + cyclic prefix (4.69 µs normal, 16.67 µs extended)
Resource element (RE): 1 subcarrier × 1 symbol slot = smallest unit
Resource block (RB): 12 subcarriers × 7 symbols (0.5 ms slot) = 84 REs
Frame: 10 ms → 10 subframes → 20 slots
Channel BWNumber of RBsSubcarriers (used)
1.4 MHz672
5 MHz25300
10 MHz50600
15 MHz75900
20 MHz1001200
This is why the EXM shows 50 RBs when testing B3 at 10 MHz and 100 RBs at 20 MHz. Each colored cell in the RB map = one resource block. Red = fully allocated and transmitting, blue/dark = idle or lower power.
4.2 FDD vs TDD — how your bands differ
FDD (Frequency Division Duplex): Uplink and downlink use separate, paired frequency bands simultaneously. The gap between UL and DL is the duplex gap.
BandUL frequency (base station RX)DL frequency (base station TX)Duplex gap
B11920–1980 MHz2110–2170 MHz130 MHz
B31710–1785 MHz1805–1880 MHz95 MHz
B8880–915 MHz925–960 MHz45 MHz
B28703–748 MHz758–803 MHz55 MHz
Your PUCCH test vectors for B3 use DL_Freq 1842.5 MHz (mid of 1805–1880 DL band) and UL_Freq 1747.5 MHz (mid of 1710–1785 UL band). The duplexer in the RU separates these — the TX filter passes 1805–1880 and the RX filter passes 1710–1785, with >50 dB isolation between them.
TDD (Time Division Duplex): UL and DL share the same frequency, alternating in time according to a configurable UL/DL ratio. B41 (2496–2690 MHz) is TDD. The base station transmits in DL subframes and receives in UL subframes. There is a Guard Period (GP) between DL and UL to allow propagation delay from far UEs to clear.
This is why B41 requires frame trigger on the EXA/EXM. Without it, you capture a mix of DL + UL time slots in the same measurement window. EVM calculated over mixed DL+UL data is meaningless — the reference signals (CRS/DMRS) are only in DL subframes.
4.3 Physical channels — DL and UL
Downlink (base station TX, what you measure with EXM Channel Power / EVM):
PDSCH: Physical Downlink Shared Channel — actual user data. The bulk of DL bandwidth. Carries IP packets to users. Uses QPSK/16QAM/64QAM/256QAM depending on channel quality.
PDCCH: Physical Downlink Control Channel — scheduling grants. Tells UEs which RBs they are allocated, what MCS to use. 1–3 OFDM symbols at the start of each subframe.
PBCH: Physical Broadcast Channel — system information (cell ID, bandwidth, frame structure). Transmitted every 40 ms. The first signal a UE decodes when searching for a cell.
CRS: Cell-specific Reference Signals — pilot tones used by UE for channel estimation and signal quality measurement (RSRP, RSRQ). Always present on specific RE positions regardless of traffic. This is what test_Tx_DLRS (downlink reference signal test) checks.
Uplink (base station RX, what you test with PUCCH waveforms):
PUSCH: Physical Uplink Shared Channel — UE data. Your sensitivity tests inject a known PUSCH waveform and measure whether the RU can decode it at the required signal level.
PUCCH: Physical Uplink Control Channel — control info only: ACK/NACK feedback (did the UE receive the downlink data?), Scheduling Request (UE asking for UL allocation), Channel Quality Indicator (CQI). Occupies the edges of the UL bandwidth (first and last 6 RBs) and frequency-hops between the two edges each slot to exploit frequency diversity.
PRACH: Physical Random Access Channel — initial access. UE sends a Zadoff-Chu preamble sequence to establish uplink timing synchronization. The base station measures the arrival time to compute Timing Advance (TA) — how early the UE must transmit to arrive at the right time.
4.4 PUCCH formats — decoding your JSON config
