EXP3 PA Classes A/B/AB/C/F — efficiency vs linearity trade-off in your GaN PA Advanced click to expand▾

PA classes — efficiency vs linearity trade-off

Class A — most linear, least efficient:
Bias point: mid-supply. Conducts for full 360° of input cycle. Gain is perfectly linear (constant). Efficiency: theoretically 25–50%, practically 15–30%. No crossover distortion. Used where linearity is critical and efficiency is secondary — e.g. small-signal driver stages. Your AAU does NOT use pure Class A — too much heat for 20W output.
Class AB — your AAU PA operating class:
Bias point: slightly above cutoff. Conducts for 180–360° of cycle. Combines best features of A and B — reasonable linearity, reasonable efficiency (~35–45% with DPD). The slight nonlinearity at crossover is corrected by DPD. This is the standard choice for cellular base station PAs. GaN technology (your PA material) enables higher efficiency than older GaAs at same output power.
Dynamic Vdd — how supply modulation improves efficiency:
Class AB PA efficiency is highest at peak power and drops at lower power levels. OFDM signals spend most of their time at low-to-medium power levels (high PAPR means peaks are rare). Dynamic Vdd reduces the PA supply voltage during low-power periods, so the PA dissipates less heat even though it's conducting. At 6 dB below peak power, Dynamic Vdd can improve efficiency from 35% to 55% — reducing heat by 30%. This is why your AAU's Dynamic Vdd configuration in the PA registers directly affects both efficiency and junction temperature.
Why PA class matters for your work
The PA in your Metro AAU RFFE is a GaN (Gallium Nitride) transistor biased and operated in a specific class that trades linearity against efficiency. Your PA efficiency test plan (Module 11 / PPT2) directly measures this. Understanding PA classes explains WHY DPD is necessary and WHY dynamic Vdd saves power.
PA classes — the complete picture
ClassConduction angleMax efficiencyLinearityUsed where
Class A360° (always on)50%Excellent — always in linear regionLow-power driver stages, test equipment
Class B180° (half cycle)78.5%Poor at zero-crossing — crossover distortionPush-pull audio, rarely in RF
Class AB180°–360° (adjustable bias)50–78%Good — biased slightly above cutoffMost base station PAs, your RENESAS F8410 operates here
Class C<180° (cutoff biased)>78.5%Very poor — only works for CW/FMTransmitters for constant-envelope signals only
Class F180° + harmonic tuning>90% theoreticalGood with DPDHigh-efficiency RF PAs, some 5G designs
DohertyTwo-amplifier combination60–70% at backed-off powerGood with DPDYour Metro AAU — the standard for LTE/5G base stations
Why Doherty is THE choice for LTE/5G base stations
A single Class AB PA has peak efficiency near saturation but very poor efficiency when backed off for PAPR headroom. At 10 dB back-off (typical for LTE OFDM): Class AB efficiency drops to ≈ 15%. A Doherty PA maintains ~60% efficiency at 6–8 dB back-off by using a carrier amplifier (always on, Class AB) and a peaking amplifier (only turns on at high power peaks, Class C). The two amplifiers combine through a quarter-wave transformer.
Doherty efficiency at output back-off (OBO): At OBO = 0 dB (saturation): η ≈ 78% (both amps at full power) At OBO = 6 dB (normal OFDM): η ≈ 60% (carrier amp efficient, peaking off) At OBO = 10 dB (deep backoff): η ≈ 45% (only carrier amp running) vs Class AB at OBO = 6 dB: η ≈ 25% (huge difference!)
How gate bias (Vgg) sets the operating class
In your GaN PA (RENESAS F8410), the gate voltage Vgg3_p sets the quiescent current which sets the conduction angle which sets the operating class. Your PA efficiency test plan tests Vgg3_p at −6.5 V (near cutoff = more Class C, lower quiescent current, more efficient), −5.5 V, and −4.5 V (more Class AB, more linear, more quiescent current). The test finds the optimal Vgg that satisfies both ACLR/EVM spec AND maximum efficiency.
Class A: why your EXA uses it (and your RU doesn't)
Test equipment uses Class A amplifiers for their excellent linearity. Your EXA internal amplifiers and your signal generator output stage are Class A — they must not add any distortion to the signal being measured. The 50% max efficiency is acceptable for instruments that run from wall power. The GaN PA in your RU runs at 40+ V drain, delivers 20 W RF, and must be as efficient as possible — that's why Doherty at Class AB is used, and why DPD linearizes the nonlinearity.
🎯 Analogy: PA efficiency is like a car engine

A car engine converts fuel to motion — but only about 25-40% of the fuel becomes actual motion; the rest is heat from the exhaust and engine block. Your PA does the same with electricity. Class A is like leaving the engine running at full throttle all the time (very inefficient). Class AB is like a well-tuned engine that only works as hard as needed. Dynamic Vdd is like a hybrid car — it reduces fuel use at low speeds (low signal levels) automatically. 148W of heat from 4 PA columns is why your AAU needs active cooling and why high ambient temperature causes power derating.

EXP4 Noise floor from first principles — thermal noise, kTB, −174 dBm/Hz derivation Advanced click to expand▾

Noise floor from first principles — thermal noise to system sensitivity

Full chain: kTB → NF → Sensitivity → EXM injection:
kTB at 290K = −174 dBm/Hz. Add 10·log(10MHz) = +70 dB → noise floor = −104 dBm. Add system NF = +5.75 dB → system noise floor = −98.25 dBm. Add SNR_req for QPSK 1/3 = −1 dB → sensitivity = −99.25 dBm (B1). EXM must inject at this power level minus cable loss correction. If cable = −2.5 dB: EXM output = −99.25 + 2.5 = −96.75 dBm to achieve −99.25 dBm at RU port. See DSA card for per-band offsets.
Why EXA DANL must be checked before RX measurements:
EXA DANL with preamp ON: −130 dBm/Hz. In 10 MHz BW: −130 + 70 = −60 dBm. Your system noise floor is −98.25 dBm — 38 dB above EXA DANL. Safe margin. But if you try to measure an antenna noise floor directly (passive, no LNA), you would be measuring the EXA noise, not the antenna. Always verify EXA DANL > 10 dB below the signal you want to measure.
When measured sensitivity is worse than expected:
Check in order: (1) Cable loss — measure with VNA, subtract from EXM output. (2) Connector torque and condition. (3) EXM output power — verify with EXA before injection. (4) EXA preamp state — must be ON for RSSI/sensitivity checks. (5) ADC_ADJUST calibration — if off, RSSI will read wrong even though physics is fine. (6) LNA health — measure NF directly with EXA NF mode.
Where −174 dBm/Hz comes from
Thermal noise is the random motion of electrons in any resistor at any temperature above absolute zero. It sets the absolute minimum noise floor of any receiver, regardless of how good the electronics are.
Thermal noise power in bandwidth B: P_noise = k × T × B k = Boltzmann constant = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K T = temperature in Kelvin (room temp = 290 K = 17°C) B = bandwidth in Hz At B = 1 Hz: P_noise = 1.38×10⁻²³ × 290 × 1 = 4.0×10⁻²¹ W Converting to dBm: P_noise = 10×log₁₀(4.0×10⁻²¹ / 10⁻³) = 10×log₁₀(4.0×10⁻¹⁸) = −174 dBm So: thermal noise density = −174 dBm per Hz at room temperature (290 K) For any bandwidth: Noise floor (dBm) = −174 + 10×log₁₀(B_Hz) B = 10 MHz (LTE): −174 + 70 = −104 dBm B = 20 MHz (LTE): −174 + 73 = −101 dBm B = 100 MHz (5G): −174 + 80 = −94 dBm
Adding noise figure to get receiver noise floor
Receiver noise floor = −174 + 10×log₁₀(BW) + NF Your RU Rx chain NF (estimated): LNA NF: ~2 dB Filter insertion loss before LNA: ~0.5 dB (adds to NF) Duplexer loss before LNA: ~0.5 dB (adds to NF) System NF ≈ 3 dB For B1 10 MHz: Noise floor = −174 + 70 + 3 = −101 dBm Required SNR for QPSK 1/3: ~−1 dB (can decode below noise floor with coding gain!) Sensitivity = −101 + (−1) = −102 dBm 3GPP REFSENS = −69 dBm → your RU easily beats this ✓
Why sensitivity tests have SUCH a wide margin from −69 dBm
The 3GPP Wide Area BS REFSENS of −69 dBm seems easy — your actual sensitivity is around −100 to −112 dBm. The 3GPP limit is set for the worst-case Wide Area BS with poor NF, high interference, and broad operating conditions. The limit is a floor — real base stations must be much better. In your RSSI calibration data: the 2 dB error margin (the practical RSSI sensitivity) is −93.5 to −95.5 dBm, showing your actual RU is ≈25 dB better than the 3GPP floor.
Noise at different temperatures (useful for temp testing)
TemperatureKelvinThermal noise densityChange from room temp
−40°C (cold outdoor)233 K−175.6 dBm/Hz−1.6 dB (quieter)
+17°C (room, 290K)290 K−174.0 dBm/Hzreference
+55°C (hot outdoor)328 K−173.0 dBm/Hz+1.0 dB (noisier)
+85°C (PA junction)358 K−172.5 dBm/Hz+1.5 dB (noisier)
This is why sensitivity specs are referenced to 290 K. When you run sensitivity tests with the unit hot (after long TX sessions), the noise floor rises slightly. Always let the RU reach thermal steady state before sensitivity tests.
EXP5 PRACH detector internals — noise estimator, peak multiplier, timing advance math Expert click to expand▾

PRACH detector internals — noise estimator, peak multiplier, false alarm

How PRACH detection decides pass/fail:
The PRACH detector correlates the received UL signal against each of the 64 possible Zadoff-Chu root sequences. For each root, the correlator produces a power profile over the cyclic shift dimension. The peak power is compared to a detection threshold: threshold = measured_noise_floor × peak_multiplier_α. If peak > threshold: PRACH detected. The noise floor is measured from non-PRACH resource blocks in the same subframe.
Peak multiplier α — the key parameter:
α is set by the RU configuration. Low α (e.g. 4 = 6 dB above noise): detects weak UEs, but more false alarms (random noise peaks exceed threshold). High α (e.g. 16 = 12 dB above noise): robust against false alarms, but misses UEs at or below threshold power. Your sensitivity test uses a specific α — the DSA power level is set so that at the rated sensitivity, the signal peak is just above threshold at the standard α value. This is why the sensitivity number is not "noise floor + NF" alone — it includes the peak_multiplier overhead.
False alarm rate — why it matters in deployment:
A false PRACH alarm causes the gNB to send a Random Access Response (RAR) to a nonexistent UE, wasting resources. High false alarm rate degrades cell capacity. Too sensitive α → many false alarms. In your lab: false alarms show up as PRACH detected count exceeding the number of EXM injections (more detections than preambles sent). Normal: detection count = injections × detection_rate. If detection count > injections: false alarm problem — α too low.
The full PRACH detection pipeline
Stage 1 — Front end: Remove CP → apply FFT → extract PRACH subcarriers (839 bins at 1.25 kHz spacing) Stage 2 — Root correlation: For each root u being tested: Correlate received signal with conjugate of root ZC: Y = X × ZC_u* Apply IFFT → get power-delay profile (839 taps, one per possible cyclic shift) Stage 3 — Noise estimation: Take the correlation output after IFFT Form noise vector: all taps EXCEPT the K preamble positions (exclude K windows) Noise_est = mean(noise_vector_power) [average of all "empty" delay taps] Stage 4 — Peak detection: For each of the K preamble windows: Find peak power in that window: P_peak Detection threshold: P_peak / Noise_est > peak_multiplier If exceeded → preamble detected at that cyclic shift Timing advance = peak_position × (1/FFT_size) × symbol_duration
What the noise estimator actually does — intuition
The correlation output has 839 delay taps. For a given root u with ZCZ=12, there are K ≈ 6–7 preamble windows (occupied delay taps) and 839 − K×Ncs ≈ 700+ "empty" taps where no valid preamble should appear. The noise estimator averages power in these empty taps — that average IS the noise floor. The peak multiplier then sets: "if the peak is X times above this noise floor, call it a detection."
The detection threshold trade-off
Higher peak_multiplier: → Fewer false alarms (noise spikes mistaken for preambles) ✓ → More missed detections (real weak preambles not detected) ✗ → Better for dense urban where random UEs cause false alarms Lower peak_multiplier: → More detections of weak preambles ✓ → More false alarms ✗ → Better for large cells where UEs are far away and weak RuAuto test_Rx_PRACH sweeps power and finds the threshold where miss detection rate = 1% This measured threshold must be ≤ PRACH_KPI (e.g. −87 dBm + DSA offset per band)
Timing advance from PRACH — how it works
The delay tap position of the detected peak = propagation delay of UE Round-trip delay = 2 × distance / c For 1 km cell: delay = 2×1000 / 3×10⁸ = 6.67 μs One PRACH delay tap = Ncs × FFT_size / (839 × subcarrier_spacing) = Ncs × 0.001 ms / 839 (for 1.25 kHz format 0 PRACH) Timing Advance command sent to UE = detected delay taps × tap_duration UE then transmits that much earlier so signal arrives aligned at eNB
Connecting PRACH to your test results
In your test_Rx_PRACH output: "timing advance avg/std" shows the measured round-trip delay and its consistency. High std dev = the detector is struggling at the noise floor (inconsistent peak position). Low std dev = clean detection. The miss-detection rate curves you see in the results are exactly the probability of the peak/noise ratio exceeding the threshold at each input power level.
EXP6 dBFS ↔ dBm conversion — the complete guide with your real calibration numbers Intermediate click to expand▾

dBFS ↔ dBm conversion — complete guide with your RU numbers

The conversion formula and where the constants come from:
P_dBm = dBFS_reading + ADC_ADJUST. ADC_ADJUST = (total RX chain gain from RU port to ADC register) in dB. This includes: LNA gain (+20 dB), VGA gain (variable, AGC-controlled), mixer conversion gain, ADC full-scale calibration. Rather than tracking all these separately, RSSI cal measures the net offset once and stores it. Example: EXM injects −97.5 dBm at RU port. ADC reads −12.5 dBFS. ADC_ADJUST = −97.5 − (−12.5) = −85. Future readings: P_dBm = dBFS + (−85).
dBFS scale — understanding what each level means:
0 dBFS: ADC output saturated (all bits = 1). This is clipping — measurement invalid.
−12 dBFS: target operating point (12 dB headroom for peaks).
−40 dBFS: low signal — AGC should have increased gain already.
−74 dBFS: quantisation noise floor (12-bit ADC limit).
Below −74 dBFS: signal lost in quantisation noise.
Common conversion errors:
Forgetting cable loss: P_at_port = EXM_output − cable_loss. Using wrong ADC channel: get_rssi 0 is B1 Col A, not B3. ADC_ADJUST drifts with temperature: recalibrate at operating temperature. ADC_ADJUST is band-specific: B1 and B3 have different values even on the same ADC chip because they use different gain settings.
The fundamental difference
dBmdBFS
What it measuresAbsolute RF power at a physical portDigital amplitude relative to ADC max
Reference point1 mW into 50Ω at the connectorADC full-scale output (maximum code)
RangeAny value (positive or negative)Always ≤ 0 dBFS (0 = clipping)
Where measuredAt RF port, after all the hardwareIn the digital domain, after ADC
Used inLink budget, test results, 3GPP specspower_monitor, get_rssi raw output
Why you CANNOT simply subtract a fixed number
Many engineers think: "dBFS to dBm = just add 50 dB (or whatever the gain is)." This is only true if the gain chain from RF port to ADC is perfectly known AND constant. In reality it varies with: temperature, frequency, which ADC channel, which RFFE, calibration state, and firmware version. This is why hardware.json has a per-ADC ADC_ADJUST vector — each ADC needs its own offset.
The conversion formula using your real calibration data
RSSI_dBm = RSSI_dBFS + ADC_ADJUST + chain_gain_compensation Where ADC_ADJUST is the measured offset from your RSSI calibration: ADC 0 (B1): ADC_ADJUST = −20.9 dBFS ADC 2 (B3): ADC_ADJUST = −20.8 dBFS ADC 5 (B1): ADC_ADJUST = −24.2 dBFS (different because different RF path) Example: ADC 0 reads −44.9 dBFS at sensitivity point → RSSI_dBm ≈ −44.9 + ADC_ADJUST + RF_gain_total The 2dB-error-margin point = −95.5 dBm (from your RSSI Results deck) So total conversion offset = −95.5 − (−44.9) = −50.6 dB Meaning: 1 dBFS at ADC 0 input = (−50.6) dBm at RU antenna port
What the get_rssi command actually does
get_rssi output for ADC 0: rssi_dbfs: raw ADC measurement in dBFS (e.g. −44.9 dBFS) rssi_dbm: rssi_dbfs + ADC_ADJUST[0] (pre-compensated using hardware.json) The firmware reads ADC_ADJUST from /etc/configs/hardware.json Adds it to the raw dBFS reading Returns the compensated dBm value If hardware.json is wrong (offset not calibrated for your unit): → get_rssi dBm is wrong by however much the offset is off → This is what the RSSI calibration procedure (your PPT1) corrects
Practical rules for your daily work

DL power_monitor> −8 dBFSNear ADC clippingReduce DL power or check CFR
UL get_rssi−44.9 dBFSAt sensitivity test point for B1This is your REFSENS measurement point
UL get_rssi−68 dBFS or worseAt or below ADC noise floorSignal too weak — cannot measure reliably

L0 Foundation — Electronics: Ohm's Law, Impedance, dB/dBm/dBc, VSWR, Smith Chart, Filters, Mixers Foundation click to expand▾

Electronics foundation — the base you build RF knowledge on

Ohm's Law to RF — the continuity:
V=IR, P=VI=V²/R=I²R in DC circuits. In RF, impedance Z replaces resistance R and includes reactance (capacitors, inductors). At RF frequencies, lumped components behave differently — a capacitor becomes a short at high freq, an inductor becomes an open. This is why RF design is about distributed elements (transmission lines, antennas) and why 50 Ω is the universal RF reference impedance.
dB/dBm — the RF number system:
Learn these rules cold: +3dB=×2 power, +10dB=×10. 0dBm=1mW, +30dBm=1W, −30dBm=1μW. Every RF calculation uses dB because gain and loss simply add. Chain gain = sum of all block gains in dB. This is the single most important concept to internalise — you use it 50× per day in RF work.
Master these before touching RF equipment. Every RF measurement is built on these foundations — Ohm's law for power calculations, dBm for every instrument reading, VSWR for every antenna match check, S-parameters for every VNA measurement.

L1 Digital Communications — Modulation (AM/FM/PSK/QAM/OFDM), Coding (CRC/Turbo/LDPC), Multiple Access (FDMA/TDMA/CDMA/OFDMA) Level 1 click to expand▾

Digital communications — modulation, coding, OFDM basics

From bits to waveform:
Digital comms: bits → symbol mapping (QAM) → pulse shaping → carrier modulation → channel → demodulation → symbol decision → bits. Each step has a quality metric: Symbol Error Rate → Bit Error Rate → Block Error Rate (BLER). 3GPP uses 5% BLER as the sensitivity threshold. The entire DSA framework is calibrating your test to this 5% BLER threshold.
Why OFDM was chosen for LTE:
OFDM converts a wideband channel into many narrow subchannels (15 kHz each). Each subchannel experiences flat fading (not frequency-selective). Frequency-domain equalization becomes trivial — one complex multiply per subcarrier. Guard bands (cyclic prefix) eliminate inter-symbol interference from multipath. The price: high PAPR (10–12 dB) requiring DPD and CFR.
LTE downlink uses OFDMA with QAM modulation on each subcarrier. Uplink uses SC-FDMA (single carrier) to keep UE PAPR low (battery saving). Your RU receives SC-FDMA from UE and transmits OFDMA to UE.

Digital comms is what the RF chain is carrying

L3 RF Measurements ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ — Power, EVM, ACLR, SEM, RSSI, Sensitivity, Dynamic Range, PA tests — where RF engineers spend their lives Core ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾

RF measurements — power, EVM, ACLR, SEM, RSSI in depth

The 5 measurements you run most often:
TX Power: output at BOB SMA vs rated target (±1 dB). ACLR: adjacent channel leakage (< −45 dBc). EVM: IQ constellation quality (< 8% for 64QAM). RSSI: receive power calibration (CLI vs DU within ±2 dB). Sensitivity: PRACH detection at threshold (>99% in 100 attempts). Everything else is derived from or feeds into these five.
SEM — Spectrum Emission Mask:
SEM verifies TX spectral purity across a wide frequency range — not just the adjacent channel (ACLR) but spurious emissions 10s of MHz away. 3GPP defines limits at multiple offset frequencies. EXA measures this in one sweep using the SEM measurement function. Failures outside the main ACLR range usually indicate harmonics (PA operating at wrong Vdd) or spurious oscillations.
This is where you live as an RF engineer. Every instrument reading, every test result, every pass/fail decision maps to this level. The goal is not just to measure but to understand WHY a measurement fails and trace it to the exact root cause in the hardware or software chain.

L4 RF Components — Full signal chain: BBU→DAC→IQ→Mixer→PLL→PA→Duplexer→Antenna (and reverse RX path) Level 4 click to expand▾

RF components — full signal chain from BBU to antenna

DL signal chain — every block:
BBU/DU (IQ data) → FHGW (IFFT, BFP, CFR, DPD) → DAC → upconverter (mixer+LO) → PA → duplexer/T-R switch → antenna. Each adds gain or loss. DPD is the most complex — adaptively pre-distorts the signal to compensate for PA nonlinearity. Without DPD, ACLR would fail by 10–15 dB. See A05 (TX chain) and A06 (RX chain) cards for full diagrams.
UL signal chain — every block:
Antenna → duplexer/T-R switch → pre-BPF → LNA → post-BPF → mixer → VGA/AGC → ADC → FHGW (FFT, BFP compress) → eCPRI → DU. NF is set by the first components: cable+duplexer+LNA. LNA gain divides all subsequent NF contributions. See NCH card for full Friis calculation. See DSA card for how NF drives sensitivity and test thresholds.

L7 O-RAN RF ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ — RU Architecture, M/C/U/S Plane, RU Capabilities, Tilt, RET, RSSI, IQ Playback, DPD, uSleep, Carrier Activation Your Work ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾

O-RAN RF — O-RU architecture, M/C/U/S planes, fronthaul timing

O-RAN planes — M/C/U/S:
M-plane (Management): configuration, SW upgrade, fault management via NETCONF/YANG. How you configure bands, power, calibration. C-plane (Control): scheduling information — which RBs active, beam index, timing. Latency sensitive (<100μs). U-plane (User): IQ data — the actual signal samples. Very high bandwidth. S-plane (Sync): timing distribution — PTP IEEE 1588 from DU to RU. Required for TDD timing.
Fronthaul timing — why ±1.5μs matters for TDD:
TDD requires all gNBs in a network to switch from DL to UL at exactly the same time. If one RU switches 5μs late, its DL transmission overlaps with another cell's UL reception → interference. PTP (Precision Time Protocol) distributes timing from GPS-locked grandmaster clock to each RU via Ethernet. Required accuracy: ±1.5μs end-to-end. GPS holdover (when GPS signal lost): clock must maintain ±1.5μs for several hours.

Test equipment — EXA, EXM, VNA — specs, settings, use cases

Instrument purpose summary:
EXA N9010B (Spectrum/Signal Analyser): measures what the RU transmits — power, ACLR, EVM, SEM. Input always from BOB SMA via 30 dB pad. IP: 10.62.2.135, port 5025. EXM E6640A (VSG): injects calibrated signals into RU for RX tests — RSSI cal, sensitivity, PRACH. Output to BOB SMA via measured cable. VNA E5071C: measures RF paths — cable loss, connector VSWR, column-to-column phase difference for beamforming cal.
Key settings per measurement:
ACLR: EXA, atten 20dB, preamp OFF, ACLR mode LTE. Power: EXA, atten 20dB, preamp OFF, power meter mode. EVM: EXA, VSA mode or EVM function. RSSI cal: EXM inject known power, EXA verify EXM accuracy first. Phase cal: VNA, SOLT cal first, IFBW 1kHz, single frequency at band centre.

RF debugging — TX power failure tree, RX sensitivity fault isolation

TX power low — fault tree:
1. Measure at BOB SMA with EXA (atten 20dB, preamp OFF). 2. Power within ±1 dB of target? PASS. 3. Power low by fixed offset → TX_GAIN register wrong or tx_calibration_eeprom.json missing (fault 12). 4. Power varies → DPD not converged (wait 60s) or PA unstable. 5. Power zero → PA disabled, check RFFE_ENABLE register, PA bias voltage. 6. Power intermittent → loose BOB SMA connector.
RX sensitivity bad — fault tree:
1. Check cable loss with VNA. Subtract from EXM output → is injected power at RU port correct? 2. Run RSSI cal check: inject −95 dBm, read get_rssi → within ±2 dB of expected? 3. If RSSI cal off: re-run cal, update ADC_ADJUST. 4. If RSSI cal correct but PRACH detection rate low: LNA NF degraded (measure NF with EXA). 5. One column fails: physical inspection of that column cable and connector. 6. All columns fail equally: DSA value wrong in tc_cadence.json.

Interview preparation — what RF test engineer interviews actually ask

The 5 questions every RF test engineer interview includes:
1. What is receiver sensitivity and how is it calculated? (Know the formula cold: −174 + 10log(BW) + NF + SNR_req)
2. What is ACLR, what is the limit, and what causes failure? (−45 dBc, PA nonlinearity, DPD)
3. What is Noise Figure and why does the LNA dominate? (Friis formula, first stage dominates)
4. Walk me through setting up a TX power measurement. (BOB SMA, 30 dB pad, EXA, atten, preamp OFF, DPD wait)
5. You get an ACLR failure. What do you check first? (DPD converged? Measurement setup correct? Rated power correct?)
How to answer "tell me about a difficult RF problem you solved":
Use the STAR format: Situation (what were you testing), Task (what failed), Action (how you debugged using 5-Why), Result (what you found and fixed). Example: "During B1 sensitivity testing on unit 26050509, I observed a 6 dB TX power deficit on B41. I suspected a calibration issue. I checked whether tx_calibration_eeprom.json was present — it was missing (fault 12). Flashing the correct cal file resolved it immediately." This shows systematic thinking, instrument knowledge, and real hands-on experience.
What interviewers are actually testing:
RF knowledge is secondary — they want to see: (1) Do you think systematically? Change one variable at a time. (2) Do you know your instruments? Can you set up EXA correctly? (3) Can you explain technical concepts simply? This matters for customer calls. (4) Do you document your work? Results, procedure, root cause. (5) Do you know when to escalate? Not everything is fixable at the bench. The beginner section Q&A at the top of this guide has full answers to the top 10 questions — read all of them before any interview.

SensitivityWhy does sensitivity differ per band?LNA NF varies with frequency (lower freq = lower NF) · Duplexer loss differs · T/R switch adds loss (TDD) · same kTB but different system NF per band → different DSA offset

S-parametersS11=-6dB. What does this mean? Is it good?S11=-6dB = 25% reflected power, VSWR≈3:1. NOT good for RF port. Good match needs S11 below -20dB (1% reflected). Root cause: impedance mismatch at antenna connector or damaged cable.
Smith ChartLoad point is at right edge of Smith Chart. What is it?Right edge = pure resistance, no reactance. If at rightmost point (R=∞) = open circuit, Γ=+1, VSWR=∞. For matching network design, you navigate Smith Chart with L/C/transmission line segments to reach centre (50Ω).
uSleepuSleep test fails — EVM spike on symbol 0. Root cause?PA bias (Vgg) ramp-up is too slow. Bias not settled by start of first active symbol. Check RENESAS bias controller timing registers. Should be settled within <5μs before symbol start.
BeamformingB1 ACLR passes per-column but fails combined. Why?Cross-column phase alignment issue. When columns combine, their signals add coherently in main lobe direction but intermodulation products from slight phase mismatch create spectral regrowth. Check IQ calibration per column, verify DPD observation covers all columns.

L18 RF System Architecture ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ — Complete signal chain: L2/L3→PHY→Baseband→IQ→DAC→Upconverter→PLL→PA→Duplexer→Antenna + reverse RX path Core ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾

RF system architecture — end to end from core to antenna

How your AAU fits in the network:
Core (AMF/SMF/UPF) ↔ gNB (O-CU ↔ O-DU ↔ FHGW ↔ O-RU/AAU) ↔ UE. Your work is at the O-RU layer — you test the Radio Unit in isolation using PW's FHGW+DU as the counterpart. O-RAN standardises the O-RU↔O-DU interface (eCPRI + 7.2x split) so the O-RU must interoperate with any compliant O-DU. This is what the RCT conformance tests verify.
Power budget end to end:
gNB TX: +43 dBm (20W) per column at antenna port. Free space loss at 1km, 2140MHz: −99.6 dB. UE receive: +43 − 99.6 = −56.6 dBm. UE sensitivity: ~−105 dBm. DL margin: 48.4 dB. UE TX: +23 dBm. Free space loss: −99.6 dB. gNB receive: +23 − 99.6 = −76.6 dBm. gNB sensitivity: −99.25 dBm. UL margin: 22.6 dB. UL is the limiting direction — this is always why coverage is UL-limited.
Know every block's purpose, failure mode, and impact on the signal. For each block ask: What does it do? What happens to the signal? What can go wrong? How does a failure manifest at the measurement point (EXA/EXM)? The complete chain from L2 bits to radiated RF and back is your mental model for all debugging.

L19 RF Impairments — IQ Imbalance, LO Leakage, DC Offset, Phase Noise, CFO, PA Nonlinearity, AM-AM/AM-PM Distortion Advanced click to expand▾

RF impairments — IQ imbalance, LO leakage, phase noise, compression

IQ imbalance — cause and effect:
I and Q paths have slightly different gain or phase due to component mismatch. Effect: constellation rotates and compresses → EVM increases. On EXA constellation display: asymmetric clusters (amplitude imbalance) or rotated clusters (phase imbalance). Spec: IQ amplitude balance < 0.5 dB, IQ phase imbalance < 1°. Root cause: analog baseband circuit tolerance in the DAC/mixer.
LO leakage — DC offset in IQ:
If the LO signal leaks to the output, it appears as a large carrier at the centre frequency. In the IQ constellation: all symbols offset from origin. In spectrum: spike at band centre frequency (DC offset in baseband maps to carrier frequency after upconversion). Spec: LO leakage < −30 dBc. Causes: mixer imbalance, LO feedthrough, ground bounce in analog baseband.
Compression — PA P1dB impact:
As input power approaches P1dB, PA gain drops. In the constellation: all points compress inward toward origin (amplitude compression). In spectrum: ACLR increases (spectral regrowth). EVM worsens. DPD is designed to operate right at P1dB and compensate, but if DPD model is wrong or not converged, compression shows through.

L20 Synchronisation — GPS/GNSS, PTP IEEE 1588, SyncE, Holdover, Frequency/Phase/Time sync — critical in O-RAN TDD Advanced click to expand▾

Synchronisation — GPS, PTP IEEE 1588, sync chain for TDD

GPS to RU sync chain:
GPS satellite → GPS receiver at site → 10 MHz + 1PPS reference output → PTP Grandmaster Clock (IEEE 1588) → Ethernet switch (transparent or boundary clock) → DU (PTP slave, also boundary clock) → FHGW (PTP slave) → RU (PTP slave). Each hop adds timing error. Budget: GPS accuracy ±50 ns, each switch hop ±100 ns, end-to-end must stay within ±1.5 μs. Your DU shows PTP status: locked/holdover/freerun.
PTP profiles for telecom — G.8275.1 vs G.8275.2:
G.8275.1: full on-path support (all switches must be PTP-aware). Achieves ±100 ns. Required for Phase 2 TDD. G.8275.2: partial support (some switches can be non-PTP-aware). Achieves ±1 μs. Adequate for Phase 1. Your deployment uses whichever the DU and network switches support. Check DU config: ptp_profile = G.8275.1 or G.8275.2.
B41 TDD testing — what sync failure looks like:
No PTP lock → DU operates in freerun → TDD frame timing is arbitrary → DL/UL collision in your own cell → EXM injection during UL window hits the RU while PA is transmitting → LNA overloaded → sensitivity measurement completely wrong → all B41 RX tests fail with no apparent hardware fault. Always verify PTP lock (DU status: ptp_state = LOCKED) before any B41 test.
TDD bands (B41) are critically dependent on phase synchronisation. If PTP sync is lost and RU enters holdover, clock drift will eventually cause TDD DL/UL switching misalignment → interference → throughput collapse. Alarm: GPS Loss or PTP Loss triggers holdover mode.
THE WHY FRAMEWORK
Why it exists
TDD B41 cannot work without timing sync
Problem solved
Unsynchronised TDD = DL/UL collision = LNA damage
Hardware
GPS receiver, PTP grandmaster, FHGW, RU PTP client
Standard
3GPP TS 36.133, IEEE 1588-2008, G.8275.1
How measured
DU PTP status: LOCKED/HOLDOVER, PTP offset stats
Pass/fail
PTP offset < ±1.5 μs continuously
Common failures
GPS loss → holdover → drift beyond ±1.5μs → B41 failure
Debug
Check GPS antenna, PTP config, holdover spec
Interview Q
Why is PTP synchronisation critical for TDD?
Customer impact
B41 cell off-air whenever GPS signal degrades
L21 Timing Advance — LTE TA, NR TA, cell radius, propagation delay L21 click to expand▾

Timing Advance — why every UE must transmit early

Why TA exists:
All UEs must arrive at the gNB at exactly the same time within the subframe window. A UE 10 km away has 33 μs propagation delay — if it transmitted at the subframe boundary, its signal arrives late and collides with the next UE. TA tells the UE to advance its transmission by 2× the propagation delay (round trip). In your lab: EXM cable ≈ 0 propagation → TA = 0. PRACH sensitivity tests still work because there is no real propagation to compensate.
How TA is measured:
When UE sends a PRACH preamble, gNB measures arrival time of correlation peak vs expected time. Offset = propagation delay. gNB sends RAR (Random Access Response) with TA value. UE advances UL timing by that amount. LTE TA granularity: 0.52 μs per step. Max TA: 0.67 ms → 100 km theoretical cell radius. TA continuously updated during call as UE moves.
NR TA vs LTE TA:
NR TA granularity is finer (0.5 μs) and includes a TA offset per carrier for multi-carrier operation. NR also introduces a TA timer — if the UE does not receive a TA update within the timer, it falls back to PRACH to re-establish timing. This is more robust but means PRACH sensitivity matters more in NR than LTE.
THE WHY FRAMEWORK
Why it exists
UL timing alignment between UEs
Problem solved
UL collision between UEs at gNB
Hardware
PRACH detector, MAC scheduler
Standard
3GPP TS 36.213, 38.213
How measured
PRACH arrival time offset measurement
Pass/fail
Within guard period window
Common failures
TA drift post-HO, cell edge timing
Debug
Check PRACH timing stats in logs
Interview Q
Explain how TA is measured and applied
Customer impact
UEs at cell edge cannot connect if TA fails
L22 Beamforming ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ — Analog/Digital/Hybrid beamforming, Beam Sweeping, Beam Management, Beam Failure Recovery Core ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾

Beamforming — analog, digital, hybrid; your 4T4R AAU

How your 4T4R AAU does beamforming:
4 TX columns (A/B/C/D), each connected to a separate PA. Phase shifter (PE44820DS) applied per column digitally. Baseband beamforming weights computed by O-DU scheduler based on UE channel feedback (CSI-RS/SRS measurements). Phase weights sent to FHGW → applied to each column's IQ stream before DAC. Result: constructive interference in desired UE direction, destructive in other directions.
MRC on the RX side — how 4 columns combine:
Maximum Ratio Combining weights each column's received signal by its own SNR quality. Column with strong LNA and clean cable gets high weight. Degraded column gets low weight automatically. Algebraically: output SNR = Σ(SNR_i) for all columns i. For 4 equal columns: output SNR = 4× single column SNR = +6 dB. This is why combined sensitivity is always 5–6 dB better than single-column sensitivity.
Beamforming gain in the link budget:
Beamforming gain (TX): for 4-column phased array, beam gain ≈ 10·log(4) = +6 dBi over isotropic per column = +6 dB EIRP improvement. With 4 columns transmitting coherently: total EIRP = single_column_power + 4_column_BF_gain = +43 dBm + 6 dB = +49 dBm EIRP (excluding antenna element gain). Antenna element gain adds another 8–12 dBi. Total EIRP can reach +60 dBm for a 4T4R AAU with panel antenna.
THE WHY FRAMEWORK
Why it exists
Beamforming is what makes your 4T4R AAU valuable
Problem solved
Single-antenna = no coverage shaping, no MRC gain
Hardware
4 PAs, 4 LNAs, PE44820DS phase shifters, ADC 4 channels
Standard
3GPP TS 36.211, O-RAN beamforming specs
How measured
VNA S21 phase per column, OTA if available
Pass/fail
All columns within ±2° phase error
Common failures
Dead column → 1.5-2dB MRC loss, beam direction error
Debug
VNA phase cal → identify which column offset → correct register
Interview Q
How does beamforming steer a beam direction?
Customer impact
Coverage holes at specific angles if beam points wrong
L23 MIMO — SISO to Massive MIMO, SU-MIMO, MU-MIMO, spatial multiplexing L23 ⭐⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾

MIMO — how multiple antennas multiply capacity

Spatial multiplexing — the core idea:
MIMO creates multiple independent spatial channels between gNB and UE using multipath scattering. Each channel carries a separate data stream. A 4×4 MIMO system can carry 4 independent streams simultaneously on the same frequency — quadrupling capacity without extra bandwidth. Richer scattering environment (indoor, urban) = better MIMO performance. Open field = poor scattering = MIMO gain disappears.
Your 4T4R AAU — MIMO in practice:
4 TX columns (A/B/C/D) with 4 PAs + 4 LNAs. TX side: typically used for beamforming (all 4 columns phase-shifted to steer beam in one direction) rather than 4-stream spatial multiplexing. RX side: MRC combining across 4 columns gives +6 dB diversity gain. Full 4-stream SU-MIMO requires UE to have 4 receive antennas — rare on phones, common on CPE. Typical: 2-stream MIMO per UE + 4T4R for beamforming gain.
MRC diversity gain — why dead RX columns matter:
Maximum Ratio Combining weights each column by its SNR. Output SNR = sum of all column SNRs. For 4 equal columns: output SNR = 4× single column = +6 dB. Each dead RX column loses 1.5-2 dB of MRC gain. In your unit 26050510: B1C, B1D dead, B3D dead → 2 columns lost for B1 = −3 dB sensitivity degradation. This is why individual column RX failures directly affect sensitivity test results.
THE WHY FRAMEWORK
Why it exists
Multiply spectral efficiency without more bandwidth
Problem solved
Single-stream capacity bottleneck
Hardware
Multiple PA/LNA/ADC per column
Standard
3GPP TS 36.211 / 38.211
How measured
EVM per layer, MRC gain measurement
Pass/fail
Per-stream EVM, diversity gain
Common failures
High column correlation, bad channel rank
Debug
Check antenna spacing, SRS config, column health
Interview Q
Difference between MIMO diversity and spatial multiplexing
Customer impact
Lower than expected peak throughput
L24 Calibration — TX/RX/IQ/Temperature/Gain/Phase/Factory/Field — the most overlooked area, critical for accurate measurements Advanced click to expand▾

Calibration — TX/RX/IQ/temperature/gain/phase all in one place

All calibration types and when to run:
TX gain cal: at factory, after PA replacement, after firmware with new DAC_SCALE. Output: tx_calibration_eeprom.json.
RX gain cal (= RSSI cal): at factory, when cable changed, when temp drift > 3 dB. Output: ADC_ADJUST in hardware.json.
IQ cal: at factory, if EVM degrades without other explanation. Corrects I/Q amplitude and phase imbalance in analog frontend.
Temp compensation cal: at factory, at multiple temperatures. Output: TEMP_COMP table in hardware.json.
Phase cal: at factory, if beamforming direction is wrong. Output: PE44820DS register values.
Which cal to run when things go wrong:
TX power wrong → TX gain cal. RSSI wrong → RSSI cal. Beam pointing wrong → phase cal. EVM degraded → IQ cal. Measurements drift with temperature → temp comp cal. All cals drifted after drop/shock → full factory recal. After firmware update changes DAC or ADC settings → TX gain cal + RSSI cal.
THE WHY FRAMEWORK
Why it exists
Calibration is what makes measurements meaningful
Problem solved
Uncalibrated RU gives wrong numbers → wrong decisions
Hardware
All RF hardware + calibration equipment
Standard
IEC 17025 (calibration lab standard)
How measured
Inject known power, measure response, compute offset
Pass/fail
ADC_ADJUST accurate to ±1dB, TX power ±0.5dB of target
Common failures
Forgetting to recal after hardware change or temp shift
Debug
Which cal? TX power wrong→TX gain cal, RSSI off→RSSI cal
Interview Q

L25 Temperature testing — RF performance at −40°C to +70°C L25 ⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾

Temperature testing — RF performance changes with heat and cold

Why temperature changes RF performance:
GaN PA transconductance decreases at high temperature → gain drops (typically −0.02 dB/°C). At cold: gain increases, risk of over-power. DPD coefficients calibrated at room temperature become invalid at extremes — the PA nonlinearity profile changes, so pre-distortion no longer matches → ACLR worsens. RSSI readings drift because ADC_ADJUST was calibrated at a specific temperature. All of these effects require TEMP_COMP (temperature compensation) tables in hardware.json.
Classic interview scenario — RSSI fails at +55°C:
RSSI cal done at +25°C → TEMP_COMP table missing → LNA gain drifts −0.5 dB at 55°C → ADC_ADJUST is now wrong by 0.5 dB → get_rssi reads 0.5 dB low → exceeds ±2 dB limit. Fix: run RSSI cal at both 25°C and 55°C, measure temperature coefficient, populate TEMP_COMP table. This exact scenario appears in real product qualification and in interviews at Ericsson, Nokia, and similar companies.
3GPP temperature test points:
3GPP TS 36.141 Annex C defines test conditions: Normal (25°C ±5°C), Extreme low (−30°C for indoor, −40°C for outdoor), Extreme high (+55°C for indoor, +55°C for outdoor with solar radiation add). All conformance tests must pass at all temperature conditions. The RU must maintain all specs across the full range — not just at room temperature. Qualification testing requires running the full RCT at each temperature point, typically 3-4 days of testing per temperature point.
THE WHY FRAMEWORK
Why it exists
Products deploy in −40 to +70°C environments
Problem solved
RF components change gain/NF with temperature
Hardware
PA, LNA, ADC, TEMP_COMP firmware
Standard
3GPP TS 36.141 Annex C environmental
How measured
Full RCT at each temperature point
Pass/fail
All specs pass at all temperatures
Common failures
RSSI drift, ACLR at cold, PA shutdown at hot
Debug
TEMP_COMP table, DPD re-convergence trigger
Interview Q
RSSI fails only at high temperature — debug
Customer impact
Field units failing in summer heat or winter cold
L26 Environmental testing — thermal, humidity, rain, salt fog, dust L26 ⭐⭐ click to expand▾

Environmental testing — the RU must survive its deployment environment

Why env testing is separate from RF testing:
An RU might pass all RF specs in a clean lab at 25°C but fail in deployment due to: condensation shorting PCB traces (humidity), connector corrosion from sea air (salt fog), solder joint cracking from thermal expansion cycles. Environmental tests simulate the full deployment lifecycle — 10-15 years of outdoor exposure — in 50-200 hours of accelerated aging. Full RF RCT is run after each environmental test to verify no performance degradation.
Thermal cycling — the most common long-term failure mode:
Temperature cycling between −40°C and +70°C expands and contracts PCB and solder joints at different rates (thermal expansion mismatch). Over 100s of cycles, solder joints develop micro-cracks → intermittent connections → RF failures that only appear in the field. Qualification: typically 200-500 thermal cycles with RF check after each block of 50. ACLR starting to degrade at cycle 150: solder joint fatigue at PA or connector.
IP rating and what it means for connector integrity:
Outdoor RU enclosures must be IP65 minimum. Testing: spray chamber with water jets for 15 minutes from all angles, verify no ingress and full RF function after. The most common IP failure: O-ring seal around a connector bulkhead degrades after thermal cycling, allowing water ingress. Water on RF PCB → corrosion → intermittent RSSI errors in field → impossible to reproduce in lab. Always inspect all gaskets and O-rings when diagnosing intermittent field failures.
THE WHY FRAMEWORK
Why it exists
Products deploy outdoors in all climates
Problem solved
Lab conditions don't represent real deployment
Hardware
All RF hardware + mechanical enclosure
Standard
IEC 60068 series, ETSI EN 300 019
How measured
Full RF RCT after each environmental stress
Pass/fail
All RF specs pass after stress
Common failures
Intermittent faults after thermal cycling
Debug
Inspect solder joints, gaskets, connectors under microscope
Interview Q
ACLR degrades in field after 6 months — how to diagnose?
Customer impact

L27 Power supply — sequencing, inrush current, ripple, brownout L27 ⭐⭐ click to expand▾

Power supply — PSU quality directly affects RF output quality

PSU ripple → spurious — a hidden RF link:
DC power supply with AC ripple at frequency f creates AM sidebands on the RF output at ±f from the carrier. A 50 Hz ripple at 50 mV p-p on the PA drain supply creates spurs at carrier ±50 Hz visible in EXA with narrow RBW. This is why PSU ripple spec exists. Always measure PSU ripple with oscilloscope before blaming RF chain for unexplained spurious emissions.
Brownout — the field failure that looks like PA fault:
"PA enters protection after 20 minutes." Classic brownout: operator site has marginal −48V supply. Under load, Vdc drops to −43V. PA Vdd droops. PA gain drops → TX power falls below threshold → power protection fires. Looks like PA hardware failure. Actually a site power problem. Test: run RCT with variable PSU, sweep Vdc from −40V to −57V, verify all RF specs across full range. Telecom spec: −48V ±10%.
Power sequencing — must be correct to avoid hardware damage:
FPGA requires: core voltage (1.0V) stable before I/O voltage (1.8V). PA requires: RF path enabled before PA bias applied. Wrong sequence = FPGA latchup or PA oscillation. Verify with oscilloscope triggered on power-on event — all rails must rise in specified order within specified timing. This is a manufacturing test step that is verified at ICT (In-Circuit Test) before each unit is shipped.
THE WHY FRAMEWORK
Why it exists
All RF performance depends on clean DC power
Problem solved
PSU problems cause RF faults that look like hardware
Hardware
PA bias circuit, FPGA power rails
Standard
ETSI EN 300 132-2 telecom power supply
How measured
RF measurement + oscilloscope simultaneously
Pass/fail
All RF specs at ±10% Vdc variation
Common failures
PA protection at brownout, spurious from ripple
Debug
Measure ripple with scope, sweep Vdc during RCT
Interview Q
TX power drops after 20 minutes — thermal or supply?
Customer impact
Site power variation causing intermittent outages
L28 Fault Management — PA Over-Temperature, VSWR Alarm, Fan Failure, GPS Loss, PTP Loss, Low Output Power, Carrier Failure Intermediate click to expand▾

Fault management — PA over-temperature, VSWR alarm, fan, power faults

PA over-temperature — the most common fault:
Trigger: junction temperature exceeds threshold (typically 85–95°C). Action: immediate PA power reduction or shutdown. Recovery: automatic when temperature drops 10°C below threshold. Root causes: (1) Ambient temperature too high (>55°C inlet), (2) Heatsink contact poor (wrong thermal paste, loose mounting screws), (3) PA operating at higher than rated power (TX_GAIN miscalibrated high), (4) Fan failed. In your lab: PA protection firing repeatedly = check ambient temp first, then PA power level, then heatsink.
VSWR alarm — when the antenna fights back:
Trigger: reflected power > threshold (VSWR > 3.0 typically). Action: PA power reduction to protect PA from load mismatch. Root causes in lab: (1) Loose BOB SMA connector, (2) Cable disconnected at antenna port, (3) Wrong cable type (wrong impedance), (4) Antenna port left open during TX test. Always connect a 50Ω termination to any unused TX port before enabling RF. VSWR fault that clears when you wiggle a cable = connector problem — replace immediately.
Fault 12 — missing tx_calibration_eeprom.json:
This specific fault caused your ~6 dB B41 power deficit on unit 26050509. The RU boots, reads tx_calibration_eeprom.json for TX gain register values. If file missing or corrupted: RU uses default register values (typically lower than calibrated), resulting in TX power 3–8 dB below target. Symptom: TX power consistently low across all columns for that band, no other faults, DPD functioning normally. Fix: flash correct tx_calibration_eeprom.json. Always verify with EXA immediately after flash before signing off.
THE WHY FRAMEWORK
Why it exists
Faults tell you what is wrong — you must interpret them
Problem solved
Unread faults → problems compound and cause outages
Hardware
PA thermal, VSWR detector, GPS receiver, power monitor
Standard
O-RAN fault management, 3GPP TS 28.545
How measured
NETCONF alarm notification, journalctl fault log
Pass/fail
All alarms correctly map to root cause, clear after fix
Common failures
Ignoring fault 12 (missing cal file) → TX power wrong
Debug
Read fault → identify component → check that component first
Interview Q

L29 Network management — NETCONF, YANG, O1 interface, M-plane L29 ⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾

Network management — how operators configure and monitor the RU remotely

NETCONF/YANG — the language of RU configuration:
NETCONF is the protocol for network device configuration over SSH (port 830). YANG defines what parameters exist and their valid ranges. O-RAN Alliance defines standard YANG models for O-RU: tx-array-carrier (frequency, bandwidth, power), rx-array-carrier, alarms (PA temperature, VSWR, GPS loss). In production, operators configure the RU entirely via NETCONF — no CLI. When you change band config or TX power via CLI in the lab, you are doing manually what the NMS does via NETCONF in deployment.
O1 interface — four management functions:
Configuration (edit-config to set frequencies, power, bandwidth), Performance Management (PM counters: RSSI per RB, ACLR history, temperature logs), Fault Management (alarm notifications: PA protection, GPS loss, carrier failure), Software Management (SW upgrade over O1). A NETCONF edit-config sets tx-carrier-frequency. A NETCONF get returns current temperature reading. An alarm notification arrives when PA protection fires.
For Ericsson/Nokia/PW interviews:
Be able to explain: NETCONF session establishment (SSH → hello → capabilities exchange → edit-config/get). Know YANG container/list/leaf. Know that oran-o-ru-hardware.yang and oran-o-ru-interfaces.yang are key O-RAN models. YANG constraint violations return rpc-error — common source of M-plane integration failures. Be able to read a YANG edit-config XML snippet and identify what it configures.
THE WHY FRAMEWORK
Why it exists
Remote config and monitoring of deployed RUs
Problem solved
Manual CLI is not scalable to 1000s of sites
Hardware
All RU hardware parameters + network stack
Standard
O-RAN WG4 M-plane spec, RFC 6241 (NETCONF)
How measured
NETCONF get-config, compare against expected YANG
Pass/fail
All parameters within YANG-defined ranges
Common failures
NETCONF session fails, wrong parameter applied
Debug
Wireshark/tcpdump on port 830 to capture NETCONF XML

L30 Transport — eCPRI, Ethernet, VLAN, QoS, fronthaul/backhaul L30 ⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾

Transport — the network path that carries your RF signal

eCPRI fronthaul — strict latency requirements:
eCPRI carries IQ data between O-RU and O-DU over Ethernet. C-plane (control: scheduling, timing) requires < 100 μs one-way latency. If fronthaul latency exceeds the budget: IQ data arrives too late for IFFT → dropped symbols → BLER increases → throughput drops. Every Ethernet switch between RU and DU adds latency — must be measured and budgeted. In your bench: FHGW and RU directly connected → fronthaul latency ≈ 1 μs.
VLAN and QoS — why misconfiguration causes intermittent RF failures:
eCPRI, PTP, and NETCONF share the same Ethernet network. Without QoS: a network burst can delay PTP timing packets → TDD sync loss → B41 DL/UL collision. VLAN separates traffic types. QoS assigns highest priority (DSCP EF) to eCPRI and PTP. Misconfigured QoS is a common field issue causing intermittent TDD frame timing errors that are impossible to reproduce in lab without load on the transport network.
Fronthaul vs backhaul — key distinction:
Fronthaul: O-RU ↔ O-DU, eCPRI, < 100 μs, < 20 km. Midhaul: O-DU ↔ O-CU, MAC/RLC PDUs, less latency-sensitive. Backhaul: O-CU ↔ Core, standard IP, tolerates higher latency. In field troubleshooting: if PRACH detection fails intermittently, check fronthaul packet loss with tcpdump on DU eCPRI interface before assuming RU hardware fault.
THE WHY FRAMEWORK
Why it exists
RU IQ data must reach DU with bounded latency
Problem solved
Fronthaul delay causes IQ loss → BLER increase
Hardware
eCPRI switch, SFP+ optics, Ethernet stack
Standard
O-RAN WG4 fronthaul spec, eCPRI spec v2.0
How measured
iperf3 throughput, Wireshark timing, ping latency
Pass/fail
eCPRI latency < 100 μs, PTP ±1.5 μs
Common failures
QoS misconfiguration → TDD sync loss under load
Debug
tcpdump fronthaul port, check PTP offset stats
Interview Q

L31 Linux — journalctl, tcpdump, grep, awk, ssh for RF engineers L31 ⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾

Linux — the operating system your RU runs on

Why RF engineers need Linux comfort:
Your RU runs embedded Linux. All RU processes (ruauto, DPD engine, NETCONF server, PTP daemon) are Linux services. When something fails in the field, you SSH into the RU and use Linux commands to: read logs, check services, capture network traffic, check CPU/memory. Without Linux, you cannot debug field issues remotely — you must physically ship the unit back.
Most useful commands for daily RCT work:
journalctl -fu ruauto: live follow ruauto test logs. grep -i "fault|error|fail" /var/log/rru/*.log | tail -50: find recent errors. tcpdump -i eth0 -n udp dst port 319: capture PTP packets. cat /sys/class/hwmon/hwmon0/temp1_input: read PA temperature directly. awk -F"," "NR>1{sum+=$3;count++} END{print sum/count}" rssi_results.csv: compute average RSSI from results.
Scripting leverage — 3× test throughput:
Engineers who automate with Python + Shell: parse 1000-line log files in 2 minutes instead of 2 hours, run multi-band sweeps overnight unattended, generate pass/fail summary reports automatically. The most valuable skill combination for a junior RF engineer wanting to stand out: Linux command line + Python SCPI automation. It demonstrates both technical depth and practical engineering efficiency.

L32 Scripting — Python SCPI, Shell automation, YAML/JSON config L32 ⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾

Scripting — automation separates good engineers from great ones

Three scripts you should be able to write today:
1. RSSI linearity sweep: inject −60 to −110 dBm in 1 dB steps with EXM, read get_rssi at each step, plot linearity, flag deviation > 2 dB. 2. Multi-band ACLR monitor: loop B1/B3/B8/B28/B41, measure ACLR per band, write JSON results, Slack alert on failure. 3. DPD convergence tracker: measure ACLR every 5s after TX enable, plot ACLR vs time, report convergence time. These three automate the most common manual verification tasks.
Python SCPI pattern:
import socket, time
class Instr:
def __init__(self,ip): self.s=socket.socket(); self.s.connect((ip,5025))
def send(self,c): self.s.send((c+chr(10)).encode())
def query(self,c): self.send(c); return self.s.recv(4096).decode().strip()
exa=Instr("10.62.2.135")
exa.send(":FREQ:CENT 2.14e9")
aclr=float(exa.query(":FETCH:ACLR?"))
print("PASS" if aclr<-45 else "FAIL", aclr)
JSON results parsing — stop reading files manually:
import json
with open("rct_results.json") as f: r=json.load(f)
fails=[t for t in r["tests"] if t["result"]=="FAIL"]
for f in fails: print(f['group']+"/"+f['test']+": "+str(f['measured']))
Processing 100 test cases: script = 2 minutes, manual = 2 hours.

L33 RF safety — SAR, EIRP limits, EMC, EMI, human exposure L33 ⭐⭐ click to expand▾

RF safety — protecting people and passing regulatory requirements

SAR vs MPE — two different metrics for two different products:
SAR (Specific Absorption Rate, W/kg): RF energy absorbed by body tissue. Used for devices held close to body (phones, tablets). FCC limit: 1.6 W/kg averaged over 1g tissue. Test: phantom head with tissue-simulating liquid. Not relevant for fixed base stations. MPE (Maximum Permissible Exposure): field strength limit at a distance from an antenna. Used for base stations. At 2 GHz: 1 mW/cm² general population limit. Creates an exclusion zone 3–10m in front of the panel.
EMC — why your RU must not interfere with neighbours:
EMC testing verifies: (1) RU does not emit unintended radiation that interferes with other equipment (emissions test), (2) RU continues to work when subjected to external interference (immunity test). CE marking requires EN 55032 (emissions) and EN 55035 (immunity). Failure: RU interferes with adjacent cellular bands, medical equipment, or airport radar. Tested in anechoic chamber with spectrum analyser measuring radiated emissions from RU in all directions.
Lab safety — what you must actually do:
In your bench: +43 dBm = 20W of RF power at antenna port. At close range: RF burns to skin, hazardous to eyes. Always use: dummy load on unused antenna ports, 30 dB attenuator between BOB SMA and EXA, shielded cables. The BOB SMA output at +13 dBm (before pad) is still above comfortable unprotected handling levels. The 30 dB pad is not optional — it protects both you and the EXA input.
THE WHY FRAMEWORK
Why it exists
Protect humans, regulatory compliance for market access
Problem solved
Without limits: RF energy causes tissue heating
Hardware
Antenna, PA, EMC shielding
Standard
FCC OET Bulletin 65, ICNIRP, CE directives
How measured
SAR: phantom measurement, MPE: field strength at distance
Pass/fail
SAR < 1.6 W/kg, MPE within limit at exclusion zone
Common failures
Forgotten attenuator, open antenna port during TX
Debug
Check test setup, use dummy load, verify attenuation

L34 Standards — 3GPP, O-RAN, ETSI, FCC, CE, PTCRB, GCF L34 ⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾

Standards — the rulebooks every RF engineer must know

3GPP — your primary reference:
All LTE and 5G NR specifications. For your work: TS 36.141 (LTE base station conformance — defines every ACLR, EVM, sensitivity limit you test against), TS 38.141-2 (NR OTA), TS 36.104 (LTE BS radio requirements), TS 38.104 (NR). When you set a pass/fail limit in tc_cadence.json, it comes from these documents. Knowing which clause defines which limit shows expertise in interviews.
O-RAN Alliance — critical for your specific job:
O-RAN WG4 defines the fronthaul interface: eCPRI compression spec, M-plane YANG models, C/U/S-plane timing requirements. When PW AAU deploys with a non-PW DU, interoperability is verified against O-RAN WG4 specs. Key document: O-RAN.WG4.CUS.0-v07.00 (fronthaul interface spec). Your RCT work on eCPRI timing and M-plane configuration directly validates WG4 requirements.
FCC vs CE — market determines what you test:
Product sold in US requires FCC ID. Product in Europe requires CE marking. Underlying RF performance (3GPP) is the same, but regulatory approval differs. FCC: certified test lab measures conducted and radiated emissions. CE: Declaration of Conformity supported by Technical File. Your RCT covers 3GPP conformance — regulatory approval is separate but uses many of the same measurements.

L35 Manufacturing — PCB assembly, factory calibration, end-of-line test, burn-in L35 ⭐⭐ click to expand▾

Manufacturing — how an RU goes from components to deployed product

Factory calibration — why it is unique per unit:
Every RU has different component values due to manufacturing tolerance. Factory calibration measures the actual performance of each specific unit and writes correction values to EEPROM (tx_calibration_eeprom.json, hardware.json). Unique to each serial number — cannot use unit 26050509 cal file on unit 26050508. When fault 12 (missing cal file) occurs, the unit uses defaults that assume perfect components → typically 3-6 dB wrong.
End-of-line testing — fast subset of full RCT:
EOL test must complete in < 30 minutes to maintain factory throughput. Tests: TX power per band per column, ACLR per band (is DPD working?), RSSI calibration verification, basic boot and connectivity. Full RCT (2-3 hours) runs on sample units per batch and on units returned from field. Your RCT framework is the detailed version of the EOL test.
Burn-in — catching infant mortality failures:
Components follow a bathtub curve: high failure rate early (manufacturing defects), then low steady-state, then increasing at end of life. Burn-in at +55°C for 24-72 hours at full TX power stresses marginal solder joints and components. What would fail in the first month of deployment fails during burn-in instead. After burn-in: another EOL test run to confirm all specs still pass.

Problem solved

L36 Certification — FCC, CE, PTCRB, GCF, operator acceptance L36 ⭐⭐ click to expand▾

Certification — the path from your bench to the operator network

Your role — saving money at the certification gate:
Your RCT work is the pre-certification validation. Goal: find and fix all failures before the product goes to an accredited test lab. Every failure found in the cert lab costs: test campaign pause ($5-10k/day), engineering fix time, re-test fee, schedule delay (weeks to months). Finding and fixing in your lab saves 10-100× the cost. Rigorous RCT is commercially critical, not just technically correct.
Operator acceptance — the final commercial gate:
Even with FCC/CE and 3GPP conformance, operators run their own acceptance tests: performance in their specific radio environment, interoperability with their DU vendor, energy efficiency (watts per Mbps), remote management via their NMS. Failure at this stage means no purchase order despite all prior certifications. Your RCT results are often submitted as evidence during operator acceptance.
Certification cost reality:
A 3GPP conformance test campaign at an accredited lab: 6-12 weeks, $50k-$200k. FCC filing: $5k-$20k. CE Declaration: $10k-$50k. Operator acceptance testing: $50k-$300k. Total certification budget for a new product: $200k-$500k. One failure requiring re-test: $20k-$50k additional. This is why pre-certification RCT investment is economically justified — catching 1 failure in your lab saves the full re-test cost.

L37 Customer acceptance — field trial, optimisation, commercial launch L37 ⭐⭐ click to expand▾

Customer acceptance — what operators actually care about in field

Why your lab margins matter to the operator:
Operator's lab acceptance team reviews your RCT results: are all 3GPP-mandated tests present? Did all pass? Are margins good (ACLR −52 dBc vs −45 limit = 7 dB margin)? Can results be reproduced? Poor margins = risk of field failures when conditions are not ideal. An operator will not accept a product that barely passes in lab conditions — field conditions (temperature, humidity, cable aging) will push it to fail.
Field trial KPIs — what the operator measures:
RSRP (coverage), SINR (quality), DL/UL throughput, PRACH success rate, handover success rate, call drop rate, energy consumption per Mbps. Your RCT tests directly predict these: bad ACLR → interference → low SINR → low throughput → unhappy operator. Understanding this chain makes you a more commercially aware RF engineer.
CAPEX vs OPEX — the business context:
CAPEX: hardware purchase, site installation. Operators want RUs that work first time (no return-to-factory). OPEX: power ($/year), maintenance. Operators want efficient RUs (lower power bill) manageable remotely (no truck roll). Your work contributes to both: good RCT = first-time-right deployment (CAPEX), automation = low maintenance (OPEX), efficiency testing = operational savings over 10-year life.

L38 KPI Correlation — Bad ACLR → Interference → Low SINR → Low CQI → Lower MCS → Lower Throughput Advanced click to expand▾

KPI Correlation — how RF quality maps to network performance

The ACLR → throughput cascade:
Bad ACLR (−42 dBc, fails −45 dBc limit) → TX signal leaks into adjacent channel → neighbour cell UEs experience interference → SINR degrades from 20 dB to 10 dB → scheduler forced from 64QAM to QPSK → throughput drops from 75 Mbps to 20 Mbps → UE experiences slow connection → operator KPI "average throughput" degrades. Every RF spec failure has a direct path to a user-visible KPI.
EVM → MCS → throughput:
High EVM (e.g. 6% for 64QAM limit 8%) → CQI reported by UE is lower → scheduler uses lower MCS → 25% throughput reduction. EVM is the TX quality metric that most directly affects user throughput. This is why operators set tight EVM specs and treat EVM failure as a revenue impact, not just a technical inconvenience.
Sensitivity → coverage → PRACH success rate:
Sensitivity 3 dB worse than spec → cell coverage radius shrinks 30% → cell edge UEs cannot attach → PRACH failure rate increases → Random Access success rate KPI degrades → operator "network availability" KPI fails. Your DSA sensitivity test directly predicts this coverage outcome.

L39 End-to-End Troubleshooting ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ — Alarm→Logs→Protocol→RF→Hardware→Software→Root Cause Core ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾

End-to-end troubleshooting — alarm → log → protocol → RF → hardware → root cause

The complete E2E chain:
Alarm (Carrier B3 Output Power Low) → logs (journalctl: DPD_STATUS=not_converged) → protocol (eCPRI link up? B3 carrier enabled?) → RF (EXA: TX power −20 dBm vs −15.7 target) → hardware (tx_calibration_eeprom.json missing for B3) → root cause: factory cal file not flashed → fix: reflash cal file → verify: power now −15.5 dBm ✓.
Tools at each layer:
Alarm: NMS dashboard, NETCONF notification. Log: journalctl, dmesg, rct_results.json. Protocol: Wireshark (eCPRI), tcpdump (NETCONF), ping (connectivity). RF: EXA (spectrum/power/ACLR), EXM (inject known signal), VNA (cable/VSWR/phase). Hardware: multimeter (bias voltages), thermal camera, oscilloscope (power rails). Root cause: 5-Why — change ONE variable at a time.
Most common E2E mistake:
Jumping to hardware replacement before exhausting software and configuration checks. Typical field failure split: 40% configuration/firmware, 30% installation (cable/connector), 20% transport/network, 10% actual hardware. Always follow the chain top-down before opening the enclosure.

L40 Product lifecycle — requirements → design → validation → deployment → maintenance L40 ⭐⭐ click to expand▾

Product lifecycle — understanding where your work fits

RF validation — the most critical quality gate:
RF validation is the gate between design and market. Every design decision (antenna spacing, PA selection, LNA choice, duplexer spec) manifests as a pass or fail in your lab. Finding failures in RF validation is good — it is the cheapest place to find them. Finding them after certification costs 100×. Finding them after deployment costs 1000× (recall, reputation damage, SLA penalties).
How your RCT connects to every lifecycle phase:
Requirements: ACLR limit (−45 dBc) comes from 3GPP TS 36.141 — you test against it. Design: link budget predicts sensitivity (−99 dBm) — you verify the prediction. Validation: your RCT is the validation. Certification: your results provide evidence for the cert lab. Maintenance: when a field unit fails, you reproduce the failure in the lab using the same RCT framework. Understanding the full lifecycle makes every test more meaningful.
CI/CD in hardware development:
Every firmware commit triggers automated smoke RCT (15 min, key tests), full RCT on release candidates (2-3 hours). Regression tracking shows if a commit broke something. PreChecks before every session catch setup issues automatically. This Agile approach finds firmware bugs early — before they reach the certification stage. Your automated scripts must be robust, fast, and unambiguous in their pass/fail output.

L41 Telecom business context — CAPEX/OPEX, energy efficiency, why operators care L41 ⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾

Telecom business context — RF engineering decisions have financial consequences

Why operators care about every dB of sensitivity:
A 1 dB sensitivity improvement extends cell coverage by ~12% (coverage radius ∝ 10^(dB/20)). More coverage = fewer sites = less CAPEX. A 3 dB improvement doubles coverage radius — halves number of sites for same coverage. This is why operators negotiate hard on sensitivity specs and why DSA sensitivity tests are commercially critical — they directly determine how much the operator spends on infrastructure.
Energy efficiency — a major commercial differentiator:
10,000-site network at 2 kW per site = 20 MW = ~$17M/year in electricity. A 10% efficiency improvement = $1.7M/year saving. uSleep (70% power reduction when idle) and Dynamic Vdd (15% average reduction) are not academic features — they are selling points that win contracts. When you test and characterise these features, you are generating data that the sales team uses in commercial negotiations.
EVM → MCS → throughput → revenue:
High EVM forces scheduler to use lower MCS (QPSK instead of 64QAM) → lower throughput → lower operator revenue per site. A cell doing 100 Mbps vs 150 Mbps due to poor EVM forcing lower MCS costs the operator 33% of that cell's revenue capacity. This is why EVM limits are tight and EVM failure is treated seriously by operators — it is a direct revenue impact, not just a technical measurement.

L42 AI for RF ⭐⭐⭐⭐ — AI-based DPD, Fault Prediction, Power Optimization, Beam Optimization, Anomaly Detection, RCA Future ⭐⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾

AI for RF — DPD, fault prediction, beam optimisation, anomaly detection

AI-based DPD — the most mature application:
Traditional DPD uses polynomial model. AI/ML DPD uses LSTM neural network to model PA nonlinearity including memory effects — more accurate, especially at high power and high PAPR. Result: 1-3 dB better ACLR. Already deployed by Ericsson and Huawei. Downside: neural network inference requires more compute → higher FPGA/DSP load.
AI fault prediction — proactive vs reactive maintenance:
Train model on historical temperature trends, RSSI variation, ACLR history. Model predicts: "this PA likely to fail within 2 weeks." Operator dispatches maintenance before failure → no outage. Your RCT measurement data (RSSI, ACLR, temperature over time) is the training data for these models. Collecting and archiving your test data properly has value beyond just pass/fail.
AI beam optimisation — replacing manual tuning:
Traditional: operators manually tune antenna tilt/power/weights site by site. AI: train on KPI data across thousands of sites, automatically optimise per site. Estimated improvement: 5-15% throughput with no hardware change. Nokia AVA and Ericsson AI-based SON already commercially deployed. Understanding how your RF measurements feed AI models makes you a more forward-looking engineer.

L43 Interview scenarios — 8 systematic debug walkthroughs L43 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾

Interview scenarios — walk through these before every RF test engineer interview

Scenario 1: ACLR degrades after software update
Step 1: Is measurement valid? Attenuation correct, preamp OFF, DPD converged (60s wait)? Step 2: Reproduce on second unit — systematic or unit-specific? Step 3: Diff the SW update — what changed? DPD algorithm? CFR threshold? DAC scale? Step 4: Roll back FW on one unit — does ACLR recover? Step 5: If rollback fixes: update changed DPD or CFR parameter. Check DPD_ENABLE, CFR_CLIP_LEVEL in changelogs. Root cause: usually CFR threshold changed → larger peaks → overdriving PA.
Scenario 2: RSSI accuracy fails only at high temperature
Step 1: Confirm failure is reproducible at +55°C. Step 2: Check TEMP_COMP table in hardware.json — populated? If empty: temperature compensation disabled → RSSI drifts. Step 3: Measure RSSI at +25°C and +55°C with same EXM injection → compute drift = X dB/°C. Step 4: Calculate required TEMP_COMP coefficient. Step 5: Run RSSI cal at both temperatures, update table. Root cause: TEMP_COMP table not calibrated or not loaded at boot.
Scenario 3: PA enters protection after 20 minutes
Step 1: Which protection? Check fault register: over-temperature vs over-current vs VSWR. Step 2: If over-temperature: thermal camera on PA, check ambient > 55°C, heatsink contact, fan. Step 3: If VSWR: VNA on antenna port — is load present? Step 4: If over-current: check PA bias vs spec, check if unit is over-driven. Monitor temperature over time — steady rise until threshold = thermal compound deficiency. Root cause in 70% of cases: thermal management, not electrical.
Scenario 4: Dynamic range fails B3 but passes B1
Step 1: Confirm back-to-back with same setup. Step 2: Check ADC channel mapping — correct ADC for B3? (ch 2/3/6/7, not ch 0/1/4/5 for B1). Step 3: Check ADC_ADJUST_B3 — calibrated correctly? Step 4: Sweep EXM −60 to −110 dBm for both bands, plot RSSI vs injected power — compare curves. Parallel but offset: ADC_ADJUST_B3 wrong → recalibrate. Different slope: hardware fault in LNA or mixer at B3 frequency. Root cause: most likely wrong ADC_ADJUST_B3.

🎯 4 More interview scenarios — practise these until automatic
Scenario 5: TX power passes at room temp but fails at +55°C
Step 1: Confirm failure is reproducible at temp (not a transient). Step 2: Check PA thermal protection status — did it fire? If yes: PA entering thermal derating before protection → heatsink issue, not calibration. Step 3: If no protection but power is low: measure actual power change vs room temp. If drift matches expected PA gain temperature coefficient (−0.02 dB/°C × 30°C = −0.6 dB): TEMP_COMP table missing for TX gain → update it. Step 4: If drift is larger than −0.6 dB: check PA Vdd at temperature — is Dynamic Vdd stepping down prematurely? Step 5: Verify TEMP_COMP_TX table is loaded at boot (check boot log). Root cause: usually missing TX gain temperature compensation.
Scenario 6: B41 PRACH detection fails intermittently — B1/B3/B8/B28 all pass
B41 is TDD — immediately suspect timing/sync. Step 1: Check DU PTP status — is it LOCKED? Even a brief GPS signal loss can cause PTP to enter holdover. Step 2: Check PTP offset over time — is it drifting beyond ±1.5 μs? Step 3: If PTP is fine: check EXA gating — are you measuring only during UL subframes? B41 PRACH arrives only in UL slots. Step 4: If gating is correct: verify EXM is synchronised to TDD frame — injection must be in correct UL subframe. Step 5: Check fronthaul latency under load — if transport QoS is misconfigured, PTP packets get delayed under traffic → sync degrades → intermittent B41 issues. Root cause: almost always PTP sync or EXA/EXM gating setup.
Scenario 7: After PA replacement, ACLR fails but TX power is correct
ACLR fail with correct power = PA is on but DPD is not working for the new PA. Step 1: Was DPD allowed to converge? PA replacement resets DPD coefficients — wait 60s after enabling TX. Step 2: If still failing after convergence: the new PA has different nonlinearity than the DPD model was trained on. The DPD coefficients calibrated for the old PA do not match the new one. Step 3: Force DPD re-adaptation — some systems require explicit re-trigger after hardware change. Step 4: Check if DPD algorithm converged at all (DPD_STATUS register). Step 5: If DPD_STATUS shows converged but ACLR still fails: PA bias may be different — check bias voltage matches spec for new PA part number. Root cause: DPD model not re-adapted after PA replacement.
Scenario 8: RSSI reads 6 dB lower than expected on one specific column
6 dB is exactly 1 bit in a 12-bit ADC — suspicious of BFP error. Step 1: Is it exactly 6 dB or approximately? If exactly 6 dB: BFP decompression fault (mantissa/exponent mismatch) → check FHGW firmware version, check eCPRI error counters. Step 2: If approximately 6 dB: check cable for that column (swap with known-good cable). Step 3: Run RSSI across all B1 columns — is it only Column X or all columns? If only one column: hardware fault on that column (LNA or cable). If all columns: ADC_ADJUST wrong for that band → re-calibrate. Step 4: Verify ADC channel mapping — is the correct get_rssi N being read for that column? (B3 Col A = get_rssi 2, not 0). Step 5: If column reads correct with EXM at full power but wrong at low power: LNA may be compressed by a strong blocker nearby during the test. Root cause: check in this order — ADC channel mapping → cable swap → LNA health → BFP error.
L44 Hands-on lab skills — spectrum analyser, VNA, oscilloscope, power meter L44 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾

Hands-on lab skills — what you must be able to do physically

EXA — the instrument you use most every day:
Must be able to: Set centre frequency, span, RBW, attenuation in under 60 seconds. Switch between ACLR, EVM, spectrum modes without manual. Know exactly which attenuation and preamp setting for which measurement. Read ACLR result and interpret pass/fail. Export trace data. Control via Python SCPI script. The EXA is your primary window into what the RU is actually transmitting.
VNA — skills that separate intermediate from senior engineers:
Must be able to: Perform full SOLT 2-port calibration in 5 minutes. Measure S11, S21, group delay without guidance. Measure cable phase at a specific frequency. Compare per-column phase for beamforming calibration. Interpret return loss results. The VNA is more complex than the EXA — engineers comfortable with it stand out significantly in interviews.
CMW500 / EXM as call box — end-to-end system testing:
CMW500 (R&S) and EXM (Keysight) simulate a complete network (eNB + UE) to run real LTE/NR calls. Used for: end-to-end throughput, handover, UE power control, real PRACH-to-data flow. Different from injecting a waveform — full L2/L3 signalling. Knowing how to set up a real call is a significant differentiator — means you can do system-level testing, not just component measurements.

📋 Instrument decision guide — which to use for which measurement
Measurement Use This Key Settings Common Mistake
TX Power EXA Atten 20dB · Preamp OFF · 30dB pad Preamp ON → input compression → wrong reading
ACLR EXA LTE ACLR mode · wait 60s DPD · RBW 100kHz Measuring before DPD convergence → false fail
EVM EXA (VSA mode) Demodulation mode · correct FRC · IFBW matters Wrong IFBW makes EVM look worse than reality
RSSI injection EXM FRC waveform · correct UL freq · verify with EXA first Injecting without verifying EXM output ±0.5dB
Cable loss VNA S21 · SOLT cal first · measure at band centre freq Skipping SOLT cal → cable + connector loss included
Phase cal VNA S21 phase · IFBW 1kHz · single freq · 30min warmup Moving cables after SOLT cal → phase measurement wrong
VSWR check VNA S11 · 1-port cal · check all connectors Not checking S11 after connecting → missing bad connector
PSU ripple Oscilloscope AC couple · 50mV/div · 1MHz BW · check PA rail DC coupling masks small AC ripple → miss the problem
Noise figure EXA (NF mode) Noise source ENR · preamp ON · cold/hot method Not entering correct ENR table → NF reads wrong
