Company knowledge — tailor your preparation to the employer

Ericsson, Nokia, Parallel Wireless — your current context:
Focus: O-RAN interoperability (can O-RU work with non-vendor O-DU?), energy efficiency (uSleep, Dynamic Vdd, W/Mbps), carrier-grade reliability (99.999% uptime), field ops (remote diagnosis, SW updates, no truck roll). For interviews: be ready to discuss O-RAN functional split, NETCONF/YANG M-plane, eCPRI fronthaul latency, and the DSA/sensitivity framework in detail. Your current RCT work at PW directly prepares you for roles here.
Apple / Google — OTA and device RF (very different domain):
Focus: Over-The-Air measurements (how well does the device radiate and receive in all directions?), SAR compliance (RF energy absorbed by human body), antenna design within a phone enclosure, co-existence (WiFi + BT + 5G all in same device without interfering), user experience metrics (call drop when holding phone a certain way?). OTA uses anechoic chambers and 3D radiation pattern measurements. The 3GPP spec for device OTA is TS 38.176. Very different from base station testing but shares RF fundamentals.
Universal skills — what every company values most:
(1) Systematic troubleshooting — find root cause without replacing things randomly. (2) Instrument fluency — set up EXA ACLR measurement correctly without checking manual. (3) Quantitative thinking — think in dB, know what 3 dB means. (4) Automation — write Python SCPI script to automate a measurement. (5) Communication — explain why ACLR matters to a non-RF engineer. These transfer across all companies. Build these first, company-specific knowledge comes with the job.

FDD vs TDD SETUP — KEY DIFFERENCES
FDD (B1/B3/B8/B28)
FREQ Channel: set DL freq
Mode: FDD LTE (e.g. B3)
Mode Setup: DL or UL direction
Source → Freq: set UL freq
Trigger polarity: Positive
Trigger delay: OFF
DL and UL are different frequencies → no timing dependency between them
TDD (B41)
FREQ Channel: same freq DL/UL
Mode: TDD LTE (B41)

WHY The "Why?" Framework — For every topic: Why does it exist? What problem? Which hardware? Which spec? How measured? Pass/fail? Debug? Interview? Customer impact? Master Framework click to expand▾

The WHY framework — 11 questions to master any RF topic

How to use the WHY framework:
For every feature, measurement, or standard you study, answer these 11 questions. This transforms memorised definitions into real understanding. A person who only answers "what is ACLR?" (definition) loses to someone who answers all 11. Use for interview preparation — structure your answers using these questions for complete, impressive responses.
The 11 questions — apply to every topic:
1. Why does it exist? 2. What problem does it solve? 3. Where is it used? 4. Which hardware blocks? 5. Which spec/clause? 6. How measured (instrument + setup)? 7. Pass/fail criteria (exact numbers)? 8. Common failures? 9. Debug approach? 10. Interview Q that tests it? 11. Customer/business impact if it fails?
Example — ACLR through all 11:
1. Prevent adjacent channel interference. 2. PA nonlinearity causing spectral regrowth. 3. Every base station TX measurement. 4. PA, DPD engine, CFR. 5. 3GPP TS 36.141 clause 6.6.1. 6. EXA ACLR LTE mode, BOB SMA + 30 dB pad, after 60s DPD convergence. 7. < −45 dBc adj, < −50 dBc alt. 8. DPD not converged, over P1dB, CFR too aggressive. 9. ACLR suddenly fails after SW update — debug approach? 10. Interference → SINR down → throughput down. 11. Regulator fine, operator SLA penalty.
This "Why?" framework is what separates senior RF engineers from those who only memorised concepts. A senior engineer can answer all 10 questions for any topic without notes. Practice answering them out loud for every module in this guide — that is your interview preparation.

NF1 Thermal noise foundation — kTB, −174 dBm/Hz, Johnson-Nyquist, noise voltage Beginner click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST Thermal noise in one sentence: Any object above −273°C (absolute zero) has electrons randomly moving around — that random movement creates a tiny electrical noise. In your RU, every resistive component (cable, duplexer, LNA input) generates this noise. The LNA then amplifies it along with the wanted signal. This is why you cannot build a perfectly silent receiver.
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
Thermal noise (kTB) sets the absolute noise floor. NF1 explains the physics. The full sensitivity formula using kTB + NF + SNR → DSA offset is in the DSA card.
→ For the complete chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

RCT bench setup — DU, AAU, instruments, connections decoded

Your bench setup — instrument roles:
EXM E6640A: Vector Signal Generator. Injects calibrated UL signals (PRACH preambles at DSA-corrected power levels) into RU BOB SMA for RX/sensitivity tests. Also generates FRC waveforms for RSSI cal.
EXA N9010B: Signal/Spectrum Analyser. Measures TX output: power, ACLR, EVM, spectrum mask. Connect via BOB SMA + 30 dB pad.
VNA E5071C: Network Analyser. Measures S21 (phase) for per-column beamforming calibration, cable loss, connector VSWR.
Connection diagram — RX test (sensitivity/RSSI):
EXM output → SMA cable (measure loss with VNA first) → RU BOB SMA port (UL column under test). EXM controls: frequency = band UL centre, power = target sensitivity + cable_loss, waveform = FRC_A1. RU CLI: get_rssi N to read ADC. DU CLI: testmac rssi to read DU RSSI. All three must agree within ±2 dB.
Connection diagram — TX test (ACLR/power):
RU BOB SMA (DL column under test) → 30 dB attenuator pad → SMA cable → EXA input. EXA: centre freq = band DL centre, atten = 10 dB (+ 30 dB pad = 40 dB total), preamp OFF, ACLR mode. Wait 60s for DPD convergence. Measure: power (compare to rated target ±1 dB), ACLR (compare to −45 dBc limit), EVM if required.

Why thermal noise is unavoidable

Thermal noise and the sensitivity floor:
Any resistive element above 0 K generates thermal noise. In your RX chain: the cable termination, the duplexer, the LNA input — all generate kTB noise. The LNA then amplifies both the incoming signal and all the noise it sees. You cannot eliminate this noise — you can only minimise the noise added after the signal enters the chain (which is what good LNA design does). This is why cryogenic receivers used in radio astronomy cool the LNA to near 0 K — it is the only way to get below the room-temperature kTB floor.
Noise voltage — how it appears on a spectrum analyser:
Noise voltage Vn = √(4kTBR). For a 50Ω system at 290K in 1MHz bandwidth: Vn = √(4 × 1.38e-23 × 290 × 1e6 × 50) = 0.895 μV = −107 dBm. On your EXA with preamp ON, this appears as the noise floor — the flat baseline across the span. When you inject a signal that rises above this floor, you can measure it. When the signal drops below it, it is lost in the noise.
📐 Real numbers — how temperature changes thermal noise
−40°C
T = 233K
kTB = −175.6 dBm/Hz
1.6 dB better than 290K
+17°C
T = 290K (reference)
kTB = −174 dBm/Hz
3GPP reference temp
+55°C
T = 328K
kTB = −173.5 dBm/Hz
0.5 dB worse
+70°C
T = 343K
kTB = −173.3 dBm/Hz
0.7 dB worse + PA derates

The thermal noise change with temperature is small (< 1 dB across the full range). What matters more at high temperature is that LNA NF increases and PA gain decreases — both effects are larger than the thermal noise change itself.

NF2 Noise Figure definition — SNR degradation, Noise Factor vs NF, receiver sensitivity formula Intermediate click to expand▾
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
NF is the SNR degradation caused by your RX chain. It is the third term in the sensitivity formula after kTB+BW. Your system NF = 5.75 dB built up from the Friis chain — see NCH card. Full sensitivity derivation is in DSA card.
→ For the complete chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.
NF + SNR_req NF = 5.75 → Sens shifts 5.75 dB worse Perfect RX (NF=0): sens = −104+(−1) = −105 Real RX (NF=5.75): sens = −99.25 dBm 5.75 dB penalty vs theoretical perfect RX

NF as SNR degradation — what it means in practice

Noise Factor vs Noise Figure:
Noise Factor (F) is the linear ratio: F = SNR_in / SNR_out. Always ≥ 1. A perfect device has F = 1. Noise Figure (NF) = 10·log(F) in dB. A perfect device has NF = 0 dB. Your system NF of 5.75 dB means F = 10^(5.75/10) = 3.76 — your chain degrades SNR by a factor of 3.76 (not 5.75 times — remember dB is logarithmic). The sensitivity formula uses NF in dB because all other terms are already in dB.
How NF directly sets your test injection level:
EXM injects at sensitivity threshold. Sensitivity = kTB_floor + NF + SNR_req. If your NF increases by 1 dB (e.g. cable gets longer, LNA degrades), sensitivity worsens by 1 dB, and EXM must inject 1 dB more power. If EXM is not recalibrated but NF increased, the test is now 1 dB too easy — you are testing above threshold without knowing it. This is why the DSA table is recalculated whenever hardware changes.
NF3 Friis cascade formula — why the LNA dominates, worked examples for your RU chain Advanced click to expand▾
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
Friis cascade formula explains how your 5.75 dB system NF is built from individual component NFs. This NF feeds directly into the sensitivity formula. See DSA card for full chain, NCH card for numerical calculation.
→ For the complete chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

Why Friis means you only need to care about the LNA

The Friis insight — one worked example:
Imagine you have a 7 dB NF mixer after your 20 dB gain LNA. Its Friis contribution is (F_mixer − 1) / G_LNA = (5.012 − 1) / 100 = 0.040 linear = 0.17 dB to system NF. Now replace that mixer with a perfect 0 dB NF mixer. System NF improvement = 0.17 dB. Barely measurable. But reduce cable loss before the LNA by 0.5 dB — system NF improves by exactly 0.5 dB, directly improving sensitivity by 0.5 dB. This is the Friis insight: optimise before the LNA, not after it.
In your lab: the pre-LNA components you can actually change:
The duplexer and pre-BPF are fixed inside the RFFE — you cannot change them. The LNA is a fixed chip — you cannot swap it. The only pre-LNA component you control in the test setup is the cable from EXM to the RU port. Shorter, lower-loss cable = better system NF in your measurement = better apparent sensitivity. This is why cable quality and measured loss matter, and why the VNA cable loss measurement is step 1 of every sensitivity test setup.
NF4 NF of passive devices — attenuators, mixers, filters, cables, your test setup Intermediate click to expand▾
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
Passive devices add NF equal to their loss — this directly worsens system NF and therefore sensitivity. Every 0.1 dB extra cable loss before the LNA = 0.1 dB worse sensitivity.
→ For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

Why passive devices add noise equal to their loss

A resistor at room temperature generates thermal noise power = kTB. When a passive component like a cable attenuates a signal by X dB, it absorbs part of the signal power and replaces it with its own thermal noise. The result: the signal level drops by X dB but the noise floor drops by less (because the component adds its own noise). The net effect is exactly X dB of SNR degradation, which is the definition of X dB noise figure.

Why position relative to LNA is everything:
The Friis formula shows that each stage's NF contribution is divided by the gain of all preceding stages. A component before the LNA (G_preceding = 1 or less) adds its full NF. A component after the LNA (G_preceding = 100 for +20 dB LNA) adds only 1/100th of its NF to the system total. This is why the design rule is: minimise all loss before the LNA, and place the LNA as early in the chain as physically possible. Your duplexer and pre-BPF must be before the LNA for functional reasons (they select the band) but their loss directly degrades sensitivity.
Attenuator placement — the most common lab mistake:
When measuring TX power with EXA, you add a 30 dB attenuator to protect the EXA from the strong TX signal. This attenuator must go between the RU TX output and the EXA input — never between the signal source and the RU RX input. If you accidentally put the 30 dB pad in the RX path during a sensitivity test, you add 30 dB to system NF, and your measured sensitivity becomes 30 dB worse than reality. Always double-check the signal path before running any RX measurement.
Connector loss — the hidden NF contributor:
A single SMA connector in good condition has approximately 0.1–0.15 dB insertion loss. That is 0.1–0.15 dB of NF contribution if it is before the LNA. In a chain with 4 connectors before the LNA (source → cable → two adapters → RU port), that is 0.4–0.6 dB of additional NF from connectors alone. A damaged or incorrectly torqued connector can have 0.3–0.5 dB extra loss, immediately visible as sensitivity degradation. This is why the VNA connector inspection checklist exists and why torque specs matter for RF measurements.
NF5 All 5 noise types — Thermal, Shot, Flicker/1f, White, Burst — with RF context Advanced click to expand▾
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
5 noise types exist. Thermal noise (kTB) is what the sensitivity formula is based on. Phase noise limits EVM. Quantisation noise limits ADC dynamic range. All three affect your daily measurements.
→ For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

The three noise types that matter most in your work

Of the five noise types, three are directly relevant to your daily testing. Thermal noise sets your sensitivity floor and is the subject of the entire DSA/NF calculation chain. Phase noise from the LO limits EVM and prevents high-order modulations from decoding. Quantisation noise from the ADC sets the dynamic range ceiling.

① Thermal noise — your sensitivity floor:
Generated by any resistive element at temperature above 0 K. Formula: P = kTB. In your RX chain, every lossy component (cable, duplexer, filter) generates thermal noise equal to its loss in power. The LNA amplifies both the signal and all the noise it sees, but its own added noise is small (NF = 2 dB). This is the noise the entire DSA framework is designed around — calculate it, characterise it per band, then test each band against its own correctly-adjusted threshold.
④ Phase noise — why it shows up in EVM failures:
The local oscillator (LO) that downconverts your RF signal to baseband is not a perfect single frequency — it has random phase jitter. This jitter appears as noise skirts around the carrier in the frequency domain. When the LO mixes with your signal, this phase jitter gets transferred to the baseband IQ constellation — the symbol points rotate slightly randomly, which increases EVM. Phase noise is why you see an EVM floor that does not improve even when SNR is excellent. For QPSK this is not a problem, but for 64QAM and 256QAM the tighter constellation margins make phase noise the limiting factor.
⑤ Quantisation noise — ADC dynamic range:
Every ADC rounds the analog signal to the nearest discrete level. With 12 bits, there are 4096 levels. The rounding error is the quantisation noise. SQNR = 6.02 × N + 1.76 = 6.02 × 12 + 1.76 = 74 dB. This means your ADC can cleanly handle signals up to 74 dB above the quantisation noise floor. If your signal swings too close to full scale (clipping), you get heavy distortion. If it is too weak (near the quantisation floor), you lose resolution. The VGA/AGC in your RX chain keeps the signal in the sweet spot — typically around −12 dBFS, well within the 74 dB dynamic range.
NF6 NF applied to your work — EXA preamp, sensitivity testing, RSSI calibration, EXM overrange Advanced click to expand▾
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
NF in practice: the EXA preamp lowers the analyser NF for measuring weak signals. Per-band NF differences (B1=2.44, B8=3.15 dB) are what drive the different DSA offsets in the test table.
→ For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

How NF directly drives everything in your daily test work

NF is not an abstract concept — it is the single number that determines what power the EXM must inject for each band, what the EXA DANL must be to measure it, and whether a sensitivity failure is a hardware problem or a calibration issue. Every time you set up a sensitivity test, you are implicitly using NF.

EXA DANL must be lower than RU sensitivity — always check:
DANL (Displayed Average Noise Level) is the EXA's own noise floor — the minimum signal it can measure. For your sensitivity test to be valid, the EXA's DANL must be significantly lower than the signal you are trying to measure at the RU output.

In your test: EXM injects at sensitivity threshold (e.g. −97.5 dBm at RU port after cable). The PRACH detector inside the RU processes this. You read the result via CLI (get_rssi) or DU RSSI — you are not measuring the raw RF signal with EXA at this point. The EXA is used for TX measurements. But if you ever try to measure a weak RX signal directly with EXA, the DANL check is critical: EXA DANL at −130 dBm/Hz across 10 MHz = −130 + 70 = −60 dBm — safely below your −98 dBm system noise floor.
Why B8 has the highest NF (3.15 dB) and highest DSA:
At 900 MHz (B8), the transistor physics in GaAs/GaN LNAs produce slightly higher noise compared to 2 GHz. Additionally, the duplexer for B8 at 900 MHz is physically larger and has higher insertion loss than at 2 GHz — the filter Q-factor degrades at lower frequencies meaning you need a wider physical filter to achieve the same selectivity, which adds loss. These two effects combine to give B8 the worst NF in your band set. B41 at 2545 MHz has the best NF (2.0 dB) because there is no duplexer — TDD uses a T/R switch which has lower loss than a duplexer.
When measured sensitivity is worse than calculated — NF-based diagnosis:
If your sensitivity test fails by X dB, and you have confirmed cable loss and EXM calibration are correct, the excess degradation must come from the RX chain NF being higher than assumed. Break it down: measure cable loss with VNA → subtract from EXM output → compare to sensitivity formula → if residual error > 1 dB, the RX chain NF is degraded. The most likely causes in order: (1) LNA compression from a too-strong signal on a different port, (2) LNA bias voltage wrong after firmware change, (3) duplexer damaged (cracked ceramic), (4) connector oxidised adding loss before LNA.
NF_CAL Noise Figure calibration — Y-factor method, ENR, hot/cold noise, what it measures and why Advanced click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST NF calibration in one sentence: This is how you measure whether your LNA and RX chain are generating as little noise as expected. You inject two known noise levels (hot and cold) and measure how much noise the chain adds — that added noise is the Noise Figure. It tells you if the hardware is healthy, but it does not write any correction values.
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
NF calibration uses the Y-factor method to measure actual system NF. This confirms whether NF matches the values used in the sensitivity formula. It does not write any correction — it only validates hardware health.
→ For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

What is NF calibration?

NF cal answers one question: how much noise does your RX chain add to the signal? This is a hardware characterisation measurement — it tells you whether the LNA, duplexer, and cable are performing to spec. It does NOT write any correction value — it just confirms (or flags) the hardware quality.

Key terms, each explained

ENR — Excess Noise Ratio
The "how much hotter than room temperature is the noise source" spec. ENR=15 dB means the source outputs noise equivalent to a resistor at 290 × 10^(15/10) ≈ 9200 K when switched ON. This is the known reference your calculation depends on. The noise source module has its ENR printed on it and also stored in its EEPROM so the EXA can read it automatically.
Y-factor
Y = N_hot / N_cold in linear power. If hot output is −60 dBm and cold output is −66 dBm, the difference is 6 dB → Y = 10^(6/10) = 3.98. The Y-factor is how much "more noise" comes out when you switch the source hot vs cold. A low Y means the DUT is adding so much noise of its own that the source temperature barely matters — i.e., high NF device. A high Y means the DUT is quiet and is faithfully amplifying the difference — i.e., low NF device.
T_hot and T_cold
T_cold = 290 K (standard room temperature, the IEEE reference). T_hot = 290 × 10^(ENR/10). When the noise source is OFF, it still generates thermal noise at 290 K — that becomes your cold reference. This is why you use the same physical source for both measurements: it removes cable and connector uncertainty from the result.
NF formula: NF = ENR − 10·log(Y−1)
Where this comes from: NF definition is SNR_in/SNR_out. For a two-port device with gain G and noise temperature T_e, the output noise is G·k·(T_cold + T_e)·B for cold input and G·k·(T_hot + T_e)·B for hot input. Taking the ratio cancels G and B, and solving for T_e gives you NF = 10·log(1 + T_e/T_0). Substituting T_e from the Y-factor ratio gives the formula above.
In your lab — no standalone noise source needed
The EXA N9010B has a built-in NF measurement mode under Meas → Noise Figure. It drives its own internal noise source through Port 1 output, sweeps frequencies, and automatically computes NF vs frequency. You connect EXA Port 1 → RU RX port (via calibrated cable), tell it your cable loss, and it plots NF(f) for you. You then read off the NF at your band centre (e.g. 1950 MHz for B1 UL). The EXA handles the Y-factor math internally.
When NF is worse than spec — what to check
If measured NF > spec by more than 1 dB: (1) Check cable loss — every 0.1 dB extra cable loss before the LNA adds 0.1 dB to measured NF. (2) Check connector torque — loose SMA can add 0.3–0.5 dB. (3) Check LNA bias — wrong supply voltage shifts NF. (4) Check for LNA compression — if signal level too high, LNA is not in its linear region and NF appears worse. (5) Duplexer damage — a damaged duplexer filter adds extra loss before the LNA, directly adding to NF.
GAIN_CAL Gain calibration — RX chain ADC_ADJUST, TX power trim, what each register means Advanced click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST Gain calibration in one sentence: This is how you teach the radio to report accurate power readings. You inject a signal of exactly known power, see what the radio reports, and find the offset between them. That offset (ADC_ADJUST) is saved so future readings are accurate. RX gain cal = RSSI cal — they are the same procedure called by two different names.
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
Gain cal (= RSSI cal for RX, power trim for TX) corrects the difference between theoretical and actual chain gain. ADC_ADJUST from RSSI cal absorbs all RX chain gain uncertainty into one offset number per band per ADC channel.
→ For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

RX Gain Calibration — what ADC_ADJUST really is

The RX chain has many components between the antenna port and the ADC register: duplexer, BPF, LNA, VGA, mixer, another BPF, then the ADC. Each one has gain or loss. Rather than calibrating each component separately, RX gain cal treats the entire chain as a black box and finds one single number — ADC_ADJUST — that converts any dBFS reading into an accurate dBm reading at the RU input port.

ADC_ADJUST
A calibration constant stored in hardware.json, one per band per ADC channel. Formula: ADC_ADJUST = P_known_at_RU_port − dBFS_reading. Once calibrated, converting any future reading is: P_dBm = dBFS + ADC_ADJUST. It absorbs the total chain gain between RU port and ADC register — so even though the LNA adds +20 dB, the VGA might be at +6 dB, and the mixer has conversion loss of −7 dB, you never need to know each individual value. The single offset does it all.
Why separate ADC_ADJUST per band and per ADC channel
Each band has a different LNA gain and filter response, so the total chain gain is different per band. B1 at 2140 MHz has slightly different gain than B3 at 1843 MHz — even though they may share physical hardware, the frequency-dependent component behaviour means each band needs its own cal constant. Per ADC channel (B1 uses ADC channels 0/1/4/5, B3 uses 2/3/6/7) further accounts for ADC input impedance variation and any mismatch in the IQ paths.
Temperature dependence — why RSSI can drift
LNA gain changes with temperature — typically −0.02 to −0.05 dB/°C for GaAs pHEMT LNAs. In a hot lab (40°C vs 25°C calibration temp), the LNA gain drops ~0.3–0.7 dB, which makes RSSI read 0.3–0.7 dB low. If you see systematic RSSI error that grows as the RU warms up, this is why. Some RU designs have temperature compensation tables that auto-correct ADC_ADJUST as a function of measured board temperature — check hardware.json for a TEMP_COMP array.

TX Gain Calibration — what TX_GAIN register controls

The TX chain starts with the baseband IQ signal at full digital scale, passes through the DPD block, DAC, upconverter, PA driver, and finally the main PA. The total gain from baseband to RF output is roughly fixed by hardware, but there is always ±2–3 dB unit-to-unit variation from component tolerances. TX gain cal trims a digital attenuator (or the PA bias point) until the output power at the coupler port exactly hits the rated target.

tx_calibration_eeprom.json
This is the file that holds the final TX_GAIN register values after calibration — one per band per column (A/B/C/D). It is written during factory calibration and stored in the RU EEPROM. When the RU boots, it reads this file and loads the register values before enabling TX. If this file is missing or corrupt, the RU falls back to default gain values which can be 6 dB low or high — this is exactly what caused the ~6 dB B41 power deficit you found on unit 26050509 (fault 12: missing tx_calibration_eeprom.json).
Coupler ratio — the BOB SMA is not antenna power
The BOB SMA port is a directional coupler output, not the main antenna port. The coupler splits a small fraction of the TX power for monitoring — typically the coupling ratio is 30 dB, meaning the BOB SMA sees 30 dB less power than what goes to the antenna. So B1 rated power at BOB SMA = −16.7 dBm corresponds to +13.3 dBm at the antenna connector, or roughly 21 W EIRP per column after antenna gain. Always measure at the BOB SMA — connecting EXA directly to the antenna port would overload it instantly.
DPD and its interaction with gain cal
DPD (Digital Pre-Distortion) must converge before you measure TX power — it actively adjusts its coefficients for 30–60 seconds after power-on or after any power level change. If you measure output power while DPD is still adapting, you will see power fluctuating ±0.5 dB and possibly a wrong ACLR. Always wait for DPD to converge (check the DPD status register or simply wait 60 s) before taking a TX power or ACLR reading used for gain calibration.
Gain cal vs RSSI cal — how they relate
They are the same operation from opposite ends of the RX chain. RSSI cal (ADC_ADJUST) calibrates the entire RX path as one unit. NF cal measures just the noise-adding property of that path. TX gain cal calibrates the TX path. All three together ensure that when EXM injects −95 dBm, the RU reports −95 dBm via get_rssi, and when the BBU commands rated TX power, the antenna port outputs exactly rated power. Any mismatch between these three is a sign something has drifted or failed.

From your Understanding Noise Figure PDF + your lab procedure · What sensitivity is physically · How DSA is derived from sensitivity · Why modulation matters · Your exact numbers

RSSI Sensitivity + dynamic range test: manual steps and automation blueprint Advanced click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST RSSI calibration in one sentence: RSSI cal is the same as RX gain calibration — inject known power from EXM, read what the ADC reports in dBFS, compute the difference (ADC_ADJUST), save it. From then on, the radio can convert any ADC reading into an accurate power in dBm. The test passes when all three sources (EXM, CLI, DU) agree within ±2 dB.
Quick link — how this connects to DSA:
RSSI cal and RX gain cal are the same procedure. It finds ADC_ADJUST: inject known power from EXM, read dBFS from ADC, compute offset. Once calibrated, the RU can report accurate dBm for any received signal level.
→ For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card.

What RSSI calibration actually is

RSSI calibration and RX gain calibration are the same procedure with different names. The goal is to find the single offset number — ADC_ADJUST — that converts any raw dBFS reading from the ADC into an accurate dBm power level at the RU antenna port. Once calibrated, P_dBm = dBFS_reading + ADC_ADJUST for any signal in that band.

The three numbers that must agree within 2 dB:

EXM output − cable loss = what arrives at the RU port (your reference, measured physically)
CLI get_rssi + ADC_ADJUST = what the RU's ADC chain reports (your calibrated reading)
DU testmac RSSI = what the baseband processing chain reports after FFT (another independent path)

All three must agree within ±2 dB. If EXM says −97.5 dBm, CLI should report −97.5 ± 2 dBm, and DU should also report −97.5 ± 2 dBm. If CLI is accurate but DU is off, the problem is in the FHGW/baseband path. If both CLI and DU are off from EXM, the ADC_ADJUST value is wrong.
Why separate ADC_ADJUST per band and per ADC channel:
B1 UL (1950 MHz) and B3 UL (1747 MHz) use different LNA gain settings, different filter responses, and different ADC input stages. Even if two ADC channels share the same physical ADC chip, the analog input path leading to each channel varies. Unit-to-unit component tolerance means the ADC_ADJUST for B1 on ADC channel 0 of unit 26050509 will differ slightly from the same channel on unit 26050508. This is precisely what RSSI cal measures and corrects — it is a per-unit, per-band, per-channel characterisation.
Common RSSI cal failures and root causes:
CLI reads 3 dB low → ADC_ADJUST was set with a different cable. Cable got swapped. Measure new cable loss with VNA and re-run cal.
CLI accurate but DU off by 2 dB → FHGW BFP decompression issue or testmac RSSI averaging window mismatch. Check FHGW firmware version.
RSSI drifts as unit warms up → LNA gain is temperature-sensitive. Re-run cal at operating temperature (after 30 min warm-up), or check if temperature compensation table (TEMP_COMP in hardware.json) is configured.
All bands off by same amount → EXM output power was wrong during cal. Re-verify EXM output with EXA before running cal.
ADC channel mapping — which channel reads which band/column:
B1 Column A → ADC channel 0  ·  B1 Column B → ADC channel 1
B1 Column C → ADC channel 4  ·  B1 Column D → ADC channel 5
B3 Column A → ADC channel 2  ·  B3 Column B → ADC channel 3
B3 Column C → ADC channel 6  ·  B3 Column D → ADC channel 7
B8/B28 use 2 RX paths (columns A and B only) → channels 0 and 1 with band-specific ADC_ADJUST values

So get_rssi 0 reads B1 Column A. get_rssi 2 reads B3 Column A. This mapping is why if Column C shows a bad RSSI reading (channel 4 for B1), you know exactly which physical LNA and cable path to inspect.
🚨 Common RSSI calibration mistakes (from real lab experience):
Mistake: Measuring cable loss at wrong frequency
Result: ADC_ADJUST off by 0.3-1 dB, RSSI always wrong by that amount
Fix: Always measure cable loss at band centre (e.g. 1950 MHz for B1 UL)
Mistake: Using wrong ADC channel number
Result: B3 cal written to ADC_ADJUST for B1 channel — completely wrong
Fix: Always verify: B1 Col A = get_rssi 0, B3 Col A = get_rssi 2
Mistake: Not verifying EXM output before injection
Result: EXM was off by 1.2 dB → ADC_ADJUST stored with 1.2 dB error
Fix: Always verify EXM output with EXA (±0.5 dB) before any cal
Mistake: Cal at room temp, field unit gets hot
Result: RSSI drifts 1-2 dB in summer — TEMP_COMP table empty
Fix: Run cal at 25°C and 55°C, populate TEMP_COMP table

B41T B41 TDD Trigger Delay — 9.9765 ms explained, why it affects sensitivity ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST — real lab finding B41 TDD shares one frequency for DL and UL — separated only in time. The EXM must inject its UL signal only during SF2 and SF7 (the only full UL subframes in Config 2). The 9.9765 ms delay aligns the ARB waveform so it lands there. If the delay toggle is OFF, injection is uncontrolled — it lands in DL subframes and the RU cannot receive it. This was the first thing to check for the B41 ~5 dB sensitivity gap on units 26050508/26050509.

Correct frame structure and what the 9.9765 ms actually does

Corrected TDD Config 2 frame — D S U D D D S U D D:
Only SF2 and SF7 are full UL subframes. SF3, SF4, SF5 and SF8, SF9 are Downlink — not UL as previously shown incorrectly.

SF Type Time UL receive window
0D0–1 ms—
1S1–2 msDwPTS 1.000–1.643 ms · GP 1.643–1.857 ms · UpPTS 1.857–2.000 ms
2U2–3 ms← FULL UL burst (PRACH / PUSCH)
3D3–4 ms—
4D4–5 ms—
5D5–6 ms—
6S6–7 msDwPTS 6.000–6.643 ms · GP 6.643–6.857 ms · UpPTS 6.857–7.000 ms
7U7–8 ms← FULL UL burst (PRACH / PUSCH)
8D8–9 ms—
9D9–10 ms—
Special Subframe Config 6 (normal CP) decoded:
Total = 14 OFDM symbols per 1 ms subframe.
DwPTS = 9 symbols = 9 × 71.35 µs = 642.9 µs (DL pilot — RU transmits)
GP = 3 symbols = 3 × 71.35 µs = 214.1 µs (guard — silence for switching + propagation)
UpPTS = 2 symbols = 2 × 71.35 µs = 142.7 µs (UL pilot — narrow window)

The GP is only 214 µs. If the EXM injection is even 0.3 ms off, the UL burst clips into the guard period and the RU ignores it. For PRACH specifically — UpPTS is only 142.7 µs — a near-zero tolerance on timing alignment.
Why 9.9765 ms — the physics drops out exactly:
10.0000 ms   one LTE TDD frame (External 2 trigger period)
− 0.0203 ms   N_TA offset = 624 × Ts = 624 / 30,720,000 = 20.3 µs (3GPP TS 36.213 — mandatory UL timing advance for TDD)
− ~0.003 ms   cable length + Tx/Rx processing latency (~3 µs empirical)
──────────
= 9.9767 ms ≈ 9.9765 ms ✓   exactly matches your EXM screen
The 23.5 µs shortfall is not arbitrary. The N_TA advance ensures the UL burst's OFDM symbols (with cyclic prefix) land cleanly inside the RU's FFT capture window — arriving slightly early so the CP absorbs propagation uncertainty rather than clipping the GP→UpPTS boundary.
Two scenarios for the B41 sensitivity gap:

Scenario A — Delay toggle OFF (what the screenshot shows):
9.9765 ms value is configured but the toggle is OFF → delay not applied → injection is uncontrolled → most UL bursts land in DL subframes (SF3/SF4/SF5) → RU cannot receive them → BLER high → sensitivity appears ~5 dB worse than real. This is the cheap fix — just turn the toggle ON.

Scenario B — Delay ON but cable offset stale:
If your cable run differs from the ~3 µs assumed when the delay was calibrated, the fine offset is slightly wrong. Even a 0.2 ms error at the GP boundary causes partial burst loss. Test: with delay ON and fixed inject power (e.g. −97 dBm), sweep delay ±200 µs around 9.9765 ms in 20 µs steps — watch UL BLER. If BLER bottoms out at exactly 9.9765 ms: alignment is correct, the 5 dB is a real RX path issue. If BLER bottoms out at a different value: recalibrate the delay for your specific cable.
✅ B41 test setup checklist
□ ARB Trigger Source → External 2
□ Ext Trig Polarity → Pos
□ Ext Trig Delay value → 9.9765 ms (9.976500 ms)
□ Ext Trig Delay toggle → ON ← confirm this — was OFF on your screenshot
□ Mode Setup → TDD Config 2, Special SF Config 6 — must match DU exactly
□ ARB bin file → correct TDD waveform (e.g. A1-3_BW10_TDD_RNTI_0.bin)
□ GPS/PTP → LOCKED (B41 TDD requires ±1.5 µs timing accuracy)
□ If B41 still 5 dB off after delay ON → sweep delay ±200 µs to confirm alignment or identify RX path issue
□ Check UL BLER at fixed power to separate "timing artifact" from "real 5 dB RX path loss"
REF RF & RCT Glossary — quick definitions of every term Reference click to expand▾

Complete term reference — every RF and RCT acronym

RF measurement terms:
DANL: Displayed Average Noise Level — EXA own noise floor (−130 dBm/Hz with preamp ON)
P1dB: 1 dB compression point — input power where PA gain drops 1 dB from linear
IIP3: Input 3rd-order Intercept Point — linearity spec for mixers
PAPR: Peak to Average Power Ratio — OFDM signal crest factor (10–12 dB)
VSWR: Voltage Standing Wave Ratio — impedance mismatch indicator (1.0 = perfect)
NF: Noise Figure — how much SNR the RX chain degrades (dB)
ENR: Excess Noise Ratio — calibrated noise source spec for NF measurement
kTB: Thermal noise power = Boltzmann × Temperature × Bandwidth = −174 dBm/Hz
SQNR: Signal to Quantisation Noise Ratio = 6.02N + 1.76 dB (12-bit → 74 dB)
System and architecture terms:
midBRD: Mid-band Board — digital processing (FPGA, DAC/ADC) for B1/B3/B41
RFFE: Radio Frequency Front End — analog RF board (PA, LNA, duplexer) per column
FHGW: Fronthaul Gateway — Low-PHY processor (IFFT/FFT, BFP, CFR, DPD)
eCPRI: evolved Common Public Radio Interface — IQ data over 10GbE
BFP: Block Floating Point — IQ compression (9+4 bit → saves ~50% bandwidth)
PE44820DS: Digital phase shifter IC per column (beamforming control)
ORX: Observation Receiver — DPD feedback ADC (samples PA output)
JESD204B: High-speed serial interface between FPGA and DAC/ADC
O-RU/O-DU/O-CU: Open RAN Radio Unit / Distributed Unit / Centralised Unit
Test framework terms:
RuAuto: PW automated RF test framework
tc_cadence.json: Test configuration file (bands, BWs, DSA offsets, limits)
rct_results.json: Output file with all measurement results and pass/fail
Group-ID: Test group category (TX_POWER, RSSI_CAL, SENSITIVITY, ACLR)
Test-ID: Specific test case within group (B1_10M_QPSK_A1)
ETM: Embedded Test Mode — partial RCT without full DU connection
FRC A1: QPSK 1/3 — the standard sensitivity test FRC (best sensitivity, FRC A1-A5)
PRACH: Physical Random Access Channel — UE's first transmission (Zadoff-Chu preamble)
TA: Timing Advance — propagation delay correction sent by gNB to UE

EXA N9010B — your primary TX measurement instrument

Key EXA specs and settings for your work:
Freq range: 10 Hz – 26.5 GHz. DANL: −163 dBm/Hz (preamp ON). Max input: +30 dBm (+20 dBm recommended with pad). Port: TCP 5025 for SCPI. Serial: MY59070653. IP: 10.62.2.135.
For ACLR: Atten 20–30 dB, preamp OFF, RBW 100 kHz, Meas→ACLR function.
For EVM: use VSA mode or dedicated EVM measurement. Input: BOB SMA + 30 dB pad.
For RSSI check: Atten 0 dB, preamp ON, narrow span around band centre.
DANL and why preamp matters:
DANL (Displayed Average Noise Level) is the EXA's own noise floor — the minimum signal it can display. With preamp OFF and 0 dB attenuation: DANL ≈ −120 dBm/Hz. With preamp ON: DANL ≈ −130 dBm/Hz. For your sensitivity tests, the signal at the RU output is around −97.5 dBm in 10 MHz = −167 dBm/Hz spectral density. EXA preamp ON gives −130 dBm/Hz — 37 dB above the signal. Fine for direct spectrum viewing. But for ACLR on TX: signal is −17 dBm at BOB SMA after pad — preamp OFF absolutely required.
Common EXA mistakes to avoid:
Preamp ON with TX signal → input compression → ACLR reads 10–15 dB better than reality (wrong, fail in field).
Attenuation too low → ADC in EXA compresses → same wrong result.
RBW too wide → noise floor appears higher → sensitivity appears worse.
Not waiting for sweep → single sweep gives noise-contaminated ACLR → always average ≥10 sweeps.
Wrong centre frequency → measuring wrong channel → wrong ACLR offsets.

Phase & Angle Calibration using VNA E5071C — Complete Guide

SOLT calibration · Phase response · Group delay · Antenna element phase matching · Beamforming calibration · Cable phase characterisation · Step-by-step procedure for your lab

VNA1 Why phase calibration matters — beamforming, MIMO, cable characterisation Beginner click to expand▾

VNA phase calibration — why phase matters for beamforming

Why phase calibration is required:
Beamforming steers the antenna beam by applying precise phase shifts to each column's TX signal. If Column B's actual phase is 5° different from Column A due to cable or connector variation, the beam will point 2° off from the commanded direction. Over a 200m cell radius, a 2° beam error means the signal maximum is 7m away from where you think it is — reducing effective coverage. Phase cal measures the actual phase of each column and corrects it in the PE44820DS phase shifter register.
What the VNA measures:
S21 at the TX band centre frequency (e.g. 2140 MHz for B1). Source: VNA Port 1 → RU BOB SMA (one column at a time). Sink: VNA Port 2 → reference point. The S21 phase for each column gives: electrical path length from BOB SMA to measurement plane. Difference between columns A, B, C, D = phase mismatch to correct. Target: all four columns within ±2° of Column A. If Column C shows −6.4°, adjust PE44820DS register for Column C by +6.4°.
VNA E5071C — key settings for phase cal:
Freq range: single point or narrow span (±10 MHz) around band centre. IFBW: 1 kHz (low noise for accurate phase). Power: −10 dBm (keep RU in linear region). Cal: SOLT full 2-port, performed at measurement cable tips. Warm-up: 30 minutes before any measurement. Format: Phase (degrees). Do NOT bend cables between cal and measurement — phase shifts by 2–5° per 90° bend.
Phase in your AAU — the core reason
Your Metro AAU has 12 antenna elements (B1/B3/B41) steered by digital phase shifters (PE44820DS). Each element must transmit at a precise phase relative to the others. The beam points in the direction where the phases add constructively. A 5° phase error on one element degrades the beam pattern — the main lobe shifts, the gain drops, and side lobes increase. This is why TX_CAL (transmit calibration) exists and why the VNA is your primary tool for verifying it.
What the VNA measures that matters for phase
VNA measurementParameterUse in your work
S21 PhasePhase of forward transmission (deg)Phase difference between two cable/filter paths. Used to match cable electrical lengths before connecting to RU antenna ports.
S11 PhasePhase of reflection (deg)Characterises antenna port impedance phase. Combined with magnitude gives full impedance on Smith chart.
Group Delay−dφ/dω (ns)How much delay the path adds vs frequency. Constant group delay = linear phase = no pulse distortion. Ripple in group delay = multipath or resonance in connector/filter.
Electrical LengthPhase converted to metresCompares electrical lengths of two cables. For beamforming: cables to all antenna elements should have matched electrical length ±1°.
Phase ImbalanceΔPhase between Port1 and Port2Directly measures the phase mismatch between two TX paths — what OB_CAL corrects for in firmware.
The three types of phase calibration you need
TypeWhat you calibrateVNA technique
1. Cable electrical length matchingSF141 test cables from FHGW BOB to EXA/EXMS21 phase at each band centre frequency → match pairs to within ±2°
2. Antenna element phase responsePhase shift introduced by each TX path (RFFE)S21 phase sweep across band → compare all 8/12 paths → identify outliers
3. Filter / duplexer phase characterisationPhase vs frequency across the passband of BPF, duplexer, triplexerS21 phase + group delay sweep → verify linear phase in passband, check group delay ripple
VNA2 VNA calibration — SOLT/SOLR, why it matters, what errors it removes Intermediate click to expand▾
PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST VNA calibration in one sentence: Before you can trust any VNA measurement, you must remove the errors introduced by the cables and connectors between the VNA and your device. SOLT calibration (Short-Open-Load-Through) does this in 12 steps. Skip it and your S21 phase measurement includes the cable electrical length — meaningless for comparing column-to-column phase.

VNA calibration — SOLT, error models, reference plane

What SOLT calibration removes:
SOLT (Short-Open-Load-Through) calibration corrects 12 systematic errors: directivity, source match, reflection tracking, transmission tracking, load match, and isolation — for both ports. After calibration, the VNA measurement reference plane moves to the tips of the calibration standard, removing cable and connector effects. Skipping cal means your S21 phase includes the electrical length of the measurement cables — meaningless for per-column phase comparison.
12-step SOLT procedure:
1. Warm up VNA 30 min. 2. Set frequency range (e.g. 2100–2180 MHz for B1). 3. Set IFBW 1 kHz. 4. Port 1: connect SHORT, press Measure. 5. Port 1: connect OPEN, press Measure. 6. Port 1: connect LOAD (50Ω), press Measure. 7. Port 2: connect SHORT. 8. Port 2: connect OPEN. 9. Port 2: connect LOAD. 10. Connect THROUGH between ports. 11. Press Apply Cal. 12. Verify: S11 of LOAD should be < −40 dB. Then connect DUT without moving cables.
What invalidates your calibration:
Bending cables after cal, changing adapters, temperature change > 10°C, loosening any connector. If in doubt: re-cal. A 5-minute re-cal is always cheaper than a wrong measurement leading to a wrong register correction.
Why you MUST calibrate before any phase measurement
The VNA measures phase at its test ports. But everything between the VNA port and your DUT (cables, adaptors, connectors) adds phase. Without calibration, you are measuring the phase of your test setup, not the DUT. A 30 cm test cable at 2 GHz adds ~72° of phase. After SOLT calibration, the reference plane moves to the cal kit connector tips — the cable phase is mathematically removed.
SOLT calibration — Short, Open, Load, Thru
SOLT removes 12 systematic error terms: Port 1: Directivity, Source Match, Reflection Tracking Port 2: Directivity, Source Match, Reflection Tracking Transmission: Forward/Reverse Tracking, Forward/Reverse Isolation Procedure: SHORT → Γ = −1 (180° reflection) — known reflection standard OPEN → Γ = +1 (0° reflection) — known reflection standard LOAD → Γ = 0 (50Ω match) — sets the reference impedance THRU → direct connection P1→P2 — sets transmission reference
Step-by-step SOLT on your E5071C
StepAction on E5071CWhy
1Set frequency range: Start = lowest band freq − 10%, Stop = highest + 10%. For B1/B3/B41: Start 1700 MHz, Stop 2700 MHz.Cal must cover the full measurement range. Outside the cal range results are uncorrected.
2Set number of points: 401 minimum, 1601 for phase accuracy. More points = smoother phase trace.Phase resolution = frequency span / (points − 1). Coarse points = phase ripple artefacts.
3Set IF BW: 1 kHz for phase measurements (narrower = lower noise = better phase accuracy).Phase noise on VNA = random phase error. Narrow IF BW reduces noise. Tradeoff: slower sweep.
4Set power: −5 to −10 dBm (keep DUT in linear region).Measuring passive components (cables, filters) — low power avoids any nonlinearity.
5Press Cal → Cal Wizard → SOLT → 2-Port.2-port cal corrects all 12 error terms including transmission phase.
6Connect SHORT to Port 1 cable tip → press SHORT → wait for sweep.Characterises Port 1 reflection. Short must be from your calibration kit (85052D or similar).
7Connect OPEN to Port 1 → press OPEN → wait.The open standard has a known fringing capacitance model — E5071C corrects for this automatically.
8Connect LOAD to Port 1 → press LOAD → wait.50Ω reference. Load quality determines directivity — use a high-quality cal kit load (>40 dB return loss).
9Repeat SHORT, OPEN, LOAD on Port 2.Port 2 has its own error terms — must be characterised independently.
10Connect Port 1 cable directly to Port 2 cable (THRU) → press THRU.This sets the transmission reference plane. After this, S21 = 0 dB / 0° = calibrated baseline.
11Press Done/Apply → Cal status shows "Cor" (corrected).All 12 error terms are now stored. Measurement uncertainty drops from ±several degrees to ±0.1–0.5°.
12Verify cal: connect a known standard (e.g. THRU). S21 should show 0.00 dB ± 0.05 dB and 0.0° ± 0.5°.Always verify cal before trusting measurements. If verification fails → redo cal (dirty connector, wrong kit).
NEVER remove or flex the cal cables after completing SOLT. Any cable movement changes the electrical length and invalidates the calibration. If you need to reposition, redo the cal from Step 6. This is the most common source of phase measurement errors in the lab.
Cal kit selection: use the Keysight 85052D (3.5mm) or 85032F (N-type) for your SF141 cables. The cal kit model number must match what is selected in the E5071C — wrong cal kit = wrong correction model = phase errors even with "Cor" showing.
VNA3 Cable electrical length & phase matching — step-by-step for your SF141 cables Intermediate click to expand▾

Cable electrical length — phase matching, propagation delay

Electrical length vs physical length:
Electromagnetic waves travel slower in coax than in free space. Velocity factor (VF) = speed in cable / speed of light. RG316 (your lab cables): VF = 0.695. A 1m RG316 cable has electrical length = 1 / (VF × c) = 1 / (0.695 × 3e8) = 4.78 ns propagation delay = 4.78 ns × 2140 MHz × 360° = 3680° electrical length. This is why cable length directly determines S21 phase — and why cables to each column must be matched in electrical length (not just physical length).
Phase matching cables for beamforming:
For accurate beamforming, the cable from each column's BOB SMA to the measurement point must be phase-matched. Use VNA to measure S21 phase of each cable at band centre frequency. Target: all cables within ±2° of each other. If one cable is 5° longer, the column will appear 5° phase-shifted — exactly the error you are trying to measure in the RU. Use matched-pair cables (same manufacturer, same batch, same length) or trim electrical length using phase extender adapters.
Port extension — moving the reference plane after cal:
If you cal at the cable tips but then add an adapter, VNA port extension moves the reference plane electrically. Measure the adapter electrical length separately. Enter as port extension delay (ps) in VNA setup. This avoids a full re-cal whenever adapters change.
Why cable phase matching matters
In your test setup, multiple cables connect the FHGW BOB SMA ports to the EXA/EXM. For multi-port measurements (e.g. comparing TX power across 4 antenna elements simultaneously using a switch matrix), each cable must have the same electrical length — otherwise you are adding cable-to-cable phase differences to your measurement. For beamforming calibration, cable phase differences directly appear as beam pointing errors.
Electrical length vs physical length
Electrical length (degrees) = 360 × f × L × √εr / c Where: f = frequency (Hz) L = physical length (metres) εr = relative permittivity of the cable dielectric c = 3×10⁸ m/s For SF141 semi-rigid cable (εr ≈ 2.1, velocity factor VF ≈ 0.695): At 2140 MHz, 1 metre of SF141: Phase = 360 × 2140e6 × 1 × √2.1 / 3e8 = 360 × 2140e6 × 1.449 / 3e8 = 360 × 10.33 = 3720° = 10.33 full wavelengths So 1 mm difference in SF141 cable length at 2140 MHz = 3.72° phase difference For beamforming: target match within ±2° = within ±0.54 mm physical length!
Procedure — measuring and matching cable electrical lengths
StepActionTarget
1Complete SOLT calibration as above (VNA2)Cal verified, S21 = 0 dB / 0°
2E5071C: Marker → Add Marker → set to band centre freq (e.g. 2140 MHz for B1)Marker 1 at exact test frequency
3Connect Cable A between Port 1 and Port 2. Read S21 phase at marker: e.g. −245.3°Record as φ_A
4Swap to Cable B. Read S21 phase: e.g. −248.7°Record as φ_B
5Phase difference = φ_B − φ_A = −3.4°Target: |ΔΦ| ≤ 2° for cable matching
6If |ΔΦ| > 2°: use E5071C Marker → Electrical Delay function. Enter the delay to null the phase difference. The display shows the equivalent physical length difference.Electrical delay shows how many mm one cable is longer
7Trim the longer cable (precision cable cutter) or select a different cable from stock.After trimming: re-measure, verify |ΔΦ| ≤ 2°
8Repeat at all band centre frequencies: 2140 (B1), 1842.5 (B3), 942.5 (B8), 780.5 (B28), 2545 (B41)Phase match verified at all operating frequencies
9Label matched cable pairs and store together. Never mix matched cables.Matched pair stored as "CAL PAIR B1/B3 - 2026-07"
Using Electrical Delay on E5071C to null cable phase
On E5071C: Scale → Electrical Delay → enter delay value in seconds This shifts the phase trace by: ΔΦ = 360 × f × delay To null a cable: measure phase at marker → compute delay = phase / (360 × f) Example: phase difference = 3.4° at 2140 MHz Required delay = 3.4 / (360 × 2140e6) = 4.41 ps Physical length = delay × c / √εr = 4.41e-12 × 3e8 / 1.449 = 0.91 mm So Cable B is 0.91 mm longer than Cable A. Trim 0.91 mm off Cable B to match.
E5071C display formats for phase work
FormatE5071C menuBest for
Phase (−180° to +180°)Format → PhaseSeeing phase vs frequency. Jumps at ±180° (phase wrapping) are normal — use "unwrap" if needed.
Unwrapped PhaseFormat → Expanded PhaseRemoves 360° jumps — shows true monotonic phase vs frequency. Essential for group delay measurement.
Group DelayFormat → Delay−dφ/df in nanoseconds. Flat = linear phase = good. Ripple = multipath or filter resonance.
Electrical LengthMarker → Electrical DelayConverts phase to metres at the marker frequency.
Smith ChartFormat → Smith ChartS11 impedance — phase of reflection vs frequency plotted on impedance plane. Use for antenna port matching.
PolarFormat → PolarS21 as magnitude + phase on polar plot. Useful for seeing phase variation with frequency.
VNA4 Antenna element phase calibration — measuring TX path phase across all 8/12 elements Advanced click to expand▾

Antenna element phase calibration — per-column measurement

Measurement procedure per column:
1. SOLT cal at cable tips. 2. Connect Port 1 to Column A BOB SMA. 3. Connect Port 2 to reference point (or use a known reference cable). 4. Measure S21 at band centre. 5. Record magnitude and phase. 6. Repeat for columns B, C, D. 7. Compute Δφ = each column phase − Column A phase. 8. Δφ > ±2° → update PE44820DS register for that column by −Δφ (opposite sign correction).
Real B1 example (unit 26050509):
Col A: −125.4° (ref). Col B: −127.1° → Δ = −1.7° (within ±2° ✓). Col C: −131.8° → Δ = −6.4° (FAIL) → adjust PE44820DS by +6.4°. Col D: −126.9° → Δ = −1.5° (within ±2° ✓). After correction: re-measure Col C → should show ≈ −125°. If not: PE44820DS register may have limited resolution (e.g. 5.625° steps) — round to nearest step.
When phase error is larger than ±5°:
Δφ > 5° usually means: cable swap (wrong cable connected to that column), connector not fully mated (1–2 turns left to tighten), or physical damage to the RF trace/connector on the BOB. Inspect physically before adjusting register — a register correction of 8° when the actual problem is a loose connector will appear to pass VNA check but drift back when temperature changes.
What you are measuring
Each of the 8 or 12 TX paths in your AAU (from FHGW DAC output to RFFE antenna port) introduces a different phase shift. Sources of inter-element phase difference: slightly different trace lengths on PCB, component tolerance in phase shifters, connector variations, filter group delay differences. The OB_CAL (observation calibration) corrects these in firmware — but first you need to MEASURE them to know how much correction is needed.
Setup for multi-element phase measurement
Test setup: VNA Port 1 → SMA cable → FHGW BOB TX_A port (reference input) VNA Port 2 → SMA cable → Antenna element N output (DUT output) Measure: S21 = (signal at element N output) / (signal at FHGW BOB input) Parameter of interest: S21 Phase at band centre frequency Repeat for all N elements (N = 0 to 7 for 8-element array) Compare: φ_element_N vs φ_element_0 (reference element) Ideal: all elements have same S21 phase (ΔΦ = 0° between any two elements) Acceptable: |ΔΦ| ≤ 5° element-to-element before firmware correction After OB_CAL: residual ΔΦ ≤ 1° (firmware compensates the rest)
Step-by-step procedure
StepActionRecord
1Power on FHGW. Activate the band under test (e.g. B1). Ensure DL carrier is NOT transmitting — you need the DAC to be driven from the VNA, not from DU traffic. Set FHGW to passthrough/loopback mode or use BOB SMA as standalone input.Band, EARFCN, channel BW
2SOLT calibrate VNA from Port 1 cable tip to Port 2 cable tip (VNA2 procedure). Cal frequency range: cover full band + ±10%.Cal verified: S21 = 0 dB / 0.0° with THRU
3Set format: S21 Phase. Add Marker 1 at exact band centre (e.g. 2140.000 MHz for B1).Marker frequency confirmed
4Connect Port 1 → TX_A0 input, Port 2 → Antenna element 0 output. This is your reference element.φ_0 = e.g. −312.5°
5Keep Port 1 connected. Move Port 2 → Antenna element 1 output.φ_1 = e.g. −315.2°. ΔΦ_1 = φ_1 − φ_0 = −2.7°
6Repeat for elements 2–7 (or 2–11 for 12-element array).ΔΦ_N for each element
7Plot ΔΦ_N vs element number. Should be approximately flat (within ±5°). Any element with |ΔΦ| > 10° → suspect that element path for hardware fault.Phase spread table
8Enter the measured ΔΦ_N values as initial correction offsets in the FHGW firmware phase calibration table (per-element phase register). OB_CAL then fine-tunes further.Per-element phase offset written to FHGW
9After OB_CAL completes: repeat VNA measurement. Residual ΔΦ should now be ≤ 1° — the firmware has corrected the hardware phase errors.Residual phase spread after cal
Phase vs frequency sweep — checking linear phase across the band
For a TX path to be usable for wideband signals (e.g. 20 MHz LTE), the phase must be LINEAR across the band (constant group delay). Nonlinear phase = group delay variation = pulse distortion = EVM degradation.
Measure: S21 Expanded Phase across full band B1: 2110 to 2170 MHz (60 MHz sweep) Good result: straight line (linear phase) → group delay flat Phase slope = −Group delay × 360 × f → constant slope = constant delay = OK Bad result: ripple in phase → resonance in filter/connector → fix connector or replace filter Acceptable group delay variation: ≤ 10 ns across the band for LTE Check formula: EVM from group delay ripple ≈ 2π × f_subcarrier × ΔGD × 100% For 15 kHz subcarrier, 5 ns GD ripple: EVM ≈ 2π × 15e3 × 5e-9 = 0.047% (negligible) For 15 kHz subcarrier, 100 ns GD ripple: EVM ≈ 0.94% (significant)
On E5071C: after measuring S21 phase, switch to Format → Delay to see group delay directly in nanoseconds. A flat trace = good linear phase. Peaks/dips in group delay at specific frequencies = resonances from imperfect connector mating, damaged cable, or filter out of spec.
VNA5 Beamforming angle calibration — mapping phase shift to beam angle, verifying PE44820DS Advanced click to expand▾

Beamforming angle calibration — phase to beam angle mapping

Beam angle formula and your numbers:
θ = arcsin(λ × Δφ_rad / (2π × d)). For B1 at 2140 MHz: λ = c/f = 3e8/2140e6 = 0.140 m. d = λ/2 = 0.070 m. Δφ = 20° = 0.349 rad → θ = arcsin(0.140 × 0.349 / (2π × 0.070)) = arcsin(0.111) = 6.4°. This means: if each consecutive column is programmed 20° more phase shift than the previous, the beam points 6.4° off boresight.
Per-band beam angle differences:
Different bands have different wavelengths and different element spacings, so the same phase step gives a different beam angle per band. B1 (2140 MHz): 20° Δφ = 6.4° beam angle. B3 (1843 MHz): 20° Δφ = 5.5°. B8 (942 MHz): 20° Δφ = 2.8°. B28 (758 MHz): 20° Δφ = 2.2°. This is why beam calibration is done per band, not once for all bands. The PE44820DS register value for a given beam direction differs by band.
Verifying beam steering with OTA measurement:
After phase cal, verify beam steering optionally using a reference antenna on a tripod at known angle from the AAU. Measure receive power at multiple angles while sweeping phase commands. Maximum received power angle should match commanded angle within ±1°. If not: re-run VNA phase cal, check PE44820DS register writes were accepted, verify mutual coupling between columns is within design spec.
From phase difference to beam angle
For a uniform linear array with element spacing d: Beam angle θ = arcsin(λ × ΔΦ / (2π × d)) Where: λ = wavelength = c/f ΔΦ = progressive phase shift between adjacent elements (radians) d = element spacing (typically λ/2 for maximum scan range) For λ/2 spacing: d = λ/2 → θ = arcsin(ΔΦ/π) ΔΦ = 0° → θ = 0° (broadside, beam perpendicular to array) ΔΦ = 30° → θ = arcsin(30/180) = 9.6° scan ΔΦ = 60° → θ = 19.5° scan ΔΦ = 90° → θ = 30° scan ΔΦ = 180° → θ = 90° (endfire — maximum scan, impractical) Your B1/B3 4-column array (12 elements): Scan range: typically ±60° in azimuth Each 1° phase step → ~0.3° beam shift (at broadside)
Verifying the phase shifter (PE44820DS) with VNA
The PE44820DS is a digitally-controlled phase shifter. It has 6 or 8 control bits, giving 64 or 256 discrete phase states. Each state should produce a predictable, repeatable phase shift. The VNA verifies: (1) each state produces the correct phase, (2) insertion loss is consistent across states, (3) there are no stuck bits.
StepActionPass criterion
1Connect VNA Port 1 → phase shifter input, Port 2 → phase shifter output. SOLT calibrate.S21 = 0 dB / 0° at state 0 (reference)
2Set phase shifter to state 0 (all bits = 0 = minimum phase shift). Record S21 phase at band centre.Reference phase φ_0
3Step through all phase states (0, 1, 2, ... 63 for 6-bit device). At each state record S21 phase and S21 magnitude.Phase: each step should increment by ~360/64 = 5.625° · Magnitude: should stay within ±0.5 dB across all states
4Plot measured phase vs state number. Should be monotonically increasing, approximately linear.Phase linearity: deviation from ideal ≤ ±2° per state
5Check magnitude variation: |S21| should not vary more than ±0.5 dB as phase state changes.Magnitude flatness across states ≤ ±0.5 dB
6Toggle bit 0 only (LSB). Phase should shift by 5.625°. Toggle bit 5 (MSB). Phase should shift by 180°.Each bit contributes correct phase weight: MSB=180°, next=90°, 45°, 22.5°, 11.25°, 5.625°
7Repeat at cold (−20°C) and hot (+55°C) if temperature chamber available. Phase shift should be within ±3° of room temperature value.Temperature coefficient ≤ 0.05°/°C typical for GaAs phase shifters
A stuck bit in the phase shifter (one bit permanently 0 or 1) causes the phase to jump by that bit weight when it should not. In your beam pattern this appears as a sidelobe spike at a fixed direction. If you see an unexplained sidelobe in OTA measurements, check the phase shifter with this procedure first.
Full TX chain phase calibration sequence (combining VNA steps)
Complete sequence for one antenna element: 1. VNA: Measure cable electrical length → confirm within ±2° of reference cable 2. VNA: Measure S21 phase of pre-PA path (FHGW BOB → phase shifter input): Set phase shifter to state 0. Record φ_prePA. 3. VNA: Measure S21 phase of full TX path (FHGW BOB → antenna port): φ_total = φ_prePA + φ_phaseShifter(state) + φ_PA + φ_filter + φ_combiner 4. FHGW CLI: Set per-element phase offset register to compensate φ_total Command: write_phase_cal_reg element_N offset_deg 5. Activate all elements simultaneously. Set all phase shifters to state 0. Measure OTA beam pattern in anechoic chamber (or near-field scanner). Verify main beam at θ = 0° (broadside) → confirms cal correct. 6. Command phase shifters to steer beam to θ = 15°, 30°, 45°. Verify beam follows at each angle within ±2°. 7. If beam angle error > 2°: re-run VNA measurement on outlier element, identify the phase error source, correct register.
VNA6 Practical VNA phase tips — common mistakes, connector care, temperature effects Intermediate click to expand▾

Practical VNA tips — common mistakes, cable handling

Six most common VNA mistakes:
1. Not warming up — LO drifts 5–10° in first 15 min. Always wait 30 min.
2. Wrong torque — SMA spec is 0.9 N·m. Over-torque destroys center pin. Always use torque wrench.
3. Cal at wrong plane — cal WITH measurement cables attached, not before.
4. Skipping isolation step — SOLT needs isolation between ports for accurate S21 at high loss.
5. Wrong IFBW — use 1 kHz for phase cal (slow but accurate), not 1 MHz (fast but noisy).
6. Moving cables after cal — phase shifts 2–5° per cable flex.
Connector inspection before every connection:
Look for: bent center pin (replace immediately), scratches on mating face (replace), debris in connector (clean with IPA and wooden toothpick — never metal). After cleaning, inspect with loupe. A bent center pin costs 2 minutes to catch and replace. A bent pin that makes contact costs a 2-day measurement mystery.
Port extension vs full recal — when to use which:
Full recal: whenever you change cable, add/remove adapter, or temperature changes > 10°C. Port extension: when you want to move reference plane by a fixed electrical delay (e.g. accounting for a short adapter). Port extension does not correct impedance mismatch — it only shifts phase. Never use port extension as a substitute for proper recal when making precision measurements.
Top phase measurement mistakes and how to avoid them
MistakeEffect on phase measurementPrevention
Not torquing connectors to specLoose connector → air gap → changed dielectric → phase error of 5–20°. Also reproducibility is terrible.Always use a torque wrench: SMA = 0.45 Nm (4 in-lb), N-type = 1.36 Nm (12 in-lb), 3.5mm = 0.9 Nm (8 in-lb).
Moving cables after calAny bend changes electrical length. A 90° flex of a semi-rigid cable causes ≈0.5–2° phase shift.Tape cables in position after cal. Use cable clamps. If cables move → redo cal.
Temperature driftVNA synthesiser and cables change phase with temperature. 1°C drift → ~0.1–0.5° phase change in cables.Warm up VNA for 30 minutes before cal. Measure in temperature-stable environment. Re-cal if room temp changes >2°C.
Wrong cal kit selectedE5071C applies wrong correction coefficients → systematic phase error of 1–5°.Confirm: Cal → Cal Kit → verify kit model matches your physical kit (85052D, 85032F, etc.).
Measuring outside cal frequency rangeNo correction applied → results uncalibrated → wrong phase.Always set measurement freq range BEFORE calibrating. Cal covers exactly the set sweep range.
Phase wrapping confusionPhase displayed as −180° to +180°. Jumps at boundaries look like discontinuities but are normal.Use Format → Expanded Phase to unwrap. Or use Electrical Delay to shift the trace away from ±180°.
Dirty or damaged connectorsEven invisible contamination → extra capacitance → phase shift AND return loss degradation.Inspect with magnifier or microscope before every connection. Clean with IPA and lint-free swab. Replace any connector with visible centre pin damage.
Too few frequency pointsPhase ripple artefacts between measured points — looks like a real resonance but is just interpolation.Use ≥401 points for component measurements. Use 1601 points for precision phase work.
SCPI commands to automate VNA phase measurement
// E5071C SCPI for automated phase measurement: // Set up measurement :SENS1:FREQ:STAR 2110000000 // Start freq: 2110 MHz (B1 band edge) :SENS1:FREQ:STOP 2170000000 // Stop freq: 2170 MHz (B1 band edge) :SENS1:SWE:POIN 1601 // 1601 points :SENS1:BWID 1000 // IF BW = 1 kHz :SOUR1:POW -10 // Source power = -10 dBm :CALC1:PAR1:DEF S21 // Measure S21 :CALC1:FORM PHAS // Format: Phase :CALC1:MARK1:STAT ON // Marker 1 ON :CALC1:MARK1:X 2140000000 // Marker at 2140 MHz // Trigger and read :TRIG:SOUR BUS // Bus trigger :TRIG:SING // Single sweep *OPC? // Wait for completion :CALC1:MARK1:Y? // Read marker 1 phase (degrees) // → e.g. -312.456 (degrees at 2140 MHz) // Read group delay :CALC1:FORM GDEL // Switch to group delay format :CALC1:MARK1:Y? // Read group delay (seconds) // → e.g. 2.341E-9 (2.341 ns at 2140 MHz) // Read full trace data :CALC1:DATA:FDAT? // Returns all 1601 phase points as CSV
Quick phase check — 5 minute procedure for daily use
Full SOLT cal takes 10–15 minutes. For a quick daily check without full cal:
Use a previously saved cal state: Recall → Cal → select last saved cal file. Valid if frequency range and cables unchanged since last full cal.
Verify with THRU: connect THRU and check S21 = 0 dB ±0.2 dB and 0° ±1°. If within tolerance → use saved cal. If not → do full SOLT.
For cable phase comparison only (relative measurement, not absolute): connect Cable A as THRU → Save trace → connect Cable B → use Data/Memory → shows ΔΦ directly. No SOLT needed for relative measurements.
E5071C memory trace: Trace → Data → Memory Save. Then Data → Show Data/Memory → displays the difference between current and saved trace. Phase difference is shown directly.
VNA7 Worked example — full B1 TX path phase calibration from scratch Expert click to expand▾

Worked example — B1 TX path phase calibration step by step

Complete 7-step procedure with your actual numbers:
① Warm up VNA E5071C 30 min.
② Set freq: 2100–2180 MHz, 201 points, IFBW 1 kHz, power −10 dBm.
③ SOLT cal at cable tips (SHORT/OPEN/LOAD each port, then THROUGH).
④ Connect Port 1 → Column A BOB SMA. Connect Port 2 → reference terminator with cable. Measure S21. Record: Mag = −16.7 dBm, Phase = −125.4°. This is the Column A baseline.
⑤ Move Port 1 to Column B. Record: −127.1° → Δ = −1.7° (PASS).
⑥ Move to Column C. Record: −131.8° → Δ = −6.4° (FAIL > ±2°). Write PE44820DS register with +6.4° correction.
⑦ Re-measure Column C after correction → confirm within ±2°.
What to do when correction does not take effect:
PE44820DS is an SPI-controlled digital phase shifter. Write via CLI: pe44820_write col_C 0x2A (register value depends on step size). Verify readback matches. If phase still wrong after register write: check SPI communication to RFFE (possible RFFE fault), check PE44820DS power supply (1.8V), check if DPD override is forcing phase (some DPD modes lock phase to calibrated values — disable DPD during phase cal).
Frequency dependence — why you calibrate at band centre:
Phase is frequency-dependent. A cable that is 0° at 2100 MHz may be +3° at 2180 MHz. Phase cal at band centre (2140 MHz for B1) gives the best average across the band. For wideband beamforming, some systems do phase cal at 3 frequencies (low edge, centre, high edge) and interpolate. Your RU uses single-frequency cal — adequate for 80 MHz B1 bandwidth where phase variation is small.
Scenario
You have a Metro AAU unit (unit 509, RFFE2 recently reflashed via JTAG). After reflash you need to verify the B1 TX path phase response on all 4 B1 antenna elements and confirm OB_CAL brings them within ±1° of each other.
Complete procedure with expected results
StepActionExpected resultIf fails
1Warm up E5071C for 30 min. Set: Start 2110 MHz, Stop 2170 MHz, 1601 pts, IF BW 1 kHz, Power −10 dBm.Sweep running cleanly—
2SOLT cal with 85052D kit. Verify: THRU → S21 = 0.00 dB / 0.0°Within ±0.05 dB / ±0.5°Redo cal. Check connectors.
3Connect Port 1 → FHGW BOB SMA TX port (B1, element 0). Port 2 → RU antenna port element 0. Format: Phase. Marker at 2140 MHz.φ_0 (e.g. −312.5°). Note S21 magnitude also = insertion loss of full TX path.If S21 magnitude < −60 dB → path is open or shorted
4Move Port 2 → element 1. Record φ_1.φ_1 (e.g. −314.8°). ΔΦ_1 = −2.3°ΔΦ > 10° → suspect phase shifter or filter in that element path
5Repeat for elements 2, 3. Build table: Element | φ_N | ΔΦ_NΔΦ_N within ±5° for all elementsAny outlier >10° → measure sub-sections (pre-PA, post-PA) to isolate
6Switch Format → Delay. Check group delay across 2110–2170 MHz for each element.Group delay flat within ±2 ns across bandGD ripple >10 ns → damaged connector or filter fault
7Enter ΔΦ_N values into FHGW phase cal registers via CLI. Command: set_tx_phase_offset element_N value_deg.CLI confirms write. No error.Write failure → check SSH connection, verify register address
8Activate OB_CAL in FHGW. CLI: run_calibration OB_CAL band B1. Wait ~2 minutes for convergence.OB_CAL completes. Reports residual phase error per element.OB_CAL fail → check observation coupler path, check switch matrix routing
9Repeat VNA measurement steps 3–5. All ΔΦ_N should now be ≤ 1°.Phase spread ≤ 1° after OB_CALStill >2° → OB_CAL did not converge. Re-run. Check PA is on and settled.
10Run test_Tx_BS_Output_Power and test_Tx_ACLR in RuAuto. These are the RF conformance validation.Tx power within ±1.5 dB of P_rated. ACLR ≥ 54 dBc.Power fail → check gain registers. ACLR fail → DPD re-adapt needed after phase cal.
Phase calibration data log template

Always save the E5071C state file (.sta) and the calibration file (.cal) after each phase calibration session. This lets you recall the exact setup next time without repeating the full procedure. File → Save → State&Cal → name it "B1_phase_cal_unit509_2026-07-13.sta".

What each element in your diagram means
Label in diagramFull nameWhat it does in the RCT setup
DUDistributed Unit (Baseband)The baseband processing unit. Sends downlink IQ data to the AAU via eCPRI fronthaul. Also handles m-plane (management) and RMAC (radio MAC) commands. In RCT this is your lab DU running l1.sh + l2.sh with testmac prompt.
figh / FHGWFronthaul GatewayThe digital front-end inside the AAU. Receives eCPRI from DU, runs DUC/DDC, CFR, DPD, drives DAC. The "FHGW RF" circle in your diagram marks where the digital chain hands off to the analog RF path (RFFE).
m-planeManagement Plane (O-RAN)Configuration and control interface over NETCONF/YANG. Used for: loading activation XML, setting carrier frequency, configuring beamforming weights, setting TX power. In your setup: netopeer2-cli connects here.
RMACRadio MACThe radio-level MAC layer commands. Handles scheduling, resource allocation, HARQ, power control between DU and RU. In RCT: the testmac> commands you type to activate the carrier and start transmission.
B1B3Band 1 + Band 3The AAU unit under test carries both B1 (2110–2170 MHz DL) and B3 (1805–1880 MHz DL) simultaneously on the same hardware. Your b0103 flavor. Both bands share the 8 DAC outputs of the FHGW (4 per band).
A, B, C, D portsAntenna columns A through DYour B1B3 AAU has 4 antenna columns (A, B, C, D). Each column carries both B1 and B3 signals. The red cables in your diagram connect from the RFFE TX output ports of each column to the EXM. In RuAuto: Tx4(A), Tx1(B), Tx8(C), Tx5(D) for B1; Tx3(A), Tx2(B), Tx7(C), Tx6(D) for B3.
EAA-Axy → RSSIElement Array A, element x×y → RSSIEAA = your antenna element addressing scheme. "Axy" = column A, element coordinates x and y. The RSSI reading per element is what get_rssi CLI returns — one reading per ADC channel (0–7), mapped to the 8 physical antenna elements across the 4 columns. B1 uses ADCs 0,1,4,5 and B3 uses ADCs 2,3,6,7.
Bxy / Cxy / DxyColumns B, C, D element readingsSame as Axy but for columns B, C, D. In your RSSI calibration: you measure RSSI for each column/element independently to build the per-ADC ADC_ADJUST offset table in hardware.json.
eCPRI + DownlinkeCPRI fronthaul carrying DL dataThe physical Ethernet connection between DU and AAU carrying: (1) IQ data (downlink carrier payload), (2) control plane timing (sync), (3) management plane config. In your lab: typically 10GbE SFP+ cable, IP-addressed, with PTP grandmaster for timing.
The 4-cable connection from AAU to EXM — exactly what those red lines are
Your diagram shows 4 red cables going from the AAU to the EXM. These connect the 4 antenna column TX outputs (A, B, C, D) on the RFFE to the EXM's 4 input ports (RF1, RF2, RF3, RF4 or via a switch matrix). Each cable carries the combined B1+B3 signal from that column — the diplexer/triplexer inside the RFFE has already combined B1 TX + B3 TX onto the single TX_A (or TX_B/C/D) port.
In practice, since the EXM has only 1–2 RF input ports, your setup uses an RF switch matrix (Mini-Circuits or similar) to route each column in turn to the EXM. RuAuto controls this switch matrix automatically — it measures column A, switches to column B, measures, switches to C, etc.
Measurement sequence for B1B3 RCT using this setup
StepDU actionAAU actionEXM measures
1. Bring up B1 carrierLoad B1 activation XML via NETCONF. Start l1.sh + l2.sh. testmac> activate B1 carrier.FHGW activates B1 DACs (channels 0,1,4,5). RFFE enables B1 PA on all 4 columns.Confirm carrier at 2140 MHz. Measure channel power. Compare to P_rated = −16.7 dBm.
2. TX power testSet ETM 1.1 (all RBs, QPSK). Max power command.Full B1 carrier transmitted on all 4 columns simultaneously.Measure each column A/B/C/D channel power. All should be within ±1.5 dB of P_rated.
3. ACLR testSame ETM 1.1, full power.DPD active, CFR active, PA at rated power.ACP measurement at 2140 MHz. Offset A: ±10 MHz, Offset B: ±20 MHz. Target: ≥54 dBc.
4. EVM testETM 3.1 (64QAM).Carrier with 64QAM modulation.Modulation Analysis mode. EVM target: ≤8% for 64QAM.
5. Switch to B3Load B3 activation XML. Activate B3 carrier at 1842.5 MHz.FHGW switches to B3 DACs (channels 2,3,6,7). B3 PA on.Repeat power/ACLR/EVM at 1842.5 MHz. P_rated = −15.7 dBm.
6. RSSI calibrationSet UL signal level via EXM signal generator output → RU antenna port.FHGW RX path active. get_rssi CLI returns 8 ADC readings.Compare EXM signal level vs get_rssi CLI dBm vs DU-reported RSSI. Gap must be ≤ ±2 dB.
What "EAA-Axy → RSSI" means — the RSSI measurement path
In the bottom of your diagram: EAA-Axy → RSSI. This is the uplink RSSI measurement chain:
EXM generates a known UL signal (e.g. at 1950 MHz for B1 UL, or 1747.5 MHz for B3 UL) at a calibrated power level
Signal travels through the EXM output → cable → antenna port A of the AAU
Inside the AAU: signal enters through the duplexer RX port → LNA → VGA → mixer → ADC channels 0,1 (for B1, column A)
get_rssi CLI on FHGW returns the ADC-measured power in dBFS and dBm for elements A0 and A1
The DU also reports RSSI via OAM/management plane (computed from IQ samples after FFT)
You compare: EXM output power → get_rssi CLI dBm → DU RSSI dBm. All three should agree within ±2 dB
Repeat for columns B (Bxy), C (Cxy), D (Dxy) — these map to ADC channels 4,5 / 6,7 / etc. per band

AAU port labelBandColumnFHGW Tx portADC channels (UL)EXM connection

The 4 red cables in your diagram are NOT connected simultaneously to 4 EXM ports — the EXM has one primary RF input (RFIO). The cables go to a Mini-Circuits RF switch (HTTP-controlled, IP-addressable). RuAuto sends a switch command, then measures on EXM, then switches to the next port. This is why RCT takes several minutes — it cycles through all port/band combinations sequentially.
